and 1800 to 2400 h for three d to capture birds and bats, respectively. All captured animals were placed in individual sacks for three or more hours to permit the collection of seeds passed in feces. Seeds recovered in feces were identified; tetrazolium was used to test for viability of a subsample of all seeds collected in the dry season (except in a few cases [e.g. Vismia guianensis D.C.] where seeds were too small for testing).

## Seed predation

We measured the fate of seeds dispersed into the abandoned pasture by observing seed groups of eleven forest tree species that we placed in the abandoned pasture. Seeds of each species were set out at 10-m intervals along two or three 100-m transects. At each location, a 25-cm diameter ring was nestled into the abandoned pasture vegetation and eight seeds were placed at equally spaced locations around the ring. The ring was then removed. Each seed was checked after 1, 4, 8, 24, 36, and 48 h following placement, and again at 3, 4, 7, 10, 20, 50, 100, and 200 d. At each visit, the presence and condition of seeds were recorded.

A similar experiment was conducted with seeds of four trees that invade abandoned pasture: Cecropia obtusa Trec. Solanum crinitum, Vismia guianensis, and Cordia multispicata. Because the seeds of these species are small (< 11 mg), we judged it impossible to follow the fate of individual seeds. Hence, ten seeds were placed at each of the 8 positions around the ring guide. The seed placements were made at 20 positions along line transects for a total of 160 seeds per species (8 × 10 × 20). This experiment was terminated after 48 h.

An additional experiment was initiated in the wet season of 1986 to examine habitat-specific differences in seed removal. We placed seeds of four species (Eugenia sp. Jacaranda copaia (Aubl.) D. don. Pouroma guianensis (Aubl.) Swartz, and Stryphnodendron pulcherrimum in three habitats (abandoned pasture, experimental forest treefall gaps (n = 2), and forest understorey). Sets of eight seeds were placed at 10-m intervals along transects using the ring guide as described above. Total seed placements were 216 per species in the abandoned pasture (8 seeds × 27 locations) and 80 per species in the understorey and gap habitats. We checked seeds daily for one week, and recorded removals.

Ants observed removing seeds, in this and the other seed placement experiments, were placed in alcohol for later identification. A 10 × 10 m grid of 90 rodent traps (Sherman: 2″ × 2.5″ × 9″) was established in the abandoned pasture and forest sites to characterize the communities of small rodents. Rodents were trapped on four consecutive nights in each site during the 1986 wet season.

## Seedling herbivory

We predicted that tree seedlings were more likely to experience herbivory in the abandoned pasture than in the forest because of larger populations of herbivores in the former. To test this prediction, plastic basins (40 cm diameter × 15 cm deep) were filled with sieved top soil from the abandoned pasture and planted with seedlings of seven species, including four tree species (Hymenaea courbaril L. Jacaranda copaia, Tabebuia serratifolia Nichols, and Vismia guianensis), two abandoned pasture shrubs [(Rolandra argentea Rottb. and Stachytarpheta cayennensis (L. C. Rich) Vahl)], and a non-forage grass common in abandoned pastures (Paspalum millegrana Ochrad.). The basins were set up in May, 1986, and maintained in a shaded nursery until February, 1987, at which time they were set in the ground flush with the mineral soil surface. A total of twenty basins were placed in each ecosystem, at 10-m intervals along two transects in the abandoned pasture site, and at 5-m intervals along transects in three 40 × 20 m treefall gaps. The basins were visited four times over a 16-d period, at which time each seedling was examined to determine the percent of foliage removed by herbivores.

## Abiotic barriers

Seedling survivorship and growth may be restricted in abandoned pastures by low soil moisture availability, low light levels, high temperature or high vapor pressure deficit. We evaluated the potential importance of this group of abiotic factors for tree establishment by measuring the survivorship and growth of seedling transplants protected from herbivores. Populations of 10 woody species, both trees and lianas, were established in the abandoned pasture and in the experimental treefall gaps as a basis of comparison.

Seedling populations were established in three 30 × 16-m blocks per ecosystem. Blocks were situated in patches dominated by grass (Paspalum pilosum and P. millegrana) in the abandoned pasture and in the three experimental treefall gaps of the forest. Within each block, seedlings were assigned to randomly selected positions in a grid, and were at least 50 cm from neighboring transplants and access paths. Fifty to one hundred seedlings of each species were planted per block; plant material was obtained from local plant populations as seed or seedling stock. Seed-propagated populations were sown in a nursery in December, 1985, one month before the onset of the rainy season. Other populations were established from young seedlings (with cotyledons still attached) that were directly transplanted into the study plots from mature and regrowth forests. Hymenaea courbaril was planted directly into the field as mechanically scarified seed. Seedlings were

transplanted in the 1986 wet season, from early February through mid-May. Each species was planted one block at a time, alternating between ecosystems to distribute the effect of time of planting. Approximately one month after each population was transplanted, plants that had died were replaced. Leaf cutter ants were eliminated from the abandoned pasture study area using the fungicidal bait Myrex® and seedlings were protected from small mammals with hardware-cloth cages. The survivorship and height of all seedling transplants were measured at the beginning of the first dry season (July 1986), at the beginning of the first wet season (January 1987), and again in February 1988.

Microclimatic measurements were made to aid in the interpretation of seedling performance in the abandoned pasture and mature forest. We measured photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD), air temperature (T) and air vapor pressure deficit (VPD) in each habitat. PPFD near the ground surface (10 cm height) was compared between ecosystems by taking simultaneous readings with LI-COR quantum sensors on sunny days (13 June, 1986, abandoned pasture vs experimental, seven-month-old treefall gaps and 19 July, 1986, abandoned pasture vs forest understorey). Readings were taken at 10 locations per ecosystem spaced at regular intervals (5 m in the abandoned pasture and gaps, 15 m in the forest) along randomly placed transects. Measurements were made synchronously near the soil surface at two-min intervals. The PPFD of full sun was measured in the abandoned pasture, between ground-level measurements, by holding the sensor above the abandoned pasture vegetation. Readings were made from 1000 to 1400 h.

Seasonal patterns of T and relative humidity (RH) were measured in the abandoned pasture, at the center of a 150-m² treefall gap, and in the mature forest during 1985 using Weathertronic hygrothermographs. VPD was calculated based on T and RH (Jones 1983). In each habitat, one Weathertronic hygrothermograph was placed in a weather cabinet with the T and RH sensors of the instrument at a height of 25 cm. The instruments were recalibrated in the field at 2-month intervals.

The drought stress of seedlings was measured in the abandoned pasture and treefall gaps by comparing pre-dawn xylem pressure potential (XPP) of seedlings of three tree species transplanted into the abandoned pasture and experimental treefall gaps: Myrcia deflexa, Tabebuia serratifolia, and Vismia guianensis. XPP was measured on 24 and 25 October, 1986, following 18 and 19 d without rain. Six randomly-selected seedlings were measured per species in each habitat. Seedling shoots were clipped between 0400 and 0500 h, sealed in plastic bags, and stored in a Styrofoam chest lined with damp cloth. XPP of the clipped shoots was measured in the field before 0630 h using a pressure chamber (PMS; Ritchie and Hinckley 1975). Clipped plants were excluded from the study of survivorship and growth.

Soil water content was measured during the month of October, 1986. Soil samples were taken from 0–5, 10–15 and 40–45 cm depths from the abandoned pasture, from the three experimental treefall gaps (&lt; 1 yr old), and from the forest understorey. Auger borings (n = 6 per habitat) were made at 10-m intervals along two transects in the abandoned pasture and mature forest, and along two transects in each of the gaps; sampling positions were advanced one meter at each successive sampling date. Water content was measured gravimetrically (fresh weight – oven dry weight [80°C])/ (o.d. weight).

## Results

### Natural patterns of seedling establishment

Tree seedling and sprout densities were highest in the experimental treefall gaps (up to 17 individuals m⁻²), lowest in the abandoned pasture (&lt; 0.24) and intermediate in the forest understorey (8.9 to 14.8). Tree seedling and sprout emergence was at least two orders of magnitude greater in the forest habitats than in the abandoned pasture. Nonetheless, 15 new seedlings/sprouts were found in the abandoned pasture plots (total area = 50 m²) over the 2-yr period, including 10 individuals of Myrcia sp., 3 individuals of Rollinia exsucca (DC ex Dunal) A. DC, one Zanthoxylum rhoifolia Lam. (a root sprout) and one S. crinitum (a root sprout). All of the Myrcia sp., the R. exsucca and the S. crinitum were found in a single plot located beneath the crown of a isolated treelet, Solanum crinitum. A single root sprout emerged in the remaining 24 plots.

The low density and diversity of tree seedlings and sprouts in the abandoned pasture was due to high mortality in addition to low rates of emergence. Although 15 tree seedlings and sprouts emerged in the 25 two-m² plots of this habitat, 13 of these seedlings and sprouts died by the final count. Hence, there was a net increase of only 0.04 individuals m⁻² (a total of two plants) over the two-yr study period. In just eight months, seedling and sprout density in the treefall gaps increased from 13.8 to 17.5 individuals m⁻² (Table 1). Overall, there was a very small pool of tree seedlings and shoots in the abandoned pasture from which larger size classes of trees could be recruited.

### Seed availability

Seeds of tree species were also rare in the abandoned pasture soil. Seeds of only three tree genera that are common in abandoned pastures (Cecropia, Solanum and Vismia) germinated from the abandoned pasture soil samples; they comprised 2% of total germinations (Table 2). The abandoned pasture had a seed bank that

Seeds were encountered under the four *S. crinitum* at all collection periods but variation among traps was high. Viable seeds of one liana and seven tree species were found in the feces of birds and viable seeds of seven tree species were found in the feces of bats. The largest seeds found in bird and bat feces had a dry mass of $16\mathrm{mg}$. Fifteen of the tree and liana seeds that occurred in the abandoned pasture were identified to genus (Table 3).

## Seed predation

For 6 out of the 11 forest seed species examined, more than $80\%$ of all the seeds placed in the abandoned pasture site were removed within 20 d (Fig. 2). For all 11 species, the probability of removal declined with time. Seed persistence also increased as a function of seed mass for the range of seed sizes that we examined in this trial (0.004 to $17.8\mathrm{g}$, $r^2 = 0.63$, Fig. 3).

Seed removal was also rapid for the four small-seeded pioneer species that we studied. Within $48\mathrm{h}$ of placement, $84\%$ of all *Cecropia obtusa* seed groups (i.e., 134 of 160 groups of 10 seeds) were removed completely. Removal percentages for the other three pioneer species were $&gt;70\%$.

In the comparison of seed removal among habitats, the highest rates were found in the abandoned pasture and the lowest rates were found in the treefall gaps. More than $90\%$ of the seeds of *Jacaranda copaia*, *Pourouma guianensis*, and *Eugenia* sp., and $50\%$ of the

During this same period, only 55% of J. copaia seeds and &lt; 10% (all other species) were removed in the treefall gaps, while removal rates in the understorey were between those in the pasture and gaps. Seed removal rates in the abandoned pasture were significantly higher than those in treefall gaps for all species except S. pulcherrimum, and were higher than rates in the understorey for P. guianensis and Eugenia sp. (AOV, Scheffe, p &lt; 0.05).

There were two principal groups of seed removers active in the open field: ants and small rodents. The most conspicuous ant species was Atta sexdens. We observed this ant removing most of the seeds of Inga sp. and Nectandra sp. placed in the abandoned pasture. We also observed the ant genera Solenopsis and Pheidole removing seeds of Bagassa guianensis Aubl., Laetia procera (P. et Endl.) Eichl., Vismia guianensis, Solanum crinitum, Cecropia obtusa, Jacarandra copaia, and Eugenia sp. In all the cases cited above, we observed the ants carrying the seeds into nests.

Seeds that were too large to be moved by ants (i.e., &gt; 0.4 g) were often attacked by rodents. For example, seed coats of Bertholletia excelsa Humb., Pourouma guianensis, and Manilkara huberi (Ducke) Stand. were frequently chewed through with the interior tissues removed. Larger, tough-coated seeds or fruits, like those of Radlkoferella macrocarpa (Hub.) Aubr., Maximiliana maripa Drude, and Endopleura uchi (Huber) Cuart. were frequently scored with rodent teeth marks, but not eaten.

Rodents were more common in the abandoned pasture than in the forest. During four nights of mammal trapping in the abandoned pasture, we caught rodents in 37% of our traps (4 nights × 90 traps per night = 360 trap nights). Seventy-six percent of all captures were Akodon lasiurus and the remainder were Oryzomys microtus. Both of these species are known to feed on seeds (C. Yohn pers. obs. of stomach contents). Mammal trapping for three nights in the forest (with 90 traps each night) produced a total of 4 captures, a catch-success rate of 1.5%; small mammals were 25 times more abundant in the abandoned pasture, based on catch-success rate. ## Seedling herbivory

Seedling herbivory was higher in the abandoned pasture than in treefall gaps of the mature forest. Within the first 16 d of the seedling basin experiment, more than one-third of the foliage had been removed from most of the tree seedlings in the abandoned pasture (*H. courbaril*, 75%, *J. copaia*, 85%, *T. serratifolia*, 55%, and *V. guianensis*, 65%) but no seedlings of any species had more than one-third foliage removal in the treefall gaps. Herbivory was higher for tree species than for shrub and grass species; no grasses and only one shrub seedling (*S. cayennensis*) exhibited herbivory in the abandoned pasture (5%). Lower rates of herbivory for shrubs and the grass may have resulted from differences in plant size, because the mean height of the shrubs and the grass at the beginning of the experiment was twice that of the trees (because of different growth rates while the basins were in the nursery). Species was a greater source of variation than initial plant height, although height alone accounted for a significant amount of variation in herbivory (p &lt; 0.001; two-way AOV). However, herbivore preferences for tree seedlings over grass and shrub seedlings is suggested by the complete absence of herbivory in experimental populations of the grass, *P. millegrana* and the forb, *R. argentea*.

The most important herbivore in this experiment was *Atta sexdens*. All of the seedlings with more than one third of their leaves removed exhibited evidence of *A*.

## Abiotic barriers

Both survivorship and height growth of transplanted seedlings were generally lower in the abandoned pasture than in the treefall gaps. Survivorship of seedlings before the first dry season was unexpectedly low in the abandoned pasture; for 8 of the 10 species studied, less than 30% of the seedlings survived from the time of planting to the onset of the dry season (July 1986, Fig. 4). During the first dry season (July, 1986 to January, 1987), survivorship of nine of the ten species transplanted was lower in the abandoned pasture than in treefall gaps. These differences were significant for B. guianensis, B. macrostachya, J. copaia, P. guianensis, and T. serratifolia (Fig. 4; p &lt; 0.05, 2 × 2 G-test of independence; Sokal and Rohlf 1969). H. courbaril survivorship was higher in the abandoned pasture, although this difference was not significant (p &gt; 0.05).

Despite a general pattern of lower survivorship in the abandoned pasture than in the treefall gaps, some seedlings in the abandoned pasture survived 20–23 months, to the end of the second dry season (February 1988). Abandoned pasture survivorship was greater than 8% of the original population for 5 of the species studied. Only 3 species had no survivors in the abandoned pasture by the end of the study period (B. guianensis, P. guianensis, and S. crinitum) and one of these (S. crinitum) had no survivors in the treefall gaps. Survivorship showed no consistent differences between blocks of each ecosystem.

Height growth of seedling transplants was greater in the treefall gaps than in the abandoned pasture for some species. The mean height of the five tallest individuals from each seedling population was less than 50 cm for those 7 species in the abandoned pasture that had at least 5 survivors at the end of the study period. Three species planted in the gaps had average maximum height &gt;250 cm (Fig. 5).

Microclimatic measurements revealed large differences in PPFD and dry season air T and air VPD among habitats. PPFD at 10 cm height in the grass/shrub vegetation of the abandoned pasture was 8–9% full sun and was intermediate to that in the 6 month-old experimental treefall gaps (17% full sun) and that in the intact forest (1% full sun). During the 1985 dry season, maximum T in the abandoned pasture was 2–7°C higher than in the 150-m² treefall gap and 6–11°C higher than in the forest understorey; maximum air VPD was 0.5–2.0 kPa higher than in the treefall gap and up to 3.0 Pa above that in the forest understorey (Table 4). During the 1985 wet season, maximum daily T and VPD were very similar in the

# Discussion

Research over the last decade has revealed that there is an inverse relationship between the duration and intensity of disturbance and the speed and vigor of forest succession following Amazonian forest disturbances (Uhl 1982, Uhl et al. 1988, Uhl et al. 1989). For example, regeneration is rapid following small-scale, short-lived disturbances such as treefalls because a good stock of advance regeneration quickly shoots up and plants arising as sprouts, as seedlings from seeds in the soil, or from dispersed seeds fill the open places. As disturbances become larger and more prolonged (e.g. conversion of forest to pasture), mechanisms of regeneration are slowly eliminated. This is not to say that forest regeneration is impossible on abandoned pastures in Amazonia. Indeed, Uhl et al. (1988), in a study of

thirteen abandoned pastures in eastern Amazonia, found that sites used for pasture for fewer than 8 yr were repopulated with trees within a few years of abandonment. Sprouting was an important means of regeneration on many of these sites: more than half of the 171 tree species identified in abandoned pastures had the ability to sprout (Uhl et al. 1988). In the present study, the prolonged period of land use (more than 15 yr), and associated fires, weeding, and herbicide application, were sufficient to eliminate sprouting roots almost completely (Table 1). As soil scraping with bulldozers expands as a pasture management practice (Mattos and Uhl 1994), the area of Amazon land depleted in residual tree roots should increase.

# Seed availability

Prolonged use of land as pasture decreased the number of sprouting roots and also severely reduced the number of tree seeds in the soil at the Vitoria study site. Approximately 700 tree seeds m⁻² were found in the forest seed bank but only 10 tree seeds m⁻² were found in the abandoned pasture seed bank. At the same time, the seed bank for grasses and forbs increased dramatically – from 15 (forest) to over 7000 (abandoned pasture) seeds m⁻².

Because of the near absence of sprouting roots persisting from the pre-existing forest (Table 1) and the depauperate seed bank in this abandoned pasture, trees had a chance of reestablishing only if their seeds were dispersed by wind or animals from the forest. The abandoned pasture study site was within 500 m of a mature forest edge (Fig. 1). Wind probably carried few tree seeds into the abandoned pasture because only 11% of the forest tree species are wind-dispersed, and for many of these the maximum dispersal distance is probably &lt; 100 m (N. Rosa, pers. comm.). Also, the study site at the Vitoria Ranch was not downwind from the forest. In some other tropical areas, wind-dispersed species are frequently the first tree invaders of old fields (Janzen 1988).

Birds and bats were the principal vectors for tree seed dispersal into the abandoned pasture. The seeds of ten tree and liana species were found in the feces of birds and bats captured in the abandoned pasture. Birds and bats that frequented the abandoned pasture were attracted by woody plants that produced abundant fleshy fruits, such as Solanum crinitum. Four hundred times more seeds fell into traps placed beneath plants of this species than in the traps placed above the surrounding grass-shrub matrix, where frugivorous birds were rarely observed perching. We have described a similar phenomenon of directed dispersal beneath the pasture-invading liana, Cordia multispicata, which also produces fleshy fruits (Vieira et al. 1994). Directed seed dispersal by birds, such as that described here, has also been

## Seed predation

The probability of a tree seed deposited in the abandoned pasture being removed by the animal community was directly related to the size of the seed (Fig. 3) and the thickness of the seed covering. Ants rapidly removed seeds of &lt;0.4 g, while larger, well-protected seeds were slowly chewed up by rodents. The only seeds placed in the abandoned pasture that developed into seedlings (4 out of 240 seeds placed – *Radlkoferella macrocarpa*) weighed 8 g, and had no natural vector for dispersal from the forest. Hence, seed vectors and seed predators favor opposing types of tree seeds in the abandoned pasture; only very small tree seeds (&lt;20 mg) were found in the seed bank, in seed traps, or in the feces of birds and bats captured in the abandoned pasture (Table 3), but much larger seeds were the most likely to survive the influence of ants and rodents.

The attractiveness of seeds to seed predators may also be related to substances present on the seed surface (Brian 1983). Seeds which were oily (e.g. *Laetia pro*

cera) or which retained fragments of pulp (e.g., Bagassa guianensis) were removed more rapidly than seeds with dry seed coats. The attractiveness of seeds may have declined over time as substances on the seed coat were washed away by rain or consumed by microorganisms, thereby explaining the decline in removal rate with time (Fig. 2).

We have assumed that trees taken into ant nests are, in effect, killed. The ant genera that we observed (Atta, Pheidole and Solenopsis) are known to consume seeds (Hölldobler and Wilson 1990). Moreover, nest chambers of Atta (Moutinho 1995) and Pheidole are usually 25 cm or deeper in the soil. In one excavated nest of Atta sexdens, viable seeds of Davilla and other genera were found in refuse chambers at 50 cm depth (P. Moutinho, pers. comm.). Even if transported seeds are not consumed by the ants, deep burial may preclude establishment. Solenopsis nests are closer to the surface or even appear as above-ground mounds during the dry season. In excavation of abandoned Solenopsis nests at our site, C. Yohn (unpubl.) encountered only seed remains. However, entire seeds were found at the entrances to the nests of Solenopsis and Pheidole suggesting that seeds may sometimes be carried to nests and then discarded.

Just as seed vectors determine which seeds arrive in an abandoned pasture, seed predators further reduce the types of seeds that may be available for tree establishment. The preferences of seed predators could influence succession. For example, Risch and Carroll (1986) found that Pheidole ants could influence weed community succession by selectively removing grass seed and thereby affecting density-dependent competitive interactions between grasses and dicots.

## Seedling herbivory

If seeds are transported to an abandoned pasture, escape seed predators, and then germinate, they still must survive and grow before tree establishment is complete. Here, too, we found that herbivory was important. All tree species placed in the abandoned

pasture in our basin experiment experienced severe herbivory on more than one half of the study individuals whereas herbivory was zero for seedling populations of the these same species set in forest treefall gaps. The large populations of generalist ant species that occurred in the abandoned pasture (Moutinho et al. 1993) resulted in high levels of both seed predation and seedling herbivory.

The ability of tree seedlings to withstand defoliation also appears to be related to seed size. For example, we measured the effect of A. sexdens, the leaf cutter ant in the abandoned pasture, on the survival and growth of the large-seeded forest tree, Radlkoferella macrocarpa, by planting seeds with and without physical barriers to the ant (D. Nepstad, unpubl.). In the absence of barriers, A. sexdens repeatedly attacked R. macrocarpa (Hub.) Aubl. seedlings by clipping leaves and shoot apices. Although the plants exposed to ants were ca half the size of protected plants one year after germination, cutter ants had little effect on the overall survival of these seedlings. Many tree seedlings, however, are more vulnerable to ant attack than R. macrocarpa. Small-seeded species, such as Bagassa guianensis and Didymopanax morototoni (Aubl.) Decne. et Pl., produce tiny seedlings that die if clipped within the first several weeks following germination. Seedling survival following cutter ant attack only seems possible if sufficient resources (e.g. carbohydrates and nutrients) and meristems are available to replace lost leaf and stem tissue.

## Abiotic factors

The Paragominas region, like half of the closed forests of Brazilian Amazonia, is characterized by an annual dry period during which rainfall is less than evapotranspiration (Nepstad et al. 1994). Surface soil water was depleted more in the abandoned pasture than in forest habitats during the dry season, perhaps because of the higher root length density in surface soil found in the abandoned pasture (Table 5). The tendency of grasses to deplete surface soil water more than the forest

vegetation they replace has been documented in several locations around the world (reviewed by D'Antonio and Vitousek 1992) and may be an important factor limiting the ability of drought-sensitive tree species to establish.

Tree seedlings planted in the abandoned pasture experienced far greater drought stress than identical seedlings planted in forest treefall gaps. Compared to the treefall gaps, where many moist tropical forest tree species successfully regenerate, the abandoned pasture was also hot and dry during the 5-month dry season (Table 4). Both drought stress and hot, dry air in the abandoned pasture were correlated with higher levels of seedling mortality and may therefore restrict the number and diversity of trees that became established in the abandoned pasture. Seedlings of gap-invading tree species may be more susceptible to drought than seedlings of shade-tolerant, canopy tree species. Gap-invading tree species lose leaf turgor at high xylem pressure potential relative to canopy and understorey tree species (Robichaux et al. 1984, Nepstad 1989), which may explain the complete dry season seedling mortality of the two gap-invading species B. guianensis and P. guianensis transplanted in the abandoned pasture (Fig. 4) and may partly explain the rareness with which the Cecropia spp. seeds that are deposited in the abandoned pasture emerge as seedlings. Although the small seeds of Cecropia and other gap-invading tree species are dispersed into abandoned pastures in the greatest numbers, seedlings of these species may be physiologically unsuited to survival and growth in the abandoned pasture when compared to seedlings of canopy and understorey species.

The data also indicate that factors other than drought stress, high temperature and high VPD may have contributed to the relatively poor performance of seedlings planted in the abandoned pasture. For example, both high levels of rainy-season mortality of seedlings in the abandoned pasture and very low rates of seedling height growth (&lt; 50 cm during 20-23 months for all species planted) indicate that these seedlings were not thriving even when rainfall was abundant. Two other factors may help explain this performance of seedlings planted in the abandoned pasture. First, seedlings planted in the abandoned pasture may have encountered high levels of competition for soil nutrients because the root length density (root length per volume of soil) of this ecosystem was four times higher than that of the mature forest and probably higher still than root length density of the treefall gaps (Table 5). Second, soil bulk density and resistance to penetration were also higher in the abandoned pasture, perhaps restricting development of seedling roots (Table 5 and D. Nepstad, unpubl.). Both of these factors significantly reduced seedling growth in an experiment conducted in the abandoned pasture at the Fazenda Vitoria study site. Seedlings of a leguminous

tree, Schizolobium amazonica, responded to complete nutrient solution only when the soil was tilled before planting. Seedlings that were planted in holes lined with plastic to exclude the roots of neighboring plants grew significantly faster than those planted in unlined holes (Nepstad 1989).

Wet season restrictions to tree seedling survival and growth in the abandoned pasture relative to the treefall gaps are unlikely to include low soil nutrient availability, since the nutrient status of the abandoned pasture was similar to that of the mature forest (Table 5). Moreover, it is unlikely that low light levels limited the survival and growth of forest tree seedlings in the abandoned pasture. Seedlings of moist tropical forest tree species appear to survive and grow better with 10–25% full sun than with 100% full sun (Fetcher et al. 1983, Oberbauer 1983, Augsburger 1984, Langenheim et al. 1984, Peters 1989). Light levels at 10 cm height in the abandoned pasture were 8–9% full sun early in the dry season and were probably sufficient to maintain seedlings of most of the region's tree species with the possible exception of high light-demanding species such as members of the genus Cecropia.

It is important to note that some tree species not included in the experiments presented here are able to overcome both wet and dry season barriers to growth in the abandoned pasture. For example, some seedlings of Sclerolobium paraensis had reached 10 m height within five yr of planting in the abandoned pasture, without fertilization (Nepstad and Uhl, unpubl.).

There are striking similarities between the controls over tropical plant succession elucidated in this paper and those revealed in decades of research on succession in old fields in Europe and North America (Grime 1977, Pickett 1982, Gross 1984, Huston and Smith 1987, McConnaughay and Bazzaz 1987, Gill and Marks 1991). Temperate zone studies of forest succession following cattle exclusion from pastures (Bormann 1953, Penfound 1964, Bullington 1973), likewise, reveal that woody species establishment is slow in the early years but by ten years a mix of grasses and trees is usually present. In both regions, biotic factors (e.g., seed dispersal, seed predation, competition) as well as abiotic factors (light, temperature, nutrient and water availability) influence the course of succession. However, the relative importance of these different biotic and abiotic controls can change over the course of succession in a given site (Finegan 1984). The general conclusion is that an array of factors act in concert to influence succession in both temperate and tropical ecosystems and that as disturbances become more severe, the number and strength of these controlling factors increases.

# Dispersal of ornithochorous seeds from forest edges in central Florida

T. R. McClanahan¹ &amp; R. W. Wolfe²
¹Friends World College, East African Centre, P.O. Box 526, Machakos, Kenya
²Center for Wetlands, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida, USA

Accepted 27.2.1987

Key words: Bird diversity, Frugivory, Ornithochory, Recruitment, Seed dispersal, Succession, Vegetation structure

## Abstract

Dispersal of ornithochorous seeds from isolated forests in the phosphate mining region of central Florida, U.S.A., were studied for two seasons (July to November) to determine patterns of dispersal. Three separate studies included (1) dispersal directly from forest edges to early successional herbs; (2) standardized perches (2 m high post with a crossbeam); and (3) snags (dead trees, 11.3 ± 2.8 m high, 21.4 ± 23.3 stem branches). Perch availability was more important than distance in predicting seed types and quantities of bird-dispersed seeds. The greatest concentration of bird-dispersed seeds were found under standard perches (255 ± 249 seeds/m²/fall) followed by snags (147 ± 85 seeds/m²/fall) and early successional vegetation (3.0 ± 4.1 seeds/m²/fall). Seed quantities dispersed to snags were positively correlated with the number of stem branches on snags. Seeds beneath standard perches were significantly lighter and less diverse than those found beneath snags. This difference is attributed to the larger percentage of forest or later successional species found beneath snags (73%) as compared to the standard perches (15%). Perches and vegetative structural development should facilitate ecological succession by increasing the quantity, quality and diversity of seed deposition.

## Introduction

Seed dispersal plays an important role in the regeneration of disturbed sites (Clements, 1916; McQuilkin, 1940; McClanahan, 1986). Seed dispersal studies typically result in leptokurtic seed distribution from a source for wind (Jemison &amp; Korstian, 1944; Boyer, 1958; Roe, 1960; Randall, 1974), avian (Auclair &amp; Cottam, 1971; Smith, 1975) and bat-dispersed seeds (Fleming &amp; Heithaus, 1981). Yet, bird and bat-dispersed species are often influenced by perching site availability. Perches such as stones (Livingston, 1972), trees (McAtee, 1947; Glyphis et al., 1981; Fleming &amp; Heithaus, 1981; Debussche et al., 1982; Uhl et al., 1982; Guevara et al., 1986) and artificial structures (McDonnell &amp; Stiles, 1983; McDonnell, 1986) are important foci which attract avian dispersers and associated seeds. These foci facilitate seed deposition and act as high density and diversity centers in vegetative regeneration (Yarranton &amp; Morrison, 1974).

In order to understand and manage ecological succession it is important to determine factors which affect seed dispersal and deposition. When desired this information can be used to assist or enhance ecological succession. This study compares the effect of distance and vegetative structure on dispersal and its probable role in ecological succession.

108

# Methods

Three sites adjacent to two floodplains were chosen for dispersal studies (Whidden Creek (WC), 27°42′N, 81°51′W; Peace River (PRa) 27°51′N, 81°48′W; (PRb) 27°50′N, 81°48′W; Elevations 100–124 m) in Polk County, Florida, USA. This area was originally vegetated by south-eastern North American temperate pine, hardwood and wetland forests (Monk, 1965, 1966). Species of frugivorous birds are associated with these forests (Martin et al., 1951). In the last few decades large areas around these sites have been mined and the floodplains are part of a few isolated remnant wetland forests surrounded by many kilometers of early successional, agricultural and mining environments. Sites were recently mined (2–8 years ago), regraded and planted with seedlings. Sites were vegetated by early successional herbs, grasses and wetland plants. The Whidden Creek site was the most topographically complex and had more wetland areas than the other sites.

Three dispersal studies were undertaken concerning direct dispersal, dispersal to standardized perches, and dispersal to snags.

1. Dispersal directly from forest edges to early successional vegetation consisted of 6 replicate transects of 5 seed traps placed at 15 m intervals (Jemison &amp; Korstian, 1944; Boyer, 1958). Transects began 15 m within the forest and ended 45 m away from the forest edge. This study was undertaken at all three sites. Two adjacent to Peace River (PRa and PRb) and one adjacent to Whidden Creek (WCa). Two sites (PRa and WCa) were studied for two years and the third (PRb) for one year. Larger (&gt;2 mm) endozoochorous seeds were identified and counted.

2. Three replicate transects of four standardized perches and a control; perches were constructed of an upright 2.5 m beam with a 1 m crossbeam nailed to the top (McDonnell &amp; Stiles, 1983). Perches were placed at 30 m intervals away from the forest edges with a seed trap fastened underneath each perch. Control traps were placed at the same intervals without a perch. Site WCa was studied for two years and site PRb for one year.

3. Seed dispersal to snags was undertaken at Whidden Creek (Debussche et al., 1982). Snags are dead trees placed in the ground with a pole-driving machine at convenient locations throughout the site. Three seed traps were placed at 1, 2 and 3 m intervals from the snag. A control trap was placed at greater than 10 m from the snag. The height, distance from the forest edge and number of stem branches off the trunk were recorded. Three snags were studied for two years and an additional five for one year.

Seed traps in the above studies were constructed from plastic seedling trays (0.135 m²) with a fiberglass mesh bottom (to prevent seeds from falling through drainage holes) and a wire covering (2.5 cm mesh) to reduce seed predation. Seed traps were visited every 2 to 4 weeks during fall months (July to November, 1983 and 1984). Seed traps beneath snags were occasionally lost or removed during the study and therefore data were analyzed on a seeds per month basis to normalize for this bias. Seeds were counted and identified to the genus except for three closely related genera (Ampelopsis, Vitis and Parthenocissus) whose seeds are difficult to distinguish and therefore identified to the family Vitaceae.

In the analysis of the data seed numbers, genera, weights (n = 20–79 seeds/species) and diversity (Simpson, 1949; Routledge, 1979) at various locations were analyzed to determine patterns of dispersal. Further, a distinction was made between forest and non-forest seeds as this was a critical distinction in dispersal patterns. Seeds from the genera Magnolia, Persea, Prunus, Celtis, Nyssa, Callicarpa, Cornus and the family Vitaceae were considered forest species. These genera are trees associated with later successional hardwood and wetland forests in Florida (Monk, 1965, 1966; Veno, 1976). Within the family Vitaceae the genera Vitis is often an early successional vine but from germination studies we found that all germinated seeds tested were from the genus Parthenocissus which is associated with later successional forests. We therefore placed this family in the forest class. Seeds from the genera Phytolacca, Rhus and Lantana were classified as non-forest or early successional genera. The genus Myrica was also classified as a non-forest genera. Although variably found in

109

Florida forests as an understory shrub, in the phosphate mining region, it is an early successional shrub. These distinctions are based on vegetation studies and successional theory within this region (Monk, 1965, 1966; Veno, 1976; Schnoes &amp; Humphrey, 1980; Rushton, 1983).

Site comparisons indicate that the greatest number of seeds were dispersed to the Whidden Creek site for both the edge and standard perch study. Observation suggests that bird activity was related to these site differences.

## Discussion

Seed dispersal by birds at these sites, for distances studied, appears to be less dependent on distance to a seed source than availability and types of perching sites. Seed dispersal to early successional vegetation was sparse as determined by edge and control studies. This suggests that even short distances will restrict dispersal of bird-dispersed forest species to early successional sites. With the addition of perches, the quantity and quality of seeds changes and the distance factor is either negligible or of secondary importance for distances studied (Guevara et al., 1986). Additionally, site characteristics such as topographic complexity, availability of standing water and vegetational development may account for site differences (McDonnell &amp; Stiles, 1983).

Previous studies on seed dispersal have shown

111

distance to be a dominant factor in predicting seed quantities. Wind-dispersed species often show an exponential decay with distance from a seed source (Boyer, 1958; Roe, 1968) and bird-dispersed species show similar patterns within forests (Auclair &amp; Cottam, 1971; Smith, 1975). Ornithochorous seeds may display this pattern due to the relative uniformity of perching sites within forests as suggested by Kitching's (1971) model. Winged seeds are limited by available wind energy and seed aerodynamics and therefore less specific in determining site location. Bird dispersal, on the other hand, is more site specific and dependent on bird behavior. Distance may eventually become a factor for bird-dispersed seeds but only as a residual factor to site attractiveness in areas close to seed sources.

Differences in dispersal patterns between standard perches and snags indicate that smaller low diversity non-forest seeds were dispersed to standard perches and larger more diverse forest seeds to snags. This may be attributed to structural differences of height and stem branchings between standard perches and snags. Studies on bird distribution (MacArthur &amp; MacArthur, 1961; Erdelen, 1984) suggest that bird abundance and diversity is largely affected by height and structural development of vegetation rather than floristic nature. More dispersing individuals and species may be using snags compared to standard perches which may account for observed seed differences. Lower seed quantities captured beneath snags compared to perches does not contradict McDonnell's (1986) positive relationship between height and seed quantities but is a result of seed dilution around snags due to their greater height and circumference. The total amount of seeds attracted by snags should be greater than standard perches.

Results support the conclusion of Debussche et al. (1982) that vegetative structure attracts seeds and should therefore facilitate (Connell &amp; Slatyer, 1977) ecological succession. This would also support the relay floristics model (Egler, 1954) as some species may have a seed deposition time delay dependent on previous structural development. Ornithochorous dispersal dependent on vegetative development may be a form of diffuse coevolution (Herrera, 1982) between plants and dipersers to in-

sure increased survival probability through deposition in an appropriate environment or may simply be an artifact of bird behavior. Dispersal mechanisms should depend on evolutionary pressures, life histories and trade offs between different dispersal options. Regardless, succession should be enhanced if seeds are available at proper times. This can be assisted by manipulating sites in order to attract a diversity of bird species which disperse later successional plant species.

# Dispersal of ornithochorous seeds from forest edges in central Florida

T. R. McClanahan¹ &amp; R. W. Wolfe²

## Abstract

Dispersal of ornithochorous seeds from isolated forests in the phosphate mining region of central Florida, U.S.A., were studied for two seasons (July to November) to determine patterns of dispersal. Three separate studies included (1) dispersal directly from forest edges to early successional herbs; (2) standardized perches (2 m high post with a crossbeam); and (3) snags (dead trees, 11.3 ± 2.8 m high, 21.4 ± 23.3 stem branches). Perch availability was more important than distance in predicting seed types and quantities of bird-dispersed seeds. The greatest concentration of bird-dispersed seeds were found under standard perches (255 ± 249 seeds/m²/fall) followed by snags (147 ± 85 seeds/m²/fall) and early successional vegetation (3.0 ± 4.1 seeds/m²/fall). Seed quantities dispersed to snags were positively correlated with the number of stem branches on snags. Seeds beneath standard perches were significantly lighter and less diverse than those found beneath snags. This difference is attributed to the larger percentage of forest or later successional species found beneath snags (73%) as compared to the standard perches (15%). Perches and vegetative structural development should facilitate ecological succession by increasing the quantity, quality and diversity of seed deposition.

## Introduction

Seed dispersal plays an important role in the regeneration of disturbed sites (Clements, 1916; McQuilkin, 1940; McClanahan, 1986). Seed dispersal studies typically result in leptokurtic seed distribution from a source for wind (Jemison &amp; Korstian, 1944; Boyer, 1958; Roe, 1960; Randall, 1974), avian (Auclair &amp; Cottam, 1971; Smith, 1975) and bat-dispersed seeds (Fleming &amp; Heithaus, 1981). Yet, bird and bat-dispersed species are often influenced by perching site availability. Perches such as stones (Livingston, 1972), trees (McAtee, 1947; Glyphis et al., 1981; Fleming &amp; Heithaus, 1981; Debussche et al., 1982; Uhl et al., 1982; Guevara et al., 1986) and artificial structures (McDonnell &amp; Stiles, 1983; McDonnell, 1986) are important foci which attract avian dispersers and associated seeds. These foci facilitate seed deposition and act as high density and diversity centers in vegetative regeneration (Yarranton &amp; Morrison, 1974).

In order to understand and manage ecological succession it is important to determine factors which affect seed dispersal and deposition. When desired this information can be used to assist or enhance ecological succession. This study compares the effect of distance and vegetative structure on dispersal and its probable role in ecological succession.

108

# Methods

Three sites adjacent to two floodplains were chosen for dispersal studies (Whidden Creek (WC), 27°42′N, 81°51′W; Peace River (PRa) 27°51′N, 81°48′W; (PRb) 27°50′N, 81°48′W; Elevations 100–124 m) in Polk County, Florida, USA. This area was originally vegetated by south-eastern North American temperate pine, hardwood and wetland forests (Monk, 1965, 1966). Species of frugivorous birds are associated with these forests (Martin et al., 1951). In the last few decades large areas around these sites have been mined and the floodplains are part of a few isolated remnant wetland forests surrounded by many kilometers of early successional, agricultural and mining environments. Sites were recently mined (2–8 years ago), regraded and planted with seedlings. Sites were vegetated by early successional herbs, grasses and wetland plants. The Whidden Creek site was the most topographically complex and had more wetland areas than the other sites.

Three dispersal studies were undertaken concerning direct dispersal, dispersal to standardized perches, and dispersal to snags.

1. Dispersal directly from forest edges to early successional vegetation consisted of 6 replicate transects of 5 seed traps placed at 15 m intervals (Jemison &amp; Korstian, 1944; Boyer, 1958). Transects began 15 m within the forest and ended 45 m away from the forest edge. This study was undertaken at all three sites. Two adjacent to Peace River (PRa and PRb) and one adjacent to Whidden Creek (WCa). Two sites (PRa and WCa) were studied for two years and the third (PRb) for one year. Larger (&gt;2 mm) endozoochorous seeds were identified and counted.

2. Three replicate transects of four standardized perches and a control; perches were constructed of an upright 2.5 m beam with a 1 m crossbeam nailed to the top (McDonnell &amp; Stiles, 1983). Perches were placed at 30 m intervals away from the forest edges with a seed trap fastened underneath each perch. Control traps were placed at the same intervals without a perch. Site WCa was studied for two years and site PRb for one year.

3. Seed dispersal to snags was undertaken at Whidden Creek (Debussche et al., 1982). Snags are dead trees placed in the ground with a pole-driving machine at convenient locations throughout the site. Three seed traps were placed at 1, 2 and 3 m intervals from the snag. A control trap was placed at greater than 10 m from the snag. The height, distance from the forest edge and number of stem branches off the trunk were recorded. Three snags were studied for two years and an additional five for one year.

Seed traps in the above studies were constructed from plastic seedling trays (0.135 m²) with a fiberglass mesh bottom (to prevent seeds from falling through drainage holes) and a wire covering (2.5 cm mesh) to reduce seed predation. Seed traps were visited every 2 to 4 weeks during fall months (July to November, 1983 and 1984). Seed traps beneath snags were occasionally lost or removed during the study and therefore data were analyzed on a seeds per month basis to normalize for this bias. Seeds were counted and identified to the genus except for three closely related genera (Ampelopsis, Vitis and Parthenocissus) whose seeds are difficult to distinguish and therefore identified to the family Vitaceae.

In the analysis of the data seed numbers, genera, weights (n = 20–79 seeds/species) and diversity (Simpson, 1949; Routledge, 1979) at various locations were analyzed to determine patterns of dispersal. Further, a distinction was made between forest and non-forest seeds as this was a critical distinction in dispersal patterns. Seeds from the genera Magnolia, Persea, Prunus, Celtis, Nyssa, Callicarpa, Cornus and the family Vitaceae were considered forest species. These genera are trees associated with later successional hardwood and wetland forests in Florida (Monk, 1965, 1966; Veno, 1976). Within the family Vitaceae the genera Vitis is often an early successional vine but from germination studies we found that all germinated seeds tested were from the genus Parthenocissus which is associated with later successional forests. We therefore placed this family in the forest class. Seeds from the genera Phytolacca, Rhus and Lantana were classified as non-forest or early successional genera. The genus Myrica was also classified as a non-forest genera. Although variably found in

109

Florida forests as an understory shrub, in the phosphate mining region, it is an early successional shrub. These distinctions are based on vegetation studies and successional theory within this region (Monk, 1965, 1966; Veno, 1976; Schnoes &amp; Humphrey, 1980; Rushton, 1983).

Site comparisons indicate that the greatest number of seeds were dispersed to the Whidden Creek site for both the edge and standard perch study. Observation suggests that bird activity was related to these site differences.

## Discussion

Seed dispersal by birds at these sites, for distances studied, appears to be less dependent on distance to a seed source than availability and types of perching sites. Seed dispersal to early successional vegetation was sparse as determined by edge and control studies. This suggests that even short distances will restrict dispersal of bird-dispersed forest species to early successional sites. With the addition of perches, the quantity and quality of seeds changes and the distance factor is either negligible or of secondary importance for distances studied (Guevara et al., 1986). Additionally, site characteristics such as topographic complexity, availability of standing water and vegetational development may account for site differences (McDonnell &amp; Stiles, 1983).

Previous studies on seed dispersal have shown

111

distance to be a dominant factor in predicting seed quantities. Wind-dispersed species often show an exponential decay with distance from a seed source (Boyer, 1958; Roe, 1968) and bird-dispersed species show similar patterns within forests (Auclair &amp; Cottam, 1971; Smith, 1975). Ornithochorous seeds may display this pattern due to the relative uniformity of perching sites within forests as suggested by Kitching's (1971) model. Winged seeds are limited by available wind energy and seed aerodynamics and therefore less specific in determining site location. Bird dispersal, on the other hand, is more site specific and dependent on bird behavior. Distance may eventually become a factor for bird-dispersed seeds but only as a residual factor to site attractiveness in areas close to seed sources.

Differences in dispersal patterns between standard perches and snags indicate that smaller low diversity non-forest seeds were dispersed to standard perches and larger more diverse forest seeds to snags. This may be attributed to structural differences of height and stem branchings between standard perches and snags. Studies on bird distribution (MacArthur &amp; MacArthur, 1961; Erdelen, 1984) suggest that bird abundance and diversity is largely affected by height and structural development of vegetation rather than floristic nature. More dispersing individuals and species may be using snags compared to standard perches which may account for observed seed differences. Lower seed quantities captured beneath snags compared to perches does not contradict McDonnell's (1986) positive relationship between height and seed quantities but is a result of seed dilution around snags due to their greater height and circumference. The total amount of seeds attracted by snags should be greater than standard perches.

Results support the conclusion of Debussche et al. (1982) that vegetative structure attracts seeds and should therefore facilitate (Connell &amp; Slatyer, 1977) ecological succession. This would also support the relay floristics model (Egler, 1954) as some species may have a seed deposition time delay dependent on previous structural development. Ornithochorous dispersal dependent on vegetative development may be a form of diffuse coevolution (Herrera, 1982) between plants and dipersers to in-

sure increased survival probability through deposition in an appropriate environment or may simply be an artifact of bird behavior. Dispersal mechanisms should depend on evolutionary pressures, life histories and trade offs between different dispersal options. Regardless, succession should be enhanced if seeds are available at proper times. This can be assisted by manipulating sites in order to attract a diversity of bird species which disperse later successional plant species.

# Dispersal of ornithochorous seeds from forest edges in central Florida

T. R. McClanahan¹ &amp; R. W. Wolfe²
¹Friends World College, East African Centre, P.O. Box 526, Machakos, Kenya

## Abstract

Dispersal of ornithochorous seeds from isolated forests in the phosphate mining region of central Florida, U.S.A., were studied for two seasons (July to November) to determine patterns of dispersal. Three separate studies included (1) dispersal directly from forest edges to early successional herbs; (2) standardized perches (2 m high post with a crossbeam); and (3) snags (dead trees, 11.3 ± 2.8 m high, 21.4 ± 23.3 stem branches). Perch availability was more important than distance in predicting seed types and quantities of bird-dispersed seeds. The greatest concentration of bird-dispersed seeds were found under standard perches (255 ± 249 seeds/m²/fall) followed by snags (147 ± 85 seeds/m²/fall) and early successional vegetation (3.0 ± 4.1 seeds/m²/fall). Seed quantities dispersed to snags were positively correlated with the number of stem branches on snags. Seeds beneath standard perches were significantly lighter and less diverse than those found beneath snags. This difference is attributed to the larger percentage of forest or later successional species found beneath snags (73%) as compared to the standard perches (15%). Perches and vegetative structural development should facilitate ecological succession by increasing the quantity, quality and diversity of seed deposition.

## Introduction

Seed dispersal plays an important role in the regeneration of disturbed sites (Clements, 1916; McQuilkin, 1940; McClanahan, 1986). Seed dispersal studies typically result in leptokurtic seed distribution from a source for wind (Jemison &amp; Korstian, 1944; Boyer, 1958; Roe, 1960; Randall, 1974), avian (Auclair &amp; Cottam, 1971; Smith, 1975) and bat-dispersed seeds (Fleming &amp; Heithaus, 1981). Yet, bird and bat-dispersed species are often influenced by perching site availability. Perches such as stones (Livingston, 1972), trees (McAtee, 1947; Glyphis et al., 1981; Fleming &amp; Heithaus, 1981; Debussche et al., 1982; Uhl et al., 1982; Guevara et al., 1986) and artificial structures (McDonnell &amp; Stiles, 1983; McDonnell, 1986) are important foci which attract avian dispersers and associated seeds. These foci facilitate seed deposition and act as high density and diversity centers in vegetative regeneration (Yarranton &amp; Morrison, 1974).

In order to understand and manage ecological succession it is important to determine factors which affect seed dispersal and deposition. When desired this information can be used to assist or enhance ecological succession. This study compares the effect of distance and vegetative structure on dispersal and its probable role in ecological succession.

108

# Methods

Three sites adjacent to two floodplains were chosen for dispersal studies (Whidden Creek (WC), 27°42′N, 81°51′W; Peace River (PRa) 27°51′N, 81°48′W; (PRb) 27°50′N, 81°48′W; Elevations 100–124 m) in Polk County, Florida, USA. This area was originally vegetated by south-eastern North American temperate pine, hardwood and wetland forests (Monk, 1965, 1966). Species of frugivorous birds are associated with these forests (Martin et al., 1951). In the last few decades large areas around these sites have been mined and the floodplains are part of a few isolated remnant wetland forests surrounded by many kilometers of early successional, agricultural and mining environments. Sites were recently mined (2–8 years ago), regraded and planted with seedlings. Sites were vegetated by early successional herbs, grasses and wetland plants. The Whidden Creek site was the most topographically complex and had more wetland areas than the other sites.

Three dispersal studies were undertaken concerning direct dispersal, dispersal to standardized perches, and dispersal to snags.

1. Dispersal directly from forest edges to early successional vegetation consisted of 6 replicate transects of 5 seed traps placed at 15 m intervals (Jemison &amp; Korstian, 1944; Boyer, 1958). Transects began 15 m within the forest and ended 45 m away from the forest edge. This study was undertaken at all three sites. Two adjacent to Peace River (PRa and PRb) and one adjacent to Whidden Creek (WCa). Two sites (PRa and WCa) were studied for two years and the third (PRb) for one year. Larger (&gt;2 mm) endozoochorous seeds were identified and counted.

2. Three replicate transects of four standardized perches and a control; perches were constructed of an upright 2.5 m beam with a 1 m crossbeam nailed to the top (McDonnell &amp; Stiles, 1983). Perches were placed at 30 m intervals away from the forest edges with a seed trap fastened underneath each perch. Control traps were placed at the same intervals without a perch. Site WCa was studied for two years and site PRb for one year.

3. Seed dispersal to snags was undertaken at Whidden Creek (Debussche et al., 1982). Snags are dead trees placed in the ground with a pole-driving machine at convenient locations throughout the site. Three seed traps were placed at 1, 2 and 3 m intervals from the snag. A control trap was placed at greater than 10 m from the snag. The height, distance from the forest edge and number of stem branches off the trunk were recorded. Three snags were studied for two years and an additional five for one year.

Seed traps in the above studies were constructed from plastic seedling trays (0.135 m²) with a fiberglass mesh bottom (to prevent seeds from falling through drainage holes) and a wire covering (2.5 cm mesh) to reduce seed predation. Seed traps were visited every 2 to 4 weeks during fall months (July to November, 1983 and 1984). Seed traps beneath snags were occasionally lost or removed during the study and therefore data were analyzed on a seeds per month basis to normalize for this bias. Seeds were counted and identified to the genus except for three closely related genera (Ampelopsis, Vitis and Parthenocissus) whose seeds are difficult to distinguish and therefore identified to the family Vitaceae.

In the analysis of the data seed numbers, genera, weights (n = 20–79 seeds/species) and diversity (Simpson, 1949; Routledge, 1979) at various locations were analyzed to determine patterns of dispersal. Further, a distinction was made between forest and non-forest seeds as this was a critical distinction in dispersal patterns. Seeds from the genera Magnolia, Persea, Prunus, Celtis, Nyssa, Callicarpa, Cornus and the family Vitaceae were considered forest species. These genera are trees associated with later successional hardwood and wetland forests in Florida (Monk, 1965, 1966; Veno, 1976). Within the family Vitaceae the genera Vitis is often an early successional vine but from germination studies we found that all germinated seeds tested were from the genus Parthenocissus which is associated with later successional forests. We therefore placed this family in the forest class. Seeds from the genera Phytolacca, Rhus and Lantana were classified as non-forest or early successional genera. The genus Myrica was also classified as a non-forest genera. Although variably found in

109

Florida forests as an understory shrub, in the phosphate mining region, it is an early successional shrub. These distinctions are based on vegetation studies and successional theory within this region (Monk, 1965, 1966; Veno, 1976; Schnoes &amp; Humphrey, 1980; Rushton, 1983).

Site comparisons indicate that the greatest number of seeds were dispersed to the Whidden Creek site for both the edge and standard perch study. Observation suggests that bird activity was related to these site differences.

## Discussion

Seed dispersal by birds at these sites, for distances studied, appears to be less dependent on distance to a seed source than availability and types of perching sites. Seed dispersal to early successional vegetation was sparse as determined by edge and control studies. This suggests that even short distances will restrict dispersal of bird-dispersed forest species to early successional sites. With the addition of perches, the quantity and quality of seeds changes and the distance factor is either negligible or of secondary importance for distances studied (Guevara et al., 1986). Additionally, site characteristics such as topographic complexity, availability of standing water and vegetational development may account for site differences (McDonnell &amp; Stiles, 1983).

Previous studies on seed dispersal have shown

111

distance to be a dominant factor in predicting seed quantities. Wind-dispersed species often show an exponential decay with distance from a seed source (Boyer, 1958; Roe, 1968) and bird-dispersed species show similar patterns within forests (Auclair &amp; Cottam, 1971; Smith, 1975). Ornithochorous seeds may display this pattern due to the relative uniformity of perching sites within forests as suggested by Kitching's (1971) model. Winged seeds are limited by available wind energy and seed aerodynamics and therefore less specific in determining site location. Bird dispersal, on the other hand, is more site specific and dependent on bird behavior. Distance may eventually become a factor for bird-dispersed seeds but only as a residual factor to site attractiveness in areas close to seed sources.

Differences in dispersal patterns between standard perches and snags indicate that smaller low diversity non-forest seeds were dispersed to standard perches and larger more diverse forest seeds to snags. This may be attributed to structural differences of height and stem branchings between standard perches and snags. Studies on bird distribution (MacArthur &amp; MacArthur, 1961; Erdelen, 1984) suggest that bird abundance and diversity is largely affected by height and structural development of vegetation rather than floristic nature. More dispersing individuals and species may be using snags compared to standard perches which may account for observed seed differences. Lower seed quantities captured beneath snags compared to perches does not contradict McDonnell's (1986) positive relationship between height and seed quantities but is a result of seed dilution around snags due to their greater height and circumference. The total amount of seeds attracted by snags should be greater than standard perches.

Results support the conclusion of Debussche et al. (1982) that vegetative structure attracts seeds and should therefore facilitate (Connell &amp; Slatyer, 1977) ecological succession. This would also support the relay floristics model (Egler, 1954) as some species may have a seed deposition time delay dependent on previous structural development. Ornithochorous dispersal dependent on vegetative development may be a form of diffuse coevolution (Herrera, 1982) between plants and dipersers to in-

sure increased survival probability through deposition in an appropriate environment or may simply be an artifact of bird behavior. Dispersal mechanisms should depend on evolutionary pressures, life histories and trade offs between different dispersal options. Regardless, succession should be enhanced if seeds are available at proper times. This can be assisted by manipulating sites in order to attract a diversity of bird species which disperse later successional plant species.

# Dispersal of ornithochorous seeds from forest edges in central Florida

T. R. McClanahan¹ &amp; R. W. Wolfe²
¹Friends World College, East African Centre, P.O. Box 526, Machakos, Kenya

## Abstract

Dispersal of ornithochorous seeds from isolated forests in the phosphate mining region of central Florida, U.S.A., were studied for two seasons (July to November) to determine patterns of dispersal. Three separate studies included (1) dispersal directly from forest edges to early successional herbs; (2) standardized perches (2 m high post with a crossbeam); and (3) snags (dead trees, 11.3 ± 2.8 m high, 21.4 ± 23.3 stem branches). Perch availability was more important than distance in predicting seed types and quantities of bird-dispersed seeds. The greatest concentration of bird-dispersed seeds were found under standard perches (255 ± 249 seeds/m²/fall) followed by snags (147 ± 85 seeds/m²/fall) and early successional vegetation (3.0 ± 4.1 seeds/m²/fall). Seed quantities dispersed to snags were positively correlated with the number of stem branches on snags. Seeds beneath standard perches were significantly lighter and less diverse than those found beneath snags. This difference is attributed to the larger percentage of forest or later successional species found beneath snags (73%) as compared to the standard perches (15%). Perches and vegetative structural development should facilitate ecological succession by increasing the quantity, quality and diversity of seed deposition.

## Introduction

Seed dispersal plays an important role in the regeneration of disturbed sites (Clements, 1916; McQuilkin, 1940; McClanahan, 1986). Seed dispersal studies typically result in leptokurtic seed distribution from a source for wind (Jemison &amp; Korstian, 1944; Boyer, 1958; Roe, 1960; Randall, 1974), avian (Auclair &amp; Cottam, 1971; Smith, 1975) and bat-dispersed seeds (Fleming &amp; Heithaus, 1981). Yet, bird and bat-dispersed species are often influenced by perching site availability. Perches such as stones (Livingston, 1972), trees (McAtee, 1947; Glyphis et al., 1981; Fleming &amp; Heithaus, 1981; Debussche et al., 1982; Uhl et al., 1982; Guevara et al., 1986) and artificial structures (McDonnell &amp; Stiles, 1983; McDonnell, 1986) are important foci which attract avian dispersers and associated seeds. These foci facilitate seed deposition and act as high density and diversity centers in vegetative regeneration (Yarranton &amp; Morrison, 1974).

In order to understand and manage ecological succession it is important to determine factors which affect seed dispersal and deposition. When desired this information can be used to assist or enhance ecological succession. This study compares the effect of distance and vegetative structure on dispersal and its probable role in ecological succession.

108

# Methods

Three sites adjacent to two floodplains were chosen for dispersal studies (Whidden Creek (WC), 27°42′N, 81°51′W; Peace River (PRa) 27°51′N, 81°48′W; (PRb) 27°50′N, 81°48′W; Elevations 100–124 m) in Polk County, Florida, USA. This area was originally vegetated by south-eastern North American temperate pine, hardwood and wetland forests (Monk, 1965, 1966). Species of frugivorous birds are associated with these forests (Martin et al., 1951). In the last few decades large areas around these sites have been mined and the floodplains are part of a few isolated remnant wetland forests surrounded by many kilometers of early successional, agricultural and mining environments. Sites were recently mined (2–8 years ago), regraded and planted with seedlings. Sites were vegetated by early successional herbs, grasses and wetland plants. The Whidden Creek site was the most topographically complex and had more wetland areas than the other sites.

Three dispersal studies were undertaken concerning direct dispersal, dispersal to standardized perches, and dispersal to snags.

1. Dispersal directly from forest edges to early successional vegetation consisted of 6 replicate transects of 5 seed traps placed at 15 m intervals (Jemison &amp; Korstian, 1944; Boyer, 1958). Transects began 15 m within the forest and ended 45 m away from the forest edge. This study was undertaken at all three sites. Two adjacent to Peace River (PRa and PRb) and one adjacent to Whidden Creek (WCa). Two sites (PRa and WCa) were studied for two years and the third (PRb) for one year. Larger (&gt;2 mm) endozoochorous seeds were identified and counted.

2. Three replicate transects of four standardized perches and a control; perches were constructed of an upright 2.5 m beam with a 1 m crossbeam nailed to the top (McDonnell &amp; Stiles, 1983). Perches were placed at 30 m intervals away from the forest edges with a seed trap fastened underneath each perch. Control traps were placed at the same intervals without a perch. Site WCa was studied for two years and site PRb for one year.

3. Seed dispersal to snags was undertaken at Whidden Creek (Debussche et al., 1982). Snags are dead trees placed in the ground with a pole-driving machine at convenient locations throughout the site. Three seed traps were placed at 1, 2 and 3 m intervals from the snag. A control trap was placed at greater than 10 m from the snag. The height, distance from the forest edge and number of stem branches off the trunk were recorded. Three snags were studied for two years and an additional five for one year.

Seed traps in the above studies were constructed from plastic seedling trays (0.135 m²) with a fiberglass mesh bottom (to prevent seeds from falling through drainage holes) and a wire covering (2.5 cm mesh) to reduce seed predation. Seed traps were visited every 2 to 4 weeks during fall months (July to November, 1983 and 1984). Seed traps beneath snags were occasionally lost or removed during the study and therefore data were analyzed on a seeds per month basis to normalize for this bias. Seeds were counted and identified to the genus except for three closely related genera (Ampelopsis, Vitis and Parthenocissus) whose seeds are difficult to distinguish and therefore identified to the family Vitaceae.

In the analysis of the data seed numbers, genera, weights (n = 20–79 seeds/species) and diversity (Simpson, 1949; Routledge, 1979) at various locations were analyzed to determine patterns of dispersal. Further, a distinction was made between forest and non-forest seeds as this was a critical distinction in dispersal patterns. Seeds from the genera Magnolia, Persea, Prunus, Celtis, Nyssa, Callicarpa, Cornus and the family Vitaceae were considered forest species. These genera are trees associated with later successional hardwood and wetland forests in Florida (Monk, 1965, 1966; Veno, 1976). Within the family Vitaceae the genera Vitis is often an early successional vine but from germination studies we found that all germinated seeds tested were from the genus Parthenocissus which is associated with later successional forests. We therefore placed this family in the forest class. Seeds from the genera Phytolacca, Rhus and Lantana were classified as non-forest or early successional genera. The genus Myrica was also classified as a non-forest genera. Although variably found in

109

Florida forests as an understory shrub, in the phosphate mining region, it is an early successional shrub. These distinctions are based on vegetation studies and successional theory within this region (Monk, 1965, 1966; Veno, 1976; Schnoes &amp; Humphrey, 1980; Rushton, 1983).

Seed types dispersed to standard perches and snags show qualitative differences (Table 4). The majority of seeds dispersed to snags were forest species (73%) whereas the majority found beneath standard perches were non-forest species (85%). This difference in seed type is further reflected by differences in average seed weights from the two studies (Mann-Whitney U-test; $p &lt; 0.0001$). Seeds beneath the snags being heavier ($33.6 \pm 11.4 \, \mathrm{mg}$) than those at the standard perches ($10.2 \pm 3.3 \, \mathrm{mg}$). Additionally, seed diversity at the genus level was greater beneath snags (Simpson's Index, $D = 0.75$) than standard perches ($D = 0.53$).

Site comparisons indicate that the greatest number of seeds were dispersed to the Whidden Creek site for both the edge and standard perch study. Observation suggests that bird activity was related to these site differences.

## Discussion

Seed dispersal by birds at these sites, for distances studied, appears to be less dependent on distance to a seed source than availability and types of perching sites. Seed dispersal to early successional vegetation was sparse as determined by edge and control studies. This suggests that even short distances will restrict dispersal of bird-dispersed forest species to early successional sites. With the addition of perches, the quantity and quality of seeds changes and the distance factor is either negligible or of secondary importance for distances studied (Guevara et al., 1986). Additionally, site characteristics such as topographic complexity, availability of standing water and vegetational development may account for site differences (McDonnell &amp; Stiles, 1983).

Previous studies on seed dispersal have shown

111

distance to be a dominant factor in predicting seed quantities. Wind-dispersed species often show an exponential decay with distance from a seed source (Boyer, 1958; Roe, 1968) and bird-dispersed species show similar patterns within forests (Auclair &amp; Cottam, 1971; Smith, 1975). Ornithochorous seeds may display this pattern due to the relative uniformity of perching sites within forests as suggested by Kitching's (1971) model. Winged seeds are limited by available wind energy and seed aerodynamics and therefore less specific in determining site location. Bird dispersal, on the other hand, is more site specific and dependent on bird behavior. Distance may eventually become a factor for bird-dispersed seeds but only as a residual factor to site attractiveness in areas close to seed sources.

Differences in dispersal patterns between standard perches and snags indicate that smaller low diversity non-forest seeds were dispersed to standard perches and larger more diverse forest seeds to snags. This may be attributed to structural differences of height and stem branchings between standard perches and snags. Studies on bird distribution (MacArthur &amp; MacArthur, 1961; Erdelen, 1984) suggest that bird abundance and diversity is largely affected by height and structural development of vegetation rather than floristic nature. More dispersing individuals and species may be using snags compared to standard perches which may account for observed seed differences. Lower seed quantities captured beneath snags compared to perches does not contradict McDonnell's (1986) positive relationship between height and seed quantities but is a result of seed dilution around snags due to their greater height and circumference. The total amount of seeds attracted by snags should be greater than standard perches.

Results support the conclusion of Debussche et al. (1982) that vegetative structure attracts seeds and should therefore facilitate (Connell &amp; Slatyer, 1977) ecological succession. This would also support the relay floristics model (Egler, 1954) as some species may have a seed deposition time delay dependent on previous structural development. Ornithochorous dispersal dependent on vegetative development may be a form of diffuse coevolution (Herrera, 1982) between plants and dipersers to in-

sure increased survival probability through deposition in an appropriate environment or may simply be an artifact of bird behavior. Dispersal mechanisms should depend on evolutionary pressures, life histories and trade offs between different dispersal options. Regardless, succession should be enhanced if seeds are available at proper times. This can be assisted by manipulating sites in order to attract a diversity of bird species which disperse later successional plant species.
