species, and a lower number of specialist-species such as strict granivores, because tolerant species (often generalists) are less affected by habitat urbanization (Claro et al., 2020).

Birds may be the most effective dispersers because birds are not stopped by buildings and can spread seed farther than other dispersion agents, and also can carry seeds in directions that passive dispersal agents such as water cannot – such as uphill. Birds might also increase the functional composition of plants assemblage (Johnson et al., 2018). For our study region, Sorocaba is located in an ecotonal region (overlap of Atlantic Rain Forest and Cerrado, or Brazilian Savanna), which could provide a species-rich local bird diversity. However, Sorocaba is a city whose urbanization process started more than 400 years ago and the impact on the local fauna is evident.

Similar to many cities around with the world, the local urban avifauna is limited in terms of biodiversity, where the order Passeriformes is dominant and represented by species vectors of dispersion seeds as Pitangus sulfuratus L. (Great Kiskadee), Z. capensis Statius Muller (Rufous-collared Sparrow); T. rufiventris Vieillot (Rufous-bellied Thrush); Tangara sayaca L. (Sayaca Tanager), among others. Yet most species are of medium-low environmental sensitivity (Stotz et al., 1996), they have limited options for perching in the typical landscape of parks. In this context installing perches might be a good and cheap option for allowing their influence to spread widely within urban park patches.

# 4.2. Implications for possible ecological-based management of public gardens

Improving the vegetation in public green spaces might extend the urban landscape permeability to biodiversity by providing propagules for ecological restoration, shelter, and foods, which benefit the movement of individuals and therefore genes among patches of valuable ecological significance (Smith et al., 2018). Our results have implications regarding the advantages of the alternatives tested here concerning the management of public parques and other urban gardens and/or forests.

Planting saplings constitutes the most common approach to maintain an arborized public space. However, when we account for all steps of this process: production of seedlings in greenhouses, transport, planting, and complementary care (water and nutrient/fertilizer supply) and the high percentage of death of these seedlings after planting (Hilbert et al., 2019), we have concluded this is a costly activity and that the level of biodiversity attained is driven by the offer of convenience and facility of some tree species which are not always attractive for animals. In other words, the cost per unit of a tree is prohibitively high and the ecological feedback is usually low (Leal et al., 2008; Parker and Bryan, 2017).

One possible alternative to nucleation techniques is to increment the biodiversity in public gardens by applying the principle of the "no intervention, letting the nature takes its course", also known as the "do nothing" strategy (Hobbs and Cramer, 2008). However, when secondary ecological succession occurs passively in urban sites dominated by bare soils, such sites usually become dominated by exotic herbaceous species, i.e., plants habitually found as colonizers of open habitats and easily dispersed (Figueroa et al., 2020). In this way, the use of nucleation

techniques might boost and direct the trajectory of colonization and help local species toward a richer habitat in a short term.

Removing the grass in some parts of the public gardens and sowing seeds in these bare places is much less expensive than planting seedlings but we also must consider the high percentage of non-germination of seeds when the local environment is hostile in terms of microclimate and/or soil. Also, the seed bank to be sown in the patch being restored is highly dependent on the availability of seeds locally which itself varies according to the season of the year. Seeds of forest species usually constitute an expensive raw material for projects of forest restoration (Pedrini and Dixon, 2020; Shaw et al. 2020b).

Installing perches or transplanting soil from an adjacent forest patch could be an advantageous alternative which improves the structural connectivity in the densely urban locals and enrichment in terms of biodiversity (Bonança et al. 2017). Such alternatives might be separately or jointly implemented in a single unit that could be similar to our sampling units - circular-shaped and 1-m diameter.

The European Union defined four main goals for building resilient landscapes and cities: a. enhancing sustainable urbanization; b. restoring degraded ecosystems; c. developing climate change adaptation and mitigation strategies; and d. improving risk management and resilience (Lafortezza et al. 2018). We believe that the use of nucleation techniques in urban places has the potential to fulfill all such four goals in anyplace worldwide in a cost-effective way and ecologically suitable way.

In terms of improvement of the efficacy of the proposed techniques, we have some suggestions for future research:what if we put more litter in each SU? We believe that it may be a potential option to double or triple the amount of material, as (i) it would provide better soil coverage, (ii) possibly the seed bank would come richer, and (iii) it could also serve as an eventual shelter for small animals (invertebrates and vertebrates;as discussed earlier, urban places usually have limited biodiversity and the birds that are dispersers of big-sized seeds (seeds ≥0.5 cm-diameter) are comparatively scarce. So, as a strategy, we suggest managers cultivate and plant trees whose seeds are big (because those species will not have the opportunity to be dispersed by the urban dispersers) and allow native vectors to disperse seeds of plant species with small-size seeds. This could permit the restoration of the places in a more natural way.

Regarding costs, we believe that installing perches and keeping them installed for one year, and afterwards removing them and reinstalling in another place would be much cheaper than planting trees if we consider the whole productive chain that is behind the “production” of a tree sapling, considering all the steps. The perches were made out of materials readily available and can be easily replaced if damaged.

## Final remarks

The results of this research are informative since urban environments around the world share many characteristics in common. This is because they are planned to perform pre-established tasks to meet human needs and interests (Itani et al. 2020).The ecological responses after this kind of human development might be similar in other urban areas worldwide; as shown for instance, by the similarities between our results and those recorded by Ma (2016) in Canada. Increasing the potential of the public square to support biodiversity could allow such spaces to be stepping stones for dispersing animals, mainly the birds (for the case of perches). Further research might include measuring the attraction power of perches in these areas to determine if they are more important as a restoration technique or enrichment.

In parks and public gardens, the anthropic factors are very relevant to consider in project design. We noted that some perches were damaged by children playing on the structures during our study. Taller perches may be better because children will not use them as a playground and the perches also might achieve another foraging stratum of birds.

Considering that in tropical regions the number of species is highly correlated with the number of individuals, we suggest that if we create conditions that allow native species to repopulate degraded areas, local public spaces will get richer in terms of biodiversity as the attraction of many individuals will increase local species diversity. More technical reclamation, based on engineering and mechanical methods, might produce monotonous, uniform stands, where structural and functional biodiversity is diminished when compared to other methods of restoration (Bechara et al. 2016; Hobbs and Cramer, 2008). We argue that this proposed strategy has the potential to be successfully implemented in urban green spaces due to the simplicity of design and implementation, respect of the natural structure and functioning (it is a nature-based alternative), and with an affordable cost-benefit.

# Improving the biodiversity in urban green spaces: A nature based approach

Karen Regina Castelli a,\*, Alexandre Marco Silva a, John B. Dunning Jr b

$^{a}$ Department of Environmental Engineering, Institute of Sciences and Technology of Sorocaba, SP, Brazil
$^{b}$ Department of Forestry and Natural Resources, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA

# ARTICLEINFO

Keywords:

Management of urban green spaces

Nature-based solutions

Urban biodiversity

Ecological restoration

# ABSTRACT

Urban green spaces have the reputation of limited potential to support biodiversity and public places located in urbanized regions normally sustain low levels of biodiversity. But there is the potential to improve such characteristics using restoration techniques that are easily implemented and cost-effective. In this study we implemented a set of nature-based interventions aiming to boost the local biodiversity of three urban parks in Sorocaba, SP, Brazil. Our interventions were designed to induce local ecological succession. In each park, we prepared nine sampling units (SU) by removing grass in a circle of  $1\mathrm{m}$  diameter each. During the period of the study, three Sus in each park were kept uncovered (control treatment), three received -forest litter collected in an adjacent, well-conserved forest fragment (transposition treatment), and in the other three SUs, we installed a perch (perch treatment). For one year following establishment of the treatment, we monitored each SU biweekly and recorded the number and identity of seedlings that germinated in the circles. We recorded fluctuations in the number of seedlings in all experimental treatments of the three parks, indicating the variable rate of survivorship among species. We recorded a total of 30 different genera, most of which were herbaceous plants of species native to the region. In terms of the category of seed dispersion syndrome, most seedlings were from species dispersed by abiochoric vectors. Asteraceae was the most common botanical family. On one hand, if the experimental techniques we tested did not achieve the expected success in terms of the number of species of shrubs and trees, on the other hand, such interventions were not harmful in that they did not result in a predominance of exotic species. We conclude that this kind of approach has the potential to be successfully implemented in urban green spaces due to the simplicity of elaboration and implementation, respect of the natural structure and functioning (it is a nature-based alternative), and with an appropriate cost-benefit.

# 1. Introduction

Urban ecosystems usually contain limited biodiversity when compared with adjacent conserved areas (Acuto et al., 2018; Mata et al., 2020). Such reduction is caused by the installation of infrastructure and facilities that humans consider to be important for logistics, transport, and welfare. Such "hardscape" installation drastically alters the local environment because of the human demand for space; vegetation is suppressed due to the impermeability of the resulting ground development, among other modifications (Weishaguna et al., 2020). Reductions in biodiversity diminish the ability of ecosystems to capture essential resources, produce biomass, or sustain ecological processes such as nutrient cycling. These ecological losses have consequences for human welfare, weakening the benefits that humans might get from nature (Nilon et al., 2017).

"Softscape" development, including urban parks, public gardens, and

street afforestation, are alternatives to this hardening of the urban environment (Zamil Zakaria et al., 2017), allowing one to enrich the urban landscape in terms of biodiversity. Such areas promote the connection within the urban matrix through linkages such as railway networks or ravines acting as stepping stones or corridors (Gelmi-Candusso and Hamaiainen, 2019; Smith et al., 2018). The high costs of maintenance and simultaneously low, inexpressive pattern of biodiversity in these softscape spaces, however, constitute an issue for the managers and decision-makers.

Urban parks and public gardens are generally composed of grassy areas (often of non-native species) with few herbaceous species. Commonly used tree and/or shrub species support weak and limited biodiversity, especially if non-native, with less power to perform some expected ecosystem services (Aronson et al., 2017). Species used in urban landscaping usually are often plants grown in greenhouses in with a low survivorship after planting. Percentage of loss of seedlings after

planting it in the definitive place.

Therefore, increasing biodiversity in urban parks is a hard task. Incorporating new plant species is costly and normally complex in terms of the logistics of seedling production. Furthermore, seeds constitute a critical and restricted raw material for restoring biodiversity and ecological functions (Frischie et al., 2020). Therefore, new alternatives for restoring biodiversity into urban areas need to be tested, and if successful, implemented. An urban strategy for ecological enhancement should consider realistic, and flexible goals to preserve and improve urban biodiversity for both, short-term benefits and long-term sustainability (Johnson and Handel, 2016).

Some nature-based alternatives to increment local biodiversity are cost-effective, simple, and have recognized opportunities to providing both a better quality of life to urban inhabitants and reducing the ecological footprint of towns through biodiversity planning practices such as integrating nature into the urban fabric (Pierce et al., 2020). By "nature-based alternatives," we refer to techniques that depend on natural dispersal of seeds into restored areas, as opposed to anthropogenic planting and maintenance. Therefore, Nucleation techniques – where one creates a location, or nucleus, from which restoration can proceed – constitute a set of nature-based solutions that blend several methods. These nucleation techniques include: artificial perches to which seed dispersing organisms such as birds are attracted; artificial shelters for seed-dispersing animals; ground-covering shrub/herbaceous plants that can become nuclei for other plant species over time; seed bank and seed rain sod block patches in which ground is prepared to be receptive to wind-blown seeds; and the planting of native trees and bromeliads in dense patches (Bechara et al., 2016). Nucleation techniques are increasingly recommended as an innovative strategy to adequately and effectively restore degraded habitats (Hulvey et al., 2017; Shaw et al., 2020a), because of the multiple benefits that might be provided. These benefits include (a) maintaining/increasing plant community diversity; (b) maintaining/enhancing pollinator habitat; (c) developing migration corridors or stepping stones; and (d) mitigating erosion (Hulvey et al., 2017; Xing et al., 2017).

One of the elements that the nucleation technique might influence is the syndrome of seed dispersal. Generally, seed dispersion in the plants is divided into two major categories according to the vector of dispersal. Biochory consists of seeds dispersed by animals with several subcategories (e.g., endozoochory, epizooochory), while abiochory, or mechanical dispersion, consists seeds dispersed by abiotic vectors, such as wind or water. Abiochory is also divided into subcategories (e.g., anemochory, barochory, hydrochory, etc.). We project that selection of the kind of intervention and nucleation technique might favor animal species as seed dispersers.

Our hypothesis is that nature-based solutions of easy construction and low cost might enrich the low-quality biodiversity in urban public spaces. To test this idea, we conducted a set of onsite interventions to understand the ecological responses of urban green spaces in Sorocaba, SP, Brazil. Specifically, we aimed to investigate: (i) the plant genera that might emerge after the implantation of the techniques; (ii) if such interventions are valuable in terms of incrementing the local biodiversity; and (iii) the factors that influence the emergence and survivor of the seedlings.

# 2. Materials and methods

We used three urban parks located in Sorocaba. These parks were Municipal Natural Park "Chico Mendes" (hereafter, CM), Biodiversity Corridors Municipal Natural Park (BIO), and Botanical Garden of Sorocaba "Irmãos Villas-Boas" (BOT). In each park, we prepared nine plots that we called sampling units (henceafter: SU). We prepared each SU by removing the grass cover within a circle of  $1\mathrm{m}$  diameter. We then implemented the interventions as described in Table 1. In each park, we prepared each SU at least  $2\mathrm{m}$  away from each other to avoid possible interferences (Castelli, 2019).

Table 1 Descriptions of the experimental treatments considered for the study.

|  Location | Experimental treatment | Explanation  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  In each park (9 Sampling Units) | Control (3 SU) | We removed the grass cover the same as we prepared all SUs but in these sites we did not add any other treatment. We kept each circle (SU) free of waste during the period of the experiment, maintaining only the seedling that germinated there. We installed one perch in each SU. Each perch was 2.5 m tall and constructed out of eucalyptus. We fixed two sticks (2 cm diameter and 1 m long) perpendicularly to the eucalyptus so that the birds could land there. As in the control SUs, we kept the basal circular area (ground) of each perch free of waste. Here we aimed to verify if this structure was able to attract seeds dispersers and if the seeds deposited there were capable of germination and survival. In a close, pristine forested area, after we got authorization, we collected the amount of forest first layer soil (10 cm) existing in 1 m2. We executed this service in nine randomly chosen points. We stocked the amount of forest litter in separated plastic bags and the following day we spread the material in each one of three SU of each park. This part of the experiment aimed to observe if the seeds existing in the forest litter were capable of germination and survival, and also whether the resulting species differed from those at the perch sites.  |
|   | Perc (3 SU) |   |
|   | Transposition (3 SU) |   |

Plants yield fruits and seeds that are adapted by morphology and nutritional content for dispersal. On the other hand, animals have morphological, physiological, and behavioral adaptations for detecting and eating fruits (Howe, 2016). Hence, attracting seed dispersers and promoting their movement into a specific locale, is required to use biochory as a mechanism toward incrementing biodiversity. For our study, this locale is where the perches were installed. Using perches has been investigated previously as an alternative to boost the seed rain and to accelerate the ecological succession (Athie and Dias, 2016).

However, we know that just a part of seeds can be dispersed by animals, and another part can be dispersed by abiotic or mechanical vectors, as wind or by itself, named, respectively, anemochoric and authocoric syndromes (Hofhuis and Hay, 2017; Seale and Nakayama, 2020). For the taxa with mechanical syndromes, if we only tested the use of perches, it is likely that the resulting biodiversity would remain incomplete and still unsuitable. To address this question, we also consider the use of a seed bank collected in a pristine forest patch located close to the study sites.

For one year we monitored each SU every two weeks to assess germination and count and identify the resulting seedlings. Each plant specimen was identified to the genus level. It was not possible to identify seedlings to the species level because the seedlings did not have the reproductive characters (flowers or fruit) necessary for finer identification. (Laughlin and Clarkson, 2018).

As a criterion for calculating the seedling, to cataloging the living individuals, we considered the initial stem structure and the emergence and expansion of the first leaves (eophylum).

We organized data in electronical sheets and after we performed inferential analysis (Sperman's correlation) and multivariate analysis (NMDS).

# 3. Results

During the period of monitoring, we found fluctuations in the

K.R. Castelli et al.

Ecological Engineering 173 (2021) 106398

number of seedlings in all experimental treatments of the three parks (Fig. 1). The frequency of seedlings in each SU changed among the dates and the experimental treatments for all three parks. For instance, at BIO the highest number of seedlings were in the transposition SUs for  $50\%$  of the sampling dates; at BOT, the highest number of seedlings was in the perch SUs for  $90\%$  of the dates, and at CM, the highest number of seedlings were in the control for  $60\%$  of the occasions.

The peak number of seedlings found in the park BIO was 82 seedlings, in a transposition SU on the last sampling date. In BOT we verified a maximum of 27 seedlings in a transposition SU; this occurred on the 8th sampling date. For CM, we observed a maximum of 39 seedlings in the Control on the 7th sampling date.

We enumerated a total of 30 genera, across the three parks and all experimental treatments. Among the parks, we observed the highest number of genera at BOT (18), followed by CM (13) and BIO (12) (Fig. 2). Regardless of the park or the experimental treatment, the herbaceous species were always the most common genera (80% of all genera, Table 2). We recorded the emergence of tree seedlings only in CM. Regarding the syndrome of dispersion, about 70% of all genera were abiochoric.

Four genera occurred in all parks: Aeschynomene spp., Baccharis spp., Emilia spp., and Macroptilium spp. In general, the most common genus was Macroptilium spp. However, the most common genus in BOT was Bidens spp. and for CM, was Emilia spp.

The genus Baccharis spp. was not found in the Perch SUs and occurred in the Control SUs only in BIO but it occurred in the Transposition SUs in all parks. On the other hand, the following genera were only found in one single location: Achyrocline spp., Ageratum spp., Alternanthera spp., Amaranthus spp., Ambrosia spp., Anadenanthera spp., Croton spp., Desmodium spp., Galinsoga spp., Ipomoea spp., Leucaena spp., Melochia spp., Mimosa spp., Phyllanthus spp., Sida spp., and Solanum spp.

From the 30 genera identified, 9 were exotic and 21 native. Of those 9 exotic genera, 5 occurred exclusively in Control SUs, and only 1 has a biochoric dispersal syndrome. Using our data about the number of genera, we performed a cluster analysis. This analysis indicated that the

feedback of the transposition treatment was quite different from the other two treatments, while that among the parks, BOT and CM were more similar than was BIO (Fig. 3).

Using NMDS analysis, we compared the number of genera between treatments and sites (Fig. 4). Two SUs were outside the  $95\%$  confidence region: a Perch SU in CM and a Control SU in BOT. A BIO control SU was close to the  $95\%$  limit. These sites were the most dissimilar of the SUs.

Comparing the number of seedlings between the last and the first sampling dates, we observe that, for BIO, in the control experimental treatment the number of seedlings decreased in the control SUs, while they increased in the other two treatments. For BOT the number of seedlings increased in all treatments. In CM however, the number of seedlings decreased in control and transposition SUs but remained constant the perch SUs.

The number of genera varied among dates of monitoring, for each experimental treatment and for each park. (Fig. 2). The number of genera was not cumulative along the sampling dates, meaning that over time, some genera rose, and others disappeared, so that the survival rate was never  $100\%$  across all species. For BIO we observed the highest diversity at control and transposition SUs at 250 days after the start of the project. For BOT, we observed the highest number of genera approximately 270 days after initiation. In CM, we observed similar conditions as at BIO, highest diversity for control and transposition at 240 days. Using Spearman's correlation between number of genera and number of seedlings, we found that just Control areas in BIO presented no significant difference  $(p = 0,1)$ . For all the other treatments, values  $p = 0,05$ , showing a strong correlation in values.

We registered genera from eleven botanical families (Table 2). The predominant botanical family was the Asteraceae (40% of the total), followed by the Fabaceae (20%). In the Asteraceae 9 of the 15 genera were characterized by abiochoric seed dispersal while 6 genera had biochoric dispersal. For Fabaceae, 3 of 6 genera had abiochoric seed dispersal, while the other 3 genera were identified as having biochoric dispersal.

# 4. Discussion

# 4.1. The ecological significance of the results of the experiment

Urban ecosystems present transformed soil conditions and processes, as well as fast shifting and often hotter microclimates, generating numerous barriers to fostering native plants or animals, or even predicting which taxon might survive in such an environment (Ma, 2016; Gelmi-Candusso and Hämäläinen, 2019). For instance, this environmental variation can differentially influence the potential germination of seeds, depending on the intrinsic characteristics of the seeds themselves (Bareke, 2018).

Across our treatments, the majority of genera we found were of native, herbaceous species. In this regards our results differed from Figueroa et al. (2020) who found that passive secondary ecological succession in urban settings generally results in a predominance of herbaceous and exotic species. According to the literature, most of genera observed in our experiment were capable of germinating in a wide range of soil pH (usually from 3.0 to 11.0). Soils from the studied parks were neutral or slightly acid (Castelli, 2019). Hence, the soil acidity does not seem to be a problem.

Although Guo et al. (2018) affirm that nutrient accumulation in the soil is a determinant characteristic of plant spread under human influence, we propose that for our experiment the strong exposure to the sun and eventual lack of water seemed to be crucial factors that drove mortality among the seedlings, and nutrients, despite being important, presented a secondary importance.

Species showed a great power of germination and capacity of

survival in disturbed sites are are typified as ruderal species. Ruderal species are stress-tolerant and hold competitive advantages since they are favored in environments with high disturbance and intense stress. They usually have short life cycles with rapid growth and a large amount of energy devoted to seed production (Guo et al., 2018; Wheeler and Peet, 2016). Some of the genera found in our experiment fit this description, such as Macroptilium spp., Solanum spp., and Sphagneticola spp. They also produce a notable amount of biomass, and are therefore important in terms of soil cover and restoration, as well as attractors of pollinators.

Since ruderal species contribute to biodiversity enrichment in urban green spaces (Guo et al., 2018), it is noticeable in our study sites the increase in species richness in the SUs after the interventions. We propose that if the SUs were kept grass-covered, the diversity levels would have been dominated solely grasses or tree species planted by humans. The dominance of herbaceous genera in our study agrees Zhang et al. (2020) who found that "ruderal species with shorter life span and smaller size become more dominant in high urbanized areas.

We expected the number of genera of shrubs and trees would be higher, especially for the transposition and perch SUs. However, the data of soils and microclimate (Castelli, 2019) explain the outcomes of survival. The rate of germination of woody species is usually modest, limiting the cost-benefit, even for species for which there have been preparation practices of the seedbed to provide an optimal germination environment for seeds (e.g., soil plowing and/or scarification, and fertilization), and the mix of species (trees) are previously determined (Shaw et al., 2020b).

Regarding the perch treatment, we note that the bird community in the parks was dominated by species with the capacity of ingesting small-sized fruits and seeds, and those small-sized seeds have naturally low potential of germination. We know that birds constitute a crucial assemblage of seed dispersers and are an important factors in making a successful restoration using perches. In urban habitats, birds could be the best dispersers of most seeds (Lopez et al., 2018). Bird communities in urban settlements might include a higher number of generalist

species, and a lower number of specialist-species such as strict granivores, because tolerant species (often generalists) are less affected by habitat urbanization (Claro et al., 2020).

Birds may be the most effective dispersers because birds are not stopped by buildings and can spread seed farther than other dispersion agents, and also can carry seeds in directions that passive dispersal agents such as water cannot – such as uphill. Birds might also increase the functional composition of plants assemblage (Johnson et al., 2018). For our study region, Sorocaba is located in an ecotonal region (overlap of Atlantic Rain Forest and Cerrado, or Brazilian Savanna), which could provide a species-rich local bird diversity. However, Sorocaba is a city whose urbanization process started more than 400 years ago and the impact on the local fauna is evident.

Similar to many cities around with the world, the local urban avifauna is limited in terms of biodiversity, where the order Passeriformes is dominant and represented by species vectors of dispersion seeds as Pitangus sulfuratus L. (Great Kiskadee), Z. capensis Statius Muller (Rufous-collared Sparrow); T. rufiventris Vieillot (Rufous-bellied Thrush); Tangara sayaca L. (Sayaca Tanager), among others. Yet most species are of medium-low environmental sensitivity (Stotz et al., 1996), they have limited options for perching in the typical landscape of parks. In this context installing perches might be a good and cheap option for allowing their influence to spread widely within urban park patches.

# 4.2. Implications for possible ecological-based management of public gardens

Improving the vegetation in public green spaces might extend the urban landscape permeability to biodiversity by providing propagules for ecological restoration, shelter, and foods, which benefit the movement of individuals and therefore genes among patches of valuable ecological significance (Smith et al., 2018). Our results have implications regarding the advantages of the alternatives tested here concerning the management of public parques and other urban gardens and/or forests.

Planting saplings constitutes the most common approach to maintain an arborized public space. However, when we account for all steps of this process: production of seedlings in greenhouses, transport, planting, and complementary care (water and nutrient/fertilizer supply) and the high percentage of death of these seedlings after planting (Hilbert et al., 2019), we have concluded this is a costly activity and that the level of biodiversity attained is driven by the offer of convenience and facility of some tree species which are not always attractive for animals. In other words, the cost per unit of a tree is prohibitively high and the ecological feedback is usually low (Leal et al., 2008; Parker and Bryan, 2017).

One possible alternative to nucleation techniques is to increment the biodiversity in public gardens by applying the principle of the "no intervention, letting the nature takes its course", also known as the "do nothing" strategy (Hobbs and Cramer, 2008). However, when secondary ecological succession occurs passively in urban sites dominated by bare soils, such sites usually become dominated by exotic herbaceous species, i.e., plants habitually found as colonizers of open habitats and easily dispersed (Figueroa et al., 2020). In this way, the use of nucleation

techniques might boost and direct the trajectory of colonization and help local species toward a richer habitat in a short term.

Removing the grass in some parts of the public gardens and sowing seeds in these bare places is much less expensive than planting seedlings but we also must consider the high percentage of non-germination of seeds when the local environment is hostile in terms of microclimate and/or soil. Also, the seed bank to be sown in the patch being restored is highly dependent on the availability of seeds locally which itself varies according to the season of the year. Seeds of forest species usually constitute an expensive raw material for projects of forest restoration (Pedrini and Dixon, 2020; Shaw et al. 2020b).

Installing perches or transplanting soil from an adjacent forest patch could be an advantageous alternative which improves the structural connectivity in the densely urban locals and enrichment in terms of biodiversity (Bonança et al. 2017). Such alternatives might be separately or jointly implemented in a single unit that could be similar to our sampling units - circular-shaped and 1-m diameter.

The European Union defined four main goals for building resilient landscapes and cities: a. enhancing sustainable urbanization; b. restoring degraded ecosystems; c. developing climate change adaptation and mitigation strategies; and d. improving risk management and resilience (Lafortezza et al. 2018). We believe that the use of nucleation techniques in urban places has the potential to fulfill all such four goals in anyplace worldwide in a cost-effective way and ecologically suitable way.

In terms of improvement of the efficacy of the proposed techniques, we have some suggestions for future research:what if we put more litter in each SU? We believe that it may be a potential option to double or triple the amount of material, as (i) it would provide better soil coverage, (ii) possibly the seed bank would come richer, and (iii) it could also serve as an eventual shelter for small animals (invertebrates and vertebrates;as discussed earlier, urban places usually have limited biodiversity and the birds that are dispersers of big-sized seeds (seeds ≥0.5 cm-diameter) are comparatively scarce. So, as a strategy, we suggest managers cultivate and plant trees whose seeds are big (because those species will not have the opportunity to be dispersed by the urban dispersers) and allow native vectors to disperse seeds of plant species with small-size seeds. This could permit the restoration of the places in a more natural way.

Regarding costs, we believe that installing perches and keeping them installed for one year, and afterwards removing them and reinstalling in another place would be much cheaper than planting trees if we consider the whole productive chain that is behind the “production” of a tree sapling, considering all the steps. The perches were made out of materials readily available and can be easily replaced if damaged.

## Final remarks

The results of this research are informative since urban environments around the world share many characteristics in common. This is because they are planned to perform pre-established tasks to meet human needs and interests (Itani et al. 2020).The ecological responses after this kind of human development might be similar in other urban areas worldwide; as shown for instance, by the similarities between our results and those recorded by Ma (2016) in Canada. Increasing the potential of the public square to support biodiversity could allow such spaces to be stepping stones for dispersing animals, mainly the birds (for the case of perches). Further research might include measuring the attraction power of perches in these areas to determine if they are more important as a restoration technique or enrichment.

In parks and public gardens, the anthropic factors are very relevant to consider in project design. We noted that some perches were damaged by children playing on the structures during our study. Taller perches may be better because children will not use them as a playground and the perches also might achieve another foraging stratum of birds.

Considering that in tropical regions the number of species is highly correlated with the number of individuals, we suggest that if we create conditions that allow native species to repopulate degraded areas, local public spaces will get richer in terms of biodiversity as the attraction of many individuals will increase local species diversity. More technical reclamation, based on engineering and mechanical methods, might produce monotonous, uniform stands, where structural and functional biodiversity is diminished when compared to other methods of restoration (Bechara et al. 2016; Hobbs and Cramer, 2008). We argue that this proposed strategy has the potential to be successfully implemented in urban green spaces due to the simplicity of design and implementation, respect of the natural structure and functioning (it is a nature-based alternative), and with an affordable cost-benefit.

# Improving the biodiversity in urban green spaces: A nature based approach

Karen Regina Castelli a,\*, Alexandre Marco Silva a, John B. Dunning Jr b

$^{a}$ Department of Environmental Engineering, Institute of Sciences and Technology of Sorocaba, SP, Brazil
$^{b}$ Department of Forestry and Natural Resources, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA

# ARTICLEINFO

Keywords:

Management of urban green spaces

Nature-based solutions

Urban biodiversity

Ecological restoration

# ABSTRACT

Urban green spaces have the reputation of limited potential to support biodiversity and public places located in urbanized regions normally sustain low levels of biodiversity. But there is the potential to improve such characteristics using restoration techniques that are easily implemented and cost-effective. In this study we implemented a set of nature-based interventions aiming to boost the local biodiversity of three urban parks in Sorocaba, SP, Brazil. Our interventions were designed to induce local ecological succession. In each park, we prepared nine sampling units (SU) by removing grass in a circle of  $1\mathrm{m}$  diameter each. During the period of the study, three Sus in each park were kept uncovered (control treatment), three received -forest litter collected in an adjacent, well-conserved forest fragment (transposition treatment), and in the other three SUs, we installed a perch (perch treatment). For one year following establishment of the treatment, we monitored each SU biweekly and recorded the number and identity of seedlings that germinated in the circles. We recorded fluctuations in the number of seedlings in all experimental treatments of the three parks, indicating the variable rate of survivorship among species. We recorded a total of 30 different genera, most of which were herbaceous plants of species native to the region. In terms of the category of seed dispersion syndrome, most seedlings were from species dispersed by abiochoric vectors. Asteraceae was the most common botanical family. On one hand, if the experimental techniques we tested did not achieve the expected success in terms of the number of species of shrubs and trees, on the other hand, such interventions were not harmful in that they did not result in a predominance of exotic species. We conclude that this kind of approach has the potential to be successfully implemented in urban green spaces due to the simplicity of elaboration and implementation, respect of the natural structure and functioning (it is a nature-based alternative), and with an appropriate cost-benefit.

# 1. Introduction

Urban ecosystems usually contain limited biodiversity when compared with adjacent conserved areas (Acuto et al., 2018; Mata et al., 2020). Such reduction is caused by the installation of infrastructure and facilities that humans consider to be important for logistics, transport, and welfare. Such "hardscape" installation drastically alters the local environment because of the human demand for space; vegetation is suppressed due to the impermeability of the resulting ground development, among other modifications (Weishaguna et al., 2020). Reductions in biodiversity diminish the ability of ecosystems to capture essential resources, produce biomass, or sustain ecological processes such as nutrient cycling. These ecological losses have consequences for human welfare, weakening the benefits that humans might get from nature (Nilon et al., 2017).

"Softscape" development, including urban parks, public gardens, and

street afforestation, are alternatives to this hardening of the urban environment (Zamil Zakaria et al., 2017), allowing one to enrich the urban landscape in terms of biodiversity. Such areas promote the connection within the urban matrix through linkages such as railway networks or ravines acting as stepping stones or corridors (Gelmi-Candusso and Hamaiainen, 2019; Smith et al., 2018). The high costs of maintenance and simultaneously low, inexpressive pattern of biodiversity in these softscape spaces, however, constitute an issue for the managers and decision-makers.

Urban parks and public gardens are generally composed of grassy areas (often of non-native species) with few herbaceous species. Commonly used tree and/or shrub species support weak and limited biodiversity, especially if non-native, with less power to perform some expected ecosystem services (Aronson et al., 2017). Species used in urban landscaping usually are often plants grown in greenhouses in with a low survivorship after planting. Percentage of loss of seedlings after

planting it in the definitive place.

Therefore, increasing biodiversity in urban parks is a hard task. Incorporating new plant species is costly and normally complex in terms of the logistics of seedling production. Furthermore, seeds constitute a critical and restricted raw material for restoring biodiversity and ecological functions (Frischie et al., 2020). Therefore, new alternatives for restoring biodiversity into urban areas need to be tested, and if successful, implemented. An urban strategy for ecological enhancement should consider realistic, and flexible goals to preserve and improve urban biodiversity for both, short-term benefits and long-term sustainability (Johnson and Handel, 2016).

Some nature-based alternatives to increment local biodiversity are cost-effective, simple, and have recognized opportunities to providing both a better quality of life to urban inhabitants and reducing the ecological footprint of towns through biodiversity planning practices such as integrating nature into the urban fabric (Pierce et al., 2020). By "nature-based alternatives," we refer to techniques that depend on natural dispersal of seeds into restored areas, as opposed to anthropogenic planting and maintenance. Therefore, Nucleation techniques – where one creates a location, or nucleus, from which restoration can proceed – constitute a set of nature-based solutions that blend several methods. These nucleation techniques include: artificial perches to which seed dispersing organisms such as birds are attracted; artificial shelters for seed-dispersing animals; ground-covering shrub/herbaceous plants that can become nuclei for other plant species over time; seed bank and seed rain sod block patches in which ground is prepared to be receptive to wind-blown seeds; and the planting of native trees and bromeliads in dense patches (Bechara et al., 2016). Nucleation techniques are increasingly recommended as an innovative strategy to adequately and effectively restore degraded habitats (Hulvey et al., 2017; Shaw et al., 2020a), because of the multiple benefits that might be provided. These benefits include (a) maintaining/increasing plant community diversity; (b) maintaining/enhancing pollinator habitat; (c) developing migration corridors or stepping stones; and (d) mitigating erosion (Hulvey et al., 2017; Xing et al., 2017).

One of the elements that the nucleation technique might influence is the syndrome of seed dispersal. Generally, seed dispersion in the plants is divided into two major categories according to the vector of dispersal. Biochory consists of seeds dispersed by animals with several subcategories (e.g., endozoochory, epizooochory), while abiochory, or mechanical dispersion, consists seeds dispersed by abiotic vectors, such as wind or water. Abiochory is also divided into subcategories (e.g., anemochory, barochory, hydrochory, etc.). We project that selection of the kind of intervention and nucleation technique might favor animal species as seed dispersers.

Our hypothesis is that nature-based solutions of easy construction and low cost might enrich the low-quality biodiversity in urban public spaces. To test this idea, we conducted a set of onsite interventions to understand the ecological responses of urban green spaces in Sorocaba, SP, Brazil. Specifically, we aimed to investigate: (i) the plant genera that might emerge after the implantation of the techniques; (ii) if such interventions are valuable in terms of incrementing the local biodiversity; and (iii) the factors that influence the emergence and survivor of the seedlings.

# 2. Materials and methods

We used three urban parks located in Sorocaba. These parks were Municipal Natural Park "Chico Mendes" (hereafter, CM), Biodiversity Corridors Municipal Natural Park (BIO), and Botanical Garden of Sorocaba "Irmãos Villas-Boas" (BOT). In each park, we prepared nine plots that we called sampling units (henceafter: SU). We prepared each SU by removing the grass cover within a circle of  $1\mathrm{m}$  diameter. We then implemented the interventions as described in Table 1. In each park, we prepared each SU at least  $2\mathrm{m}$  away from each other to avoid possible interferences (Castelli, 2019).

Table 1 Descriptions of the experimental treatments considered for the study.

|  Location | Experimental treatment | Explanation  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  In each park (9 Sampling Units) | Control (3 SU) | We removed the grass cover the same as we prepared all SUs but in these sites we did not add any other treatment. We kept each circle (SU) free of waste during the period of the experiment, maintaining only the seedling that germinated there. We installed one perch in each SU. Each perch was 2.5 m tall and constructed out of eucalyptus. We fixed two sticks (2 cm diameter and 1 m long) perpendicularly to the eucalyptus so that the birds could land there. As in the control SUs, we kept the basal circular area (ground) of each perch free of waste. Here we aimed to verify if this structure was able to attract seeds dispersers and if the seeds deposited there were capable of germination and survival. In a close, pristine forested area, after we got authorization, we collected the amount of forest first layer soil (10 cm) existing in 1 m2. We executed this service in nine randomly chosen points. We stocked the amount of forest litter in separated plastic bags and the following day we spread the material in each one of three SU of each park. This part of the experiment aimed to observe if the seeds existing in the forest litter were capable of germination and survival, and also whether the resulting species differed from those at the perch sites.  |
|   | Perc (3 SU) |   |
|   | Transposition (3 SU) |   |

Plants yield fruits and seeds that are adapted by morphology and nutritional content for dispersal. On the other hand, animals have morphological, physiological, and behavioral adaptations for detecting and eating fruits (Howe, 2016). Hence, attracting seed dispersers and promoting their movement into a specific locale, is required to use biochory as a mechanism toward incrementing biodiversity. For our study, this locale is where the perches were installed. Using perches has been investigated previously as an alternative to boost the seed rain and to accelerate the ecological succession (Athie and Dias, 2016).

However, we know that just a part of seeds can be dispersed by animals, and another part can be dispersed by abiotic or mechanical vectors, as wind or by itself, named, respectively, anemochoric and authocoric syndromes (Hofhuis and Hay, 2017; Seale and Nakayama, 2020). For the taxa with mechanical syndromes, if we only tested the use of perches, it is likely that the resulting biodiversity would remain incomplete and still unsuitable. To address this question, we also consider the use of a seed bank collected in a pristine forest patch located close to the study sites.

For one year we monitored each SU every two weeks to assess germination and count and identify the resulting seedlings. Each plant specimen was identified to the genus level. It was not possible to identify seedlings to the species level because the seedlings did not have the reproductive characters (flowers or fruit) necessary for finer identification. (Laughlin and Clarkson, 2018).

As a criterion for calculating the seedling, to cataloging the living individuals, we considered the initial stem structure and the emergence and expansion of the first leaves (eophylum).

We organized data in electronical sheets and after we performed inferential analysis (Sperman's correlation) and multivariate analysis (NMDS).

# 3. Results

During the period of monitoring, we found fluctuations in the

K.R. Castelli et al.

number of seedlings in all experimental treatments of the three parks (Fig. 1). The frequency of seedlings in each SU changed among the dates and the experimental treatments for all three parks. For instance, at BIO the highest number of seedlings were in the transposition SUs for  $50\%$  of the sampling dates; at BOT, the highest number of seedlings was in the perch SUs for  $90\%$  of the dates, and at CM, the highest number of seedlings were in the control for  $60\%$  of the occasions.

The peak number of seedlings found in the park BIO was 82 seedlings, in a transposition SU on the last sampling date. In BOT we verified a maximum of 27 seedlings in a transposition SU; this occurred on the 8th sampling date. For CM, we observed a maximum of 39 seedlings in the Control on the 7th sampling date.

We enumerated a total of 30 genera, across the three parks and all experimental treatments. Among the parks, we observed the highest number of genera at BOT (18), followed by CM (13) and BIO (12) (Fig. 2). Regardless of the park or the experimental treatment, the herbaceous species were always the most common genera (80% of all genera, Table 2). We recorded the emergence of tree seedlings only in CM. Regarding the syndrome of dispersion, about 70% of all genera were abiochoric.

Four genera occurred in all parks: Aeschynomene spp., Baccharis spp., Emilia spp., and Macroptilium spp. In general, the most common genus was Macroptilium spp. However, the most common genus in BOT was Bidens spp. and for CM, was Emilia spp.

The genus Baccharis spp. was not found in the Perch SUs and occurred in the Control SUs only in BIO but it occurred in the Transposition SUs in all parks. On the other hand, the following genera were only found in one single location: Achyrocline spp., Ageratum spp., Alternanthera spp., Amaranthus spp., Ambrosia spp., Anadenanthera spp., Croton spp., Desmodium spp., Galinsoga spp., Ipomoea spp., Leucaena spp., Melochia spp., Mimosa spp., Phyllanthus spp., Sida spp., and Solanum spp.

From the 30 genera identified, 9 were exotic and 21 native. Of those 9 exotic genera, 5 occurred exclusively in Control SUs, and only 1 has a biochoric dispersal syndrome. Using our data about the number of genera, we performed a cluster analysis. This analysis indicated that the

feedback of the transposition treatment was quite different from the other two treatments, while that among the parks, BOT and CM were more similar than was BIO (Fig. 3).

Using NMDS analysis, we compared the number of genera between treatments and sites (Fig. 4). Two SUs were outside the  $95\%$  confidence region: a Perch SU in CM and a Control SU in BOT. A BIO control SU was close to the  $95\%$  limit. These sites were the most dissimilar of the SUs.

Comparing the number of seedlings between the last and the first sampling dates, we observe that, for BIO, in the control experimental treatment the number of seedlings decreased in the control SUs, while they increased in the other two treatments. For BOT the number of seedlings increased in all treatments. In CM however, the number of seedlings decreased in control and transposition SUs but remained constant the perch SUs.

The number of genera varied among dates of monitoring, for each experimental treatment and for each park. (Fig. 2). The number of genera was not cumulative along the sampling dates, meaning that over time, some genera rose, and others disappeared, so that the survival rate was never  $100\%$  across all species. For BIO we observed the highest diversity at control and transposition SUs at 250 days after the start of the project. For BOT, we observed the highest number of genera approximately 270 days after initiation. In CM, we observed similar conditions as at BIO, highest diversity for control and transposition at 240 days. Using Spearman's correlation between number of genera and number of seedlings, we found that just Control areas in BIO presented no significant difference  $(p = 0,1)$ . For all the other treatments, values  $p = 0,05$ , showing a strong correlation in values.

We registered genera from eleven botanical families (Table 2). The predominant botanical family was the Asteraceae (40% of the total), followed by the Fabaceae (20%). In the Asteraceae 9 of the 15 genera were characterized by abiochoric seed dispersal while 6 genera had biochoric dispersal. For Fabaceae, 3 of 6 genera had abiochoric seed dispersal, while the other 3 genera were identified as having biochoric dispersal.

# 4. Discussion

# 4.1. The ecological significance of the results of the experiment

Urban ecosystems present transformed soil conditions and processes, as well as fast shifting and often hotter microclimates, generating numerous barriers to fostering native plants or animals, or even predicting which taxon might survive in such an environment (Ma, 2016; Gelmi-Candusso and Hämäläinen, 2019). For instance, this environmental variation can differentially influence the potential germination of seeds, depending on the intrinsic characteristics of the seeds themselves (Bareke, 2018).

Across our treatments, the majority of genera we found were of native, herbaceous species. In this regards our results differed from Figueroa et al. (2020) who found that passive secondary ecological succession in urban settings generally results in a predominance of herbaceous and exotic species. According to the literature, most of genera observed in our experiment were capable of germinating in a wide range of soil pH (usually from 3.0 to 11.0). Soils from the studied parks were neutral or slightly acid (Castelli, 2019). Hence, the soil acidity does not seem to be a problem.

Although Guo et al. (2018) affirm that nutrient accumulation in the soil is a determinant characteristic of plant spread under human influence, we propose that for our experiment the strong exposure to the sun and eventual lack of water seemed to be crucial factors that drove mortality among the seedlings, and nutrients, despite being important, presented a secondary importance.

Species showed a great power of germination and capacity of

survival in disturbed sites are are typified as ruderal species. Ruderal species are stress-tolerant and hold competitive advantages since they are favored in environments with high disturbance and intense stress. They usually have short life cycles with rapid growth and a large amount of energy devoted to seed production (Guo et al., 2018; Wheeler and Peet, 2016). Some of the genera found in our experiment fit this description, such as Macroptilium spp., Solanum spp., and Sphagneticola spp. They also produce a notable amount of biomass, and are therefore important in terms of soil cover and restoration, as well as attractors of pollinators.

Since ruderal species contribute to biodiversity enrichment in urban green spaces (Guo et al., 2018), it is noticeable in our study sites the increase in species richness in the SUs after the interventions. We propose that if the SUs were kept grass-covered, the diversity levels would have been dominated solely grasses or tree species planted by humans. The dominance of herbaceous genera in our study agrees Zhang et al. (2020) who found that "ruderal species with shorter life span and smaller size become more dominant in high urbanized areas.

We expected the number of genera of shrubs and trees would be higher, especially for the transposition and perch SUs. However, the data of soils and microclimate (Castelli, 2019) explain the outcomes of survival. The rate of germination of woody species is usually modest, limiting the cost-benefit, even for species for which there have been preparation practices of the seedbed to provide an optimal germination environment for seeds (e.g., soil plowing and/or scarification, and fertilization), and the mix of species (trees) are previously determined (Shaw et al., 2020b).

Regarding the perch treatment, we note that the bird community in the parks was dominated by species with the capacity of ingesting small-sized fruits and seeds, and those small-sized seeds have naturally low potential of germination. We know that birds constitute a crucial assemblage of seed dispersers and are an important factors in making a successful restoration using perches. In urban habitats, birds could be the best dispersers of most seeds (Lopez et al., 2018). Bird communities in urban settlements might include a higher number of generalist

species, and a lower number of specialist-species such as strict granivores, because tolerant species (often generalists) are less affected by habitat urbanization (Claro et al., 2020).

Birds may be the most effective dispersers because birds are not stopped by buildings and can spread seed farther than other dispersion agents, and also can carry seeds in directions that passive dispersal agents such as water cannot – such as uphill. Birds might also increase the functional composition of plants assemblage (Johnson et al., 2018). For our study region, Sorocaba is located in an ecotonal region (overlap of Atlantic Rain Forest and Cerrado, or Brazilian Savanna), which could provide a species-rich local bird diversity. However, Sorocaba is a city whose urbanization process started more than 400 years ago and the impact on the local fauna is evident.

Similar to many cities around with the world, the local urban avifauna is limited in terms of biodiversity, where the order Passeriformes is dominant and represented by species vectors of dispersion seeds as Pitangus sulfuratus L. (Great Kiskadee), Z. capensis Statius Muller (Rufous-collared Sparrow); T. rufiventris Vieillot (Rufous-bellied Thrush); Tangara sayaca L. (Sayaca Tanager), among others. Yet most species are of medium-low environmental sensitivity (Stotz et al., 1996), they have limited options for perching in the typical landscape of parks. In this context installing perches might be a good and cheap option for allowing their influence to spread widely within urban park patches.

# 4.2. Implications for possible ecological-based management of public gardens

Improving the vegetation in public green spaces might extend the urban landscape permeability to biodiversity by providing propagules for ecological restoration, shelter, and foods, which benefit the movement of individuals and therefore genes among patches of valuable ecological significance (Smith et al., 2018). Our results have implications regarding the advantages of the alternatives tested here concerning the management of public parques and other urban gardens and/or forests.

Planting saplings constitutes the most common approach to maintain an arborized public space. However, when we account for all steps of this process: production of seedlings in greenhouses, transport, planting, and complementary care (water and nutrient/fertilizer supply) and the high percentage of death of these seedlings after planting (Hilbert et al., 2019), we have concluded this is a costly activity and that the level of biodiversity attained is driven by the offer of convenience and facility of some tree species which are not always attractive for animals. In other words, the cost per unit of a tree is prohibitively high and the ecological feedback is usually low (Leal et al., 2008; Parker and Bryan, 2017).

One possible alternative to nucleation techniques is to increment the biodiversity in public gardens by applying the principle of the "no intervention, letting the nature takes its course", also known as the "do nothing" strategy (Hobbs and Cramer, 2008). However, when secondary ecological succession occurs passively in urban sites dominated by bare soils, such sites usually become dominated by exotic herbaceous species, i.e., plants habitually found as colonizers of open habitats and easily dispersed (Figueroa et al., 2020). In this way, the use of nucleation

techniques might boost and direct the trajectory of colonization and help local species toward a richer habitat in a short term.

Removing the grass in some parts of the public gardens and sowing seeds in these bare places is much less expensive than planting seedlings but we also must consider the high percentage of non-germination of seeds when the local environment is hostile in terms of microclimate and/or soil. Also, the seed bank to be sown in the patch being restored is highly dependent on the availability of seeds locally which itself varies according to the season of the year. Seeds of forest species usually constitute an expensive raw material for projects of forest restoration (Pedrini and Dixon, 2020; Shaw et al. 2020b).

Installing perches or transplanting soil from an adjacent forest patch could be an advantageous alternative which improves the structural connectivity in the densely urban locals and enrichment in terms of biodiversity (Bonança et al. 2017). Such alternatives might be separately or jointly implemented in a single unit that could be similar to our sampling units - circular-shaped and 1-m diameter.

The European Union defined four main goals for building resilient landscapes and cities: a. enhancing sustainable urbanization; b. restoring degraded ecosystems; c. developing climate change adaptation and mitigation strategies; and d. improving risk management and resilience (Lafortezza et al. 2018). We believe that the use of nucleation techniques in urban places has the potential to fulfill all such four goals in anyplace worldwide in a cost-effective way and ecologically suitable way.

In terms of improvement of the efficacy of the proposed techniques, we have some suggestions for future research:what if we put more litter in each SU? We believe that it may be a potential option to double or triple the amount of material, as (i) it would provide better soil coverage, (ii) possibly the seed bank would come richer, and (iii) it could also serve as an eventual shelter for small animals (invertebrates and vertebrates;as discussed earlier, urban places usually have limited biodiversity and the birds that are dispersers of big-sized seeds (seeds ≥0.5 cm-diameter) are comparatively scarce. So, as a strategy, we suggest managers cultivate and plant trees whose seeds are big (because those species will not have the opportunity to be dispersed by the urban dispersers) and allow native vectors to disperse seeds of plant species with small-size seeds. This could permit the restoration of the places in a more natural way.

Regarding costs, we believe that installing perches and keeping them installed for one year, and afterwards removing them and reinstalling in another place would be much cheaper than planting trees if we consider the whole productive chain that is behind the “production” of a tree sapling, considering all the steps. The perches were made out of materials readily available and can be easily replaced if damaged.

## Final remarks

The results of this research are informative since urban environments around the world share many characteristics in common. This is because they are planned to perform pre-established tasks to meet human needs and interests (Itani et al. 2020).The ecological responses after this kind of human development might be similar in other urban areas worldwide; as shown for instance, by the similarities between our results and those recorded by Ma (2016) in Canada. Increasing the potential of the public square to support biodiversity could allow such spaces to be stepping stones for dispersing animals, mainly the birds (for the case of perches). Further research might include measuring the attraction power of perches in these areas to determine if they are more important as a restoration technique or enrichment.

In parks and public gardens, the anthropic factors are very relevant to consider in project design. We noted that some perches were damaged by children playing on the structures during our study. Taller perches may be better because children will not use them as a playground and the perches also might achieve another foraging stratum of birds.

Considering that in tropical regions the number of species is highly correlated with the number of individuals, we suggest that if we create conditions that allow native species to repopulate degraded areas, local public spaces will get richer in terms of biodiversity as the attraction of many individuals will increase local species diversity. More technical reclamation, based on engineering and mechanical methods, might produce monotonous, uniform stands, where structural and functional biodiversity is diminished when compared to other methods of restoration (Bechara et al. 2016; Hobbs and Cramer, 2008). We argue that this proposed strategy has the potential to be successfully implemented in urban green spaces due to the simplicity of design and implementation, respect of the natural structure and functioning (it is a nature-based alternative), and with an affordable cost-benefit.

# Improving the biodiversity in urban green spaces: A nature based approach

Karen Regina Castelli a,\*, Alexandre Marco Silva a, John B. Dunning Jr b

$^{a}$ Department of Environmental Engineering, Institute of Sciences and Technology of Sorocaba, SP, Brazil
$^{b}$ Department of Forestry and Natural Resources, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA

# ARTICLEINFO

Keywords:

Management of urban green spaces

Nature-based solutions

Urban biodiversity

Ecological restoration

# ABSTRACT

Urban green spaces have the reputation of limited potential to support biodiversity and public places located in urbanized regions normally sustain low levels of biodiversity. But there is the potential to improve such characteristics using restoration techniques that are easily implemented and cost-effective. In this study we implemented a set of nature-based interventions aiming to boost the local biodiversity of three urban parks in Sorocaba, SP, Brazil. Our interventions were designed to induce local ecological succession. In each park, we prepared nine sampling units (SU) by removing grass in a circle of  $1\mathrm{m}$  diameter each. During the period of the study, three Sus in each park were kept uncovered (control treatment), three received -forest litter collected in an adjacent, well-conserved forest fragment (transposition treatment), and in the other three SUs, we installed a perch (perch treatment). For one year following establishment of the treatment, we monitored each SU biweekly and recorded the number and identity of seedlings that germinated in the circles. We recorded fluctuations in the number of seedlings in all experimental treatments of the three parks, indicating the variable rate of survivorship among species. We recorded a total of 30 different genera, most of which were herbaceous plants of species native to the region. In terms of the category of seed dispersion syndrome, most seedlings were from species dispersed by abiochoric vectors. Asteraceae was the most common botanical family. On one hand, if the experimental techniques we tested did not achieve the expected success in terms of the number of species of shrubs and trees, on the other hand, such interventions were not harmful in that they did not result in a predominance of exotic species. We conclude that this kind of approach has the potential to be successfully implemented in urban green spaces due to the simplicity of elaboration and implementation, respect of the natural structure and functioning (it is a nature-based alternative), and with an appropriate cost-benefit.

# 1. Introduction

Urban ecosystems usually contain limited biodiversity when compared with adjacent conserved areas (Acuto et al., 2018; Mata et al., 2020). Such reduction is caused by the installation of infrastructure and facilities that humans consider to be important for logistics, transport, and welfare. Such "hardscape" installation drastically alters the local environment because of the human demand for space; vegetation is suppressed due to the impermeability of the resulting ground development, among other modifications (Weishaguna et al., 2020). Reductions in biodiversity diminish the ability of ecosystems to capture essential resources, produce biomass, or sustain ecological processes such as nutrient cycling. These ecological losses have consequences for human welfare, weakening the benefits that humans might get from nature (Nilon et al., 2017).

"Softscape" development, including urban parks, public gardens, and

street afforestation, are alternatives to this hardening of the urban environment (Zamil Zakaria et al., 2017), allowing one to enrich the urban landscape in terms of biodiversity. Such areas promote the connection within the urban matrix through linkages such as railway networks or ravines acting as stepping stones or corridors (Gelmi-Candusso and Hamaiainen, 2019; Smith et al., 2018). The high costs of maintenance and simultaneously low, inexpressive pattern of biodiversity in these softscape spaces, however, constitute an issue for the managers and decision-makers.

Urban parks and public gardens are generally composed of grassy areas (often of non-native species) with few herbaceous species. Commonly used tree and/or shrub species support weak and limited biodiversity, especially if non-native, with less power to perform some expected ecosystem services (Aronson et al., 2017). Species used in urban landscaping usually are often plants grown in greenhouses in with a low survivorship after planting. Percentage of loss of seedlings after

planting it in the definitive place.

Therefore, increasing biodiversity in urban parks is a hard task. Incorporating new plant species is costly and normally complex in terms of the logistics of seedling production. Furthermore, seeds constitute a critical and restricted raw material for restoring biodiversity and ecological functions (Frischie et al., 2020). Therefore, new alternatives for restoring biodiversity into urban areas need to be tested, and if successful, implemented. An urban strategy for ecological enhancement should consider realistic, and flexible goals to preserve and improve urban biodiversity for both, short-term benefits and long-term sustainability (Johnson and Handel, 2016).

Some nature-based alternatives to increment local biodiversity are cost-effective, simple, and have recognized opportunities to providing both a better quality of life to urban inhabitants and reducing the ecological footprint of towns through biodiversity planning practices such as integrating nature into the urban fabric (Pierce et al., 2020). By "nature-based alternatives," we refer to techniques that depend on natural dispersal of seeds into restored areas, as opposed to anthropogenic planting and maintenance. Therefore, Nucleation techniques – where one creates a location, or nucleus, from which restoration can proceed – constitute a set of nature-based solutions that blend several methods. These nucleation techniques include: artificial perches to which seed dispersing organisms such as birds are attracted; artificial shelters for seed-dispersing animals; ground-covering shrub/herbaceous plants that can become nuclei for other plant species over time; seed bank and seed rain sod block patches in which ground is prepared to be receptive to wind-blown seeds; and the planting of native trees and bromeliads in dense patches (Bechara et al., 2016). Nucleation techniques are increasingly recommended as an innovative strategy to adequately and effectively restore degraded habitats (Hulvey et al., 2017; Shaw et al., 2020a), because of the multiple benefits that might be provided. These benefits include (a) maintaining/increasing plant community diversity; (b) maintaining/enhancing pollinator habitat; (c) developing migration corridors or stepping stones; and (d) mitigating erosion (Hulvey et al., 2017; Xing et al., 2017).

One of the elements that the nucleation technique might influence is the syndrome of seed dispersal. Generally, seed dispersion in the plants is divided into two major categories according to the vector of dispersal. Biochory consists of seeds dispersed by animals with several subcategories (e.g., endozoochory, epizooochory), while abiochory, or mechanical dispersion, consists seeds dispersed by abiotic vectors, such as wind or water. Abiochory is also divided into subcategories (e.g., anemochory, barochory, hydrochory, etc.). We project that selection of the kind of intervention and nucleation technique might favor animal species as seed dispersers.

Our hypothesis is that nature-based solutions of easy construction and low cost might enrich the low-quality biodiversity in urban public spaces. To test this idea, we conducted a set of onsite interventions to understand the ecological responses of urban green spaces in Sorocaba, SP, Brazil. Specifically, we aimed to investigate: (i) the plant genera that might emerge after the implantation of the techniques; (ii) if such interventions are valuable in terms of incrementing the local biodiversity; and (iii) the factors that influence the emergence and survivor of the seedlings.

# 2. Materials and methods

We used three urban parks located in Sorocaba. These parks were Municipal Natural Park "Chico Mendes" (hereafter, CM), Biodiversity Corridors Municipal Natural Park (BIO), and Botanical Garden of Sorocaba "Irmãos Villas-Boas" (BOT). In each park, we prepared nine plots that we called sampling units (henceafter: SU). We prepared each SU by removing the grass cover within a circle of  $1\mathrm{m}$  diameter. We then implemented the interventions as described in Table 1. In each park, we prepared each SU at least  $2\mathrm{m}$  away from each other to avoid possible interferences (Castelli, 2019).

Table 1 Descriptions of the experimental treatments considered for the study.

|  Location | Experimental treatment | Explanation  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  In each park (9 Sampling Units) | Control (3 SU) | We removed the grass cover the same as we prepared all SUs but in these sites we did not add any other treatment. We kept each circle (SU) free of waste during the period of the experiment, maintaining only the seedling that germinated there. We installed one perch in each SU. Each perch was 2.5 m tall and constructed out of eucalyptus. We fixed two sticks (2 cm diameter and 1 m long) perpendicularly to the eucalyptus so that the birds could land there. As in the control SUs, we kept the basal circular area (ground) of each perch free of waste. Here we aimed to verify if this structure was able to attract seeds dispersers and if the seeds deposited there were capable of germination and survival. In a close, pristine forested area, after we got authorization, we collected the amount of forest first layer soil (10 cm) existing in 1 m2. We executed this service in nine randomly chosen points. We stocked the amount of forest litter in separated plastic bags and the following day we spread the material in each one of three SU of each park. This part of the experiment aimed to observe if the seeds existing in the forest litter were capable of germination and survival, and also whether the resulting species differed from those at the perch sites.  |
|   | Perc (3 SU) |   |
|   | Transposition (3 SU) |   |

Plants yield fruits and seeds that are adapted by morphology and nutritional content for dispersal. On the other hand, animals have morphological, physiological, and behavioral adaptations for detecting and eating fruits (Howe, 2016). Hence, attracting seed dispersers and promoting their movement into a specific locale, is required to use biochory as a mechanism toward incrementing biodiversity. For our study, this locale is where the perches were installed. Using perches has been investigated previously as an alternative to boost the seed rain and to accelerate the ecological succession (Athie and Dias, 2016).

However, we know that just a part of seeds can be dispersed by animals, and another part can be dispersed by abiotic or mechanical vectors, as wind or by itself, named, respectively, anemochoric and authocoric syndromes (Hofhuis and Hay, 2017; Seale and Nakayama, 2020). For the taxa with mechanical syndromes, if we only tested the use of perches, it is likely that the resulting biodiversity would remain incomplete and still unsuitable. To address this question, we also consider the use of a seed bank collected in a pristine forest patch located close to the study sites.

For one year we monitored each SU every two weeks to assess germination and count and identify the resulting seedlings. Each plant specimen was identified to the genus level. It was not possible to identify seedlings to the species level because the seedlings did not have the reproductive characters (flowers or fruit) necessary for finer identification. (Laughlin and Clarkson, 2018).

As a criterion for calculating the seedling, to cataloging the living individuals, we considered the initial stem structure and the emergence and expansion of the first leaves (eophylum).

We organized data in electronical sheets and after we performed inferential analysis (Sperman's correlation) and multivariate analysis (NMDS).

# 3. Results

During the period of monitoring, we found fluctuations in the
