reaching an average height of 15 m (Lovett et al., 2006) but can grow up to 30 m (Meunier et al., 2010). The rapid growth rate of N. macrocalyx has been reported by Bussmann (1999) who examined the growth of 12 East African forest tree species in Mount Kenya. The study found that the length increment of N. macrocalyx branches (39.1 cm/year) was approximately 75% higher than that of primary forest species included in the study. The diameter at breast height (dbh) increment of 1-5 year old trees was 2.9 cm/year, being highest among all studied trees, the dbh increment of 20-50 year old trees was 1.92 cm/year and for trees older than 50 years, 1.48 cm/year. N. macrocalyx has a short trunk and a wide crown with large leaves. The fruit is a trilobed 1.5 × 1.0 cm capsule bearing three ellipsoid seeds (7 × 5 mm) (Meunier et al., 2010), which are dispersed by animals (Chapman et al., 1999). N. macrocalyx trees in KNP have been found to flower and fruit by the age of 6 years (authors' personal observation).

## 2.3. Experimental design and data collection

Our experiment was established in plantation clear-cuts that had not been colonized by trees. A gap was defined as an open area restricted by a boundary of woody species at least 2 m in height. Where forest boundary was difficult to define, individual large trees or dense woody shrubs were used as boundaries. Seventeen gaps were selected using random stratified sampling of different sized gaps. Gap size was measured by measuring the distance from the gap center to the forest edge toward each cardinal point. The average gap size was 436 m² (SD ± 279.4 and ranged from 113 to 1115 m²).

N. macrocalyx seeds were collected during April-May 2006 from KNP and adjacent areas from multiple trees within 10 km of the park to ensure genetic variation. Seeds were randomly divided into two groups; the first group was dried and stored, and the second group was planted into a grassland soil nursery. The seeds and nursery seedlings were planted in the selected forest gaps in early

September 2006, when the mean height of the seedlings was 34 cm (SD ± 11.6 and ranged from 10.2 to 61.0 cm). Eight randomly selected plots were established in each gap; four with transplanted seedlings (4 seedlings/plot) and four with seeds (10 seeds/plot, lightly covered with soil). The seedlings were planted in a square plot with 2 m spacing. For each seedling, an area of 50 × 50 cm was first cleared from vegetation and the seedlings were planted in the middle of these cleared areas. For the seeds, an area of 50 × 50 cm was cleared from vegetation on each plot. Two parallel lines with 10 cm spacing were established and in each line, five seeds were sown with 5 cm spacing. All seeds were sown during the same day. At the time of planting, the gaps were dominated by a dense tangle of herbaceous plants, shrubs and grasses, such as L. camara and P. purpurea.

The survival and growth of N. macrocalyx was monitored on a monthly basis for the first 19 months and again in 2012. In 2012, the N. macrocalyx canopy areas were also measured using a vertical projection of the tree crowns by measuring the length of two lines across the crown area along the longest axis and perpendicular to the longest axis. In cases where trees formed a continuous canopy, a single canopy area was measured for the entire plot. The mean canopy area was 18 m² (SD ± 3.4 and ranged from 10 to 26 m²).

In August 2012 all naturally established indigenous tree seedlings under the N. macrocalyx patches, or "nuclei", were identified and numbered. Only recruits less than 3 m tall were recorded to ensure that seedlings/saplings had recruited after the establishment of N. macrocalyx nuclei. Recruits between 0.2 and 1 m were recorded as seedlings, and between 1 and 3 m as saplings. Shrubs, such as Ficus asperifolia (Moraceae) and Piper sp. were excluded from the seedling data. For recording, we followed the Botanical names accepted by Tropicos (2015). Growth of the identified seedlings/saplings was monitored every three months for one year. Seedling turnover was monitored by recording all deaths and identifying and tagging all newly found seedlings. Signs of elephant visits and their effect on the established seedlings were

T. Piiroinen et al./Forest Ecology and Management 345 (2015) 21-28

also recorded. The *N. macrocalyx* canopy measurements were used to estimate the average canopy size for each gap. The size of the average canopy area on each gap was then used to establish a control site of the same size within the same gap but randomly located outside the nuclei to enable comparison. The size of each control site was measured with a measuring tape and the site was temporarily marked for the duration of the study. All seedlings in the control sites were identified and monitored. Understory vegetation cover for each *N. macrocalyx* nuclei and control site was visually estimated by three observers using two $1\mathrm{m}^2$ plots per site and a ten-degree scale from $0\%$ to $100\%$ of coverage. The average percentage of the two plots per site and estimates given by the three observers was then used for the analyses. Ground vegetation height was measured for each nuclei and control site from two randomly selected locations.

## 2.4. Data analysis

Paired-samples $t$-test in SPSS version 19.0.0 (SPSS, 2010) was used to examine the differences between the two planting strategies (seeding and transplantation) in terms of *N. macrocalyx* seedling survival and growth. Paired-samples $t$-test was also used to compare the areas under the nuclei and control sites in terms of their ground vegetation cover and vegetation height. The density of recruited seedlings was calculated as the number of seedlings per hectare. Since the density data was zero-skewed, nonparametric analyses were used. Densities were described with medians, but also means were provided to allow comparison with related studies. Wilcoxon signed rank nonparametric test was used to assess differences in densities of naturally recruited seedlings between areas under the nuclei and control sites.

A multidimensional scaling (MDS) was used to visualize, and an unreplicated block design PERMANOVA to test for statistical differences between the seedling communities under the nuclei and control sites. Primer 6 version 6.1.13 and PERMANOVA + version 1.0.3 (Primer, 2009) were used for this analysis. Fourth-root transformed values were used in the analysis in order to down-weight the influence of the most common species and the Bray-Curtis similarity index was calculated with a dummy variable 1 for the tree species counts.

## 3. Results

## 3.1. Establishment of nuclei

Six years after planting, *N. macrocalyx* was present in all 17 gaps. A total of 158 (58%) of the transplanted seedlings and 161 (66%) of the germinated seeds had survived. There was no significant difference between the two planting methods in terms of tree survival or growth (Paired-sample $t$-test; $df = 16$, $P &gt; 0.05$). The mean height of the *N. macrocalyx* trees was $701\mathrm{cm}$ ($\mathrm{SD} \pm 295$ and ranged from 90 to $1210\mathrm{cm}$). The percentage of ground vegetation cover and height were both significantly lower under *N. macrocalyx* nuclei than in the control sites (Paired-sample $t$-test; $df = 16$, $P = 0.001$ and $df = 16$, $P = 0.039$ respectively, Fig. 2a and b).

## 3.2. Recruitment under the nuclei

A total of 636 recruits representing 25 tree species had emerged under the nuclei six years after planting of the nucleus trees. The density of recruits was significantly higher under the nuclei compared to the control sites (Wilcoxon sign rank test; $n = 17$, $z = -2.107$, $P = 0.035$, Fig. 3). The mean density of recruits under *N. macrocalyx* nuclei was $1475.3\mathrm{ha}^{-1}$ ($Mdn = 985.9$, $IQR = 842.7-1497.7$) and in the control sites $849.2\mathrm{ha}^{-1}$ ($Mdn = 555.6$, $IQR = 0-892.9$).

All tree species that recruited under the nuclei were indigenous and relatively common in KNP (Table 1). From the 25 recruited species, $36\%$ were early successional and $64\%$ late successional, $92\%$ were animal dispersed and $8\%$ (only two species) wind dispersed. The majority of recruits were seedlings $(77\%)$ followed by saplings $(23\%)$. (15%), Rytigynia sp. (6%), Diospyros abyssinica (4%), N. macrocalyx (3%), Millettia dura (3%) and Maesa lanceolata (2%). The remaining 18 species constituted only 8% of the total number of recruits. In control sites, recruits represented only six species, which were also found to recruit under the nuclei. The majority of recruits were seedlings (89%) followed by saplings (11%) and the most common species by far was again A. grandibracteata (69%) followed by D. abyssinica (20%). The remaining four species constituted only 11% of the total number of recruits. N. macrocalyx was found to recruit under the nuclei but not in the control sites.

The PERMANOVA test showed a significant difference in the seedling communities between the areas under  $N$ . macrocalyx nuclei and control sites (PERMANOVA;  $df = 1$ , Pseudo- $F = 16.96$ ,  $R^2 = 30.2$ ,  $P = 0.0001$ , Fig. 4).

Turnover of recruits was high; after the initial survey we marked an additional 244 new recruits but recorded a loss of

267 seedlings or saplings under the nuclei, and marked an additional four recruits but recorded a loss of 29 in control sites. This indicated an annual mortality rate of  $30\%$  and  $83\%$  of recruits under the nuclei and control sites, respectively. Consequently, at the end of the survey the total number of recruits had reduced from the initial survey by  $3\%$  under the nuclei and by  $86\%$  in control sites. For practical reasons it was not possible to determine death causes for the recruits since this would have required a more frequent monitoring interval. However, we did find that 11 of the 17 nucleus sites and 5 out of the 17 control sites were visited by elephants and the visits had caused damage to or mortality of the naturally recruited seedlings in 9 and 2 sites respectively. The mortality caused by elephants varied considerably. They seemed to have spent more time in some gaps, resulting in the destruction of a large number of recruited seedlings, whereas in some gaps they had just passed through without any damage to the seedlings. In general the seedling mortality caused by elephants constituted a relatively small proportion of the overall mortality.

# 4. Discussion

Applied nucleation is based on the strategy that islands or patches of trees in a degraded area are able to promote seedling recruitment and to restore forest cover (Corbin and Holl, 2012). Compared to other restoration techniques, there are indications that applied nucleation is faster than natural colonization process but cheaper than planting the entire area. Our results support those of e.g. Albornoz et al. (2013), Holl et al. (2013), Zahawi et al. (2013), Holl and Zahawi (2014) and Zwiener et al. (2014) who found that seedling recruitment was higher under the tree patches, i.e. nuclei compared to areas without nucleus trees.

Our results indicate that the characteristics of  $N$  macrocalyx make it a good nucleus tree. Six years after planting of  $N$  macrocalyx in the gaps of the early successional forest we found that the tallest trees were more than  $10\mathrm{m}$  in height and the canopy areas reached up to  $26\mathrm{m}^2$ . We found indications that  $N$  macrocalyx had altered gap conditions, since the difference in the ground vegetation cover and height between areas under  $N$  macrocalyx

nuclei and the adjacent control sites were different (Fig. 2a and b). Study by Bussmann (1999) from Mount Kenya Forest concluded that indigenous pioneer species, such as N. macrocalyx could be highly useful for fast reforestation efforts due to their fast growth rates. Research from other locations has also attempted to identify suitable nucleus species. For example a recently published study by Mullah et al. (2014) from the Mau Forest in Kenya found a positive interaction between abundance and richness of tree saplings and the density of N. macrocalyx, supporting our findings that N. macrocalyx can intensify natural recruitment. Holl et al. (2011) tested nucleation with tree species that have high survival rate, rapid growth and extensive canopy development in a premontane rainforest zone in Costa Rica. The study found that Inga edulis was particularly well suited for restoration due to its rapid canopy development providing shade and a favorable microclimate (Holl et al. 2011) as well as resources for animals (Fink et al. 2009). Toh et al. (1999) recommended planting of large-fruited or wind-dispersed species that might otherwise have difficulty in colonizing degraded sites, provided that they are able to quickly attract seed dispersers.

Many of the ecological and morphological characteristics of N. macrocalyx support its use as a nucleation tree. N. macrocalyx has large leaves, a wide crown and a rapid growth rate and it has been found to be able to grow through a thick tangle of herbaceous plants commonly present in post-logging gaps (Piiroinen et al. 2014). The fruits of N. macrocalyx might attract frugivores that, in addition to foraging on N. macrocalyx fruits, disperse seeds of other trees under the N. macrocalyx canopies in their faeces. In addition, N. macrocalyx grows and forms new leaves more or less throughout the year (Roininen and Kasenene, unpublished study) and has a relatively high level of insect herbivory on its leaves (Kasenene and Roininen, 1999). These might be some of the characteristics of a good nucleus tree.

All species that recruited under the nuclei were indigenous and relatively common in KNP. The most common species, A. grandibracteata, is wind dispersed. This is in line with previous studies where it was recorded as an early colonizer in former pine plantations (e.g. Kasenene, 2007 and references therein). However, most species in this study were animal dispersed and late successional such as C. anisata, Rytigynia sp. and D. abyssinica. In particular, the abundance of the larger seeded, late successional species, such as Monodora myristica (which was not found in control sites), suggest that the nuclei attracted primates, supported by the finding of Balcomb and Chapman (2003) who found that primates dispersed more than 85% of M. myristica seeds in KNP. These findings are important in terms of future development of the gaps, since primates have been found to be the key seed dispersers in KNP (Lambert, 2011). We found that elephants visited the nucleus sites more frequently than the control sites. Previous research from the grasslands of KNP found that elephants often visited isolated trees in search of shelter from the sun and while resting under the crowns, the elephants deposited seeds of species such as Prunus africana, Balanites wilsoniana, Chrysophyllum albidum, Aeglopsis eggelingii, Dovyalis spinossisima, Oncoba spinosa and Dasylepsis eggelingii in their faeces (Majid et al. 2011). From these species, P. africana and B. wilsoniana were also found in our study gaps. Elephant-caused mortality of the recruited seedlings varied considerably across the gaps but our findings indicate that mortality caused by elephants was not substantial and the seed dispersal ability of elephants might overrule their negative effects on tree regeneration. For example, it has been found that B. wilsoniana does not have other effective dispersers in addition to elephants (Cochrane, 2003) and indeed we only found B. wilsoniana seedlings under the nuclei. Similarly, even though elephants visited the N. macrocalyx gaps, they did not debark or actively break or fell N. macrocalyx trees (authors' personal observation). Elephants have been reported to be selective in which trees they damage (Struhsaker et al. 1996, Ssali et al. 2013). A study by from Bwindi Impenetrable National Park by Ssali et al. (2013) found that N. macrocalyx was common in the study area but compared to many other trees such as Newtonia buchananii, Myrianthus holstii and C. albidum, N. macrocalyx was relatively neglected by elephants and thus escaped elephant damage. Since elephants in KNP have been found to favor the post-logging gaps (Struhsaker et al. 1996, Lawes and Chapman, 2006), the finding that N. macrocalyx is not preferred by elephants might further increase its value as a potential nucleus tree.

We also found N. macrocalyx recruits only under the nucleus trees but noted their absence from the control sites. This might imply that the nuclei acted as a seed source and that the N. macrocalyx seedlings were able to establish under the nuclei, but that the denser and taller vegetation in the control sites limited the establishment of the seedlings. This may further demonstrate the need for planting nucleus trees or maintaining such pioneer species to enhance forest restoration.

Our study was conducted in a former pine plantation that had been established for economic purposes on grasslands created by agricultural practices. Several studies conducted at these plantations in KNP before or right after they were clear-cut recorded positive findings indicating that the pine plantation had enhanced natural recruitment when compared to the intact grasslands (e.g. Zanne and Chapman, 2001, Kasenene, 2007). A study conducted shortly after clearing of the plantations by Kasenene (2007) found strong indications of improved natural regeneration of indigenous species, particularly in former Cupressus and Pinus plantations. The study recorded higher densities of Polyscias fulva (n ha^{-1} 23.8 pitsawn and 18.4 sawmilled) and Trema orientalis (n ha^{-1} 21.6 pitsawn and 231.5 sawmilled) which are often identified as the early colonizers in KNP (e.g. Chapman and Chapman, 1997), but we recorded no T. orientalis seedlings in our study plots and only a few P. fulva (11.6 n ha^{-1}) under the N. macrocalyx canopies. Kasenene (2007) also recorded high densities of Albizia sp. C. anisata and D. abyssinica, which is in line with our findings of the most common recruits; but, in general, the densities recorded by our study were lower compared to the densities recorded by Kasenene (2007), particularly at the control sites. The only exception was that we recorded higher densities of N. macrocalyx under the nuclei, likely as a result of seed rain from the nucleus trees. Even though the study by Kasenene (2007) is not directly comparable to our study reported here, a comparison of the two provides indication that the seedling communities in the former pine plantations have changed since the plantation was clear-cut.

A recent study found indications that succession is taking place in these former pine plantation clear-cuts, but that recovery is slow and reaching a later successional stage could take a minimum of 60 years, but most likely hundreds of years (Roininen and Valtonen, University of Eastern Finland, unpublished study). Our results support these projections. We found that indigenous trees recruited to the gaps, but the recruitment was relatively low in the control sites and seedling turnover was higher in the control sites compared to areas under the nuclei. Considering that the areas under the nuclei had higher recruit densities, hosted a higher number of different tree species compared to control sites and that a larger percentage of recruits were at a sapling stage implies that the established nuclei may accelerate forest recovery.

## Conclusions

Applied nucleation is quite poorly studied as a restoration method (Corbin and Holl, 2012) and based on literature review, we found that applied nucleation studies in afrotropical rainforests

T. Piiroinen et al./Forest Ecology and Management 345 (2015) 21-28

seem to be particularly limited even though it has excellent potential as a restoration method. Our results show that planting nuclei of an indigenous tree species, in this case a relatively common, early successional species with animal dispersed seeds, large leaves and a wide crown, was able to establish through a dense cover of herbaceous plants and facilitate natural recruitment of a wide range of other indigenous tree species. This supports findings from previous studies, which found that applied nucleation offers a good alternative to larger-scale re-planting when the aim is natural forest recovery. The loss of tropical forest cover is alarming and there is an urgent need to develop cost-effective restoration strategies since leaving areas under natural regeneration is not always effective. Our study examined whether planting nucleus trees in former pine plantation clear-cuts was able to enhance natural recruitment in gaps where succession was found to be slow. Our results provide positive indications that both transplanted and seeded *N. macrocalyx* nucleus trees were able to survive and form patches of continuous canopy in plantation clear-cuts. Moreover, we found that a viable seedling community of indigenous tree species had been established under the nuclei with a good potential to take over after the nucleus trees eventually die.

# Natural establishment of indigenous trees under planted nuclei: A study from a clear-felled pine plantation in an afrotropical rain forest

# ABSTRACT

Applied nucleation has been proposed as a cost-effective reforestation alternative to large-scale re-planting or establishing plantations with exotic tree species. We tested applied nucleation in a regenerating clear-cut pine plantation in Kibale National Park, Uganda, where natural succession had been slow. We planted Neoboutonia macrocalyx, a relatively common indigenous pioneer tree species with animal dispersed seeds and a wide crown, in the pine plantation clear-cuts as seeds and transplanted seedlings. After six years of monitoring the growth of the nucleus trees we identified all naturally recruited seedlings under the nuclei and adjacent control sites without planted nuclei. We monitored the growth and turnover of the recruited seedlings for one year and examined the ground vegetation structure under the nuclei and control sites. We found that the N. macrocalyx nucleus trees had survived equally well if planted as seeds or transplanted seedlings and had attained heights up to ten meters tall. Understory vegetation structure under the established nuclei was less dense ($P = 0.001$) and shorter ($P = 0.039$) compared to control sites. We also found that natural recruitment of indigenous tree species under the nuclei was higher compared to control sites. The seedling density under the nuclei was significantly higher ($P = 0.035$), and there was a significant difference in the composition of seedling communities ($P = 0.0001$) with a larger number of different tree species found under the nuclei. We found that a viable seedling community had been established with a good potential to take over when planted nucleus trees eventually die. Our results show that planting nucleus trees can increase recruitment of indigenous tree species in locations where natural succession is otherwise slow.

# 1. Introduction

There is an urgent need to develop cost-effective and ecologically sound forest restoration strategies in the tropics in order to curb the loss of ecosystem services (Lamb et al., 2005), conserve biodiversity (Laurance and Useche, 2009), reduce carbon emissions (van der Werf et al., 2009) and reverse altered hydrological cycles (Sheil and Murdiyarso, 2009). More than half of the tropical moist forest cover has been reduced to less than $50\%$ of tree cover (Asner et al., 2009). Achard et al. (2014) estimated forest cover changes in the tropics in 1990–2000 and 2000–2010 and recorded a net forest loss in humid tropical forests to be 4.0 million ha per year in the 1990s and 3.2 million ha per year in the 2000s, whilst the total cover of humid tropical forests in 2010 was 972 million ha. Rightly, restoration of degraded ecosystems has been recognized

as an increasingly important global environmental policy target (Aronson and Alexander, 2013).

The most economic reforestation strategy is to leave logged or otherwise degraded areas to regenerate naturally (Lamb et al., 2005). However, this strategy is sometimes inefficient. Degradation may have resulted in topsoil loss and reduced soil fertility impairing reforestation potential. Woody shrubs and herbaceous plants can also encroach upon the recovering stands, thereby suppressing tree recruitment and resulting in arrested succession (Paul et al., 2004). Moreover, a considerable factor impeding forest recovery is lack of seed dispersal (Holl, 1999; Holl et al., 2000). Most tropical rainforest seeds remain viable only for a short time in the soil, even if they form part of the soil seed bank (Vázquez-Yanes and Orozco-Segovia, 1993). Therefore, succession in degraded lands depends on recently dispersed seeds (Holl, 1999). The majority of tropical tree species depend on animals for dispersal (Howe, 1984); however, most animals avoid open areas since they offer few resources for frugivores, limited shelter from predators and no trees for birds to perch or bats to fly (Schupp et al., 1989).

http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.foreco.2015.02.027

0378-1127/© 2015 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

Active reforestation in the tropics is often carried out by establishing industrial monocultures with a limited number of species belonging to a small number of genera (particularly Pinus, Eucalyptus and Acacia) (Lamb et al. 2005). However, according to Lamb et al. (2005), even though these monocultures may be economically profitable, they fail to provide the same level of goods and services once provided by the indigenous forest. Restoration planting offers an alternative approach and is carried out particularly when attempting to re-establish indigenous forest ecosystems and the services they provide. This can be done by re-planting an entire area either with small number of pioneer tree species or by densely planting a greater number of species representing later successional stages (e.g. Parrotta et al. 1997, Lamb, 1998, Lamb et al. 2005, Rodrigues et al. 2009, Holl, 2012). However, application of these approaches is often limited by their high cost (Holl et al. 2011).

The restoration approach referred to as applied nucleation can offer a cost-effective alternative to extensive re-planting, but despite some promising results it has been relatively little studied (Corbin and Holl, 2012). This technique builds on the nucleation hypothesis (Robinson and Handel, 2000, Zahawi and Augspurger, 2006) by promoting the natural recovery process using a small number of pioneer tree species established in patches to create canopy cover and facilitate recruitment of other tree species (Yarranton and Morrison, 1974). The established tree islands or “nuclei” can also trap wind-dispersed seeds (Franks, 2003, Zahawi et al. 2013) as well as attract animal seed dispersers that would otherwise avoid open areas, allowing natural recruitment and the forested area to expand (Schlawin and Zahawi, 2008). The nuclei then shade out grasses and other competing plants, which favors germination, natural establishment of tree seedlings and increases the rate of forest expansion over time (Elliot et al. 2003). Examples of recent research on applied nucleation include a study by Albornoz et al. (2013) who examined the nucleation process in a burned area of an evergreen temperate rainforest in Chile. The study recorded higher tree regeneration under remnant tree patches compared to open areas and found that whereas open areas were waterlogged, the areas under patches were not and the patches also attracted bird seed-dispersers. Peterson et al. (2014) tested nucleation hypothesis in abandoned pastureland in Costa Rica and found indications that only larger (>40--50 cm DBH and taller than 20 m) isolated trees enhanced recruitment whereas smaller trees did not. The same study also found that in addition to larger trees, patches of other microsites, such as nurse logs and steep slopes promoted tree recruitment to a similar degree compared to larger isolated trees. Similarly, natural tree recruitment was examined on former pasture sites in a tropical premontane forest zone in Costa Rica by applying two restoration strategies, planting trees throughout and planting different sized tree islands and comparing the active restoration sites to control sites undergoing passive restoration (Holl et al. 2011, Holl et al. 2013, Zahawi et al. 2013). The studies found that both active restoration methods increased the abundance and diversity of tree recruitment and the active restoration sites had a higher level of animal-dispersed tree species compared to passive restoration sites. The studies found that the level of tree recruitment in the island treatment was similar to the more intensive plantations, concluding that applied nucleation has good potential as a restoration strategy since it yields similar results to larger scale planting but is less expensive to implement.

Our study examined experimentally if planting patches of an indigenous, early successional tree species in clear-cut pine plantation gaps can facilitate natural forest regeneration by forming recruitment nuclei for other tree species. We asked (i) Do planted N. macrocalyx Pax tree seeds and seedlings survive and grow to form patches of canopy cover in clear-cut plantation gaps where natural succession has been found to be slow? (ii) Is natural establishment of indigenous tree seedlings under the nuclei higher compared to adjacent open areas and hence (iii) Is applied nucleation an effective restoration technique in areas where natural regeneration is slow? According to nucleation hypothesis (Zahawi and Augspurger, 2006), under established nuclei we expected to see less dense and shorter understory vegetation cover, higher density of naturally recruited seedlings and differences in seedling communities when compared to control sites.

## Methods

### Study area

This study was carried out in Kibale National Park (KNP), Uganda (Fig. 1) (0°13′ to 0°41′N and 30°19′ to 30°32′E, 795 km^{2}). The altitude ranges between 1110 and 1590 m above sea level and the area has two distinct rainy seasons from March to April and from September to November (Struhsaker, 1997). The annual rainfall monitored between 1990 and 2011 at the Makerere University Biological Field Station was 1696 mm (Chapman and Chapman unpublished data after Chapman et al. 2013). The soil has been characterized as dark gray to red sandy loams or sandy clays with a soil fertility ranging from fair or favorable to good (McKey et al. 1978). The KNP comprises different habitats including swamps, grasslands, mature forest and colonizing forest patches (Struhsaker, 1997).

The forest also contained exotic softwood plantations (mainly Pinus and Cupressus) that were established in grasslands in the late 1960s and early 1970s (Fimbel and Fimbel, 1996). The grasslands themselves were presumably a result of former agricultural activities in the forest (Kingston, 1967 after Fimbel and Fimbel, 1996). The forest was granted a national park status in 1993 (Struhsaker, 1997) after which the softwood plantations have gradually been logged in order to allow natural forest recovery. The KNP also contains a variety of canopy gaps resulting from logging of the plantations (Chapman et al. 2010) and selective logging of mature forest (Paul et al. 2004). The management strategy was to leave these cleared areas to regenerate naturally, but succession in the gaps has been slow or even arrested, and the gaps are commonly dominated by grasses, shrubs and herbs, such as Pennisetum purpurea and Acanthus pubescens (e.g. Paul et al. 2004, Lawes and Chapman, 2006) and Lantana camara (authors' personal observation).

Our study was established at the vicinity of the Makerere University Biological Field Station, in the former Nyakatojo plantation that was logged during 1995--1999. The study was established in gaps where trees had not recruited naturally.

### Study species

We used Neoboutonia macrocalyx Pax (Euphorbiaceae) since it is a relatively common early successional tree species across East Africa and therefore a tree that one could expect to find in the plantation clear-cuts. The distribution of N. macrocalyx ranges across the montane forests of central and eastern Africa (Lovett et al. 2006), such as Kibale forest in Uganda and Mt. Kenya forest in Kenya where it has been found to colonize post-logging gaps (author's personal observation). It is also found in some lowland rainforests like Kakamega in Kenya and Semuliki National Park in Uganda (Roininen personal observation). It usually grows in open areas, especially along valley bottoms and swamps (Chapman et al. 1999) and in secondary and partially logged forests (Kasenene and Roininen, 1999), but it is uncommon in low-light environments (Chapman et al. 2008). It is a medium sized tree

reaching an average height of 15 m (Lovett et al., 2006) but can grow up to 30 m (Meunier et al., 2010). The rapid growth rate of N. macrocalyx has been reported by Bussmann (1999) who examined the growth of 12 East African forest tree species in Mount Kenya. The study found that the length increment of N. macrocalyx branches (39.1 cm/year) was approximately 75% higher than that of primary forest species included in the study. The diameter at breast height (dbh) increment of 1-5 year old trees was 2.9 cm/year, being highest among all studied trees, the dbh increment of 20-50 year old trees was 1.92 cm/year and for trees older than 50 years, 1.48 cm/year. N. macrocalyx has a short trunk and a wide crown with large leaves. The fruit is a trilobed 1.5 × 1.0 cm capsule bearing three ellipsoid seeds (7 × 5 mm) (Meunier et al., 2010), which are dispersed by animals (Chapman et al., 1999). N. macrocalyx trees in KNP have been found to flower and fruit by the age of 6 years (authors' personal observation).

## 2.3. Experimental design and data collection

Our experiment was established in plantation clear-cuts that had not been colonized by trees. A gap was defined as an open area restricted by a boundary of woody species at least 2 m in height. Where forest boundary was difficult to define, individual large trees or dense woody shrubs were used as boundaries. Seventeen gaps were selected using random stratified sampling of different sized gaps. Gap size was measured by measuring the distance from the gap center to the forest edge toward each cardinal point. The average gap size was 436 m² (SD ± 279.4 and ranged from 113 to 1115 m²).

N. macrocalyx seeds were collected during April-May 2006 from KNP and adjacent areas from multiple trees within 10 km of the park to ensure genetic variation. Seeds were randomly divided into two groups; the first group was dried and stored, and the second group was planted into a grassland soil nursery. The seeds and nursery seedlings were planted in the selected forest gaps in early

September 2006, when the mean height of the seedlings was 34 cm (SD ± 11.6 and ranged from 10.2 to 61.0 cm). Eight randomly selected plots were established in each gap; four with transplanted seedlings (4 seedlings/plot) and four with seeds (10 seeds/plot, lightly covered with soil). The seedlings were planted in a square plot with 2 m spacing. For each seedling, an area of 50 × 50 cm was first cleared from vegetation and the seedlings were planted in the middle of these cleared areas. For the seeds, an area of 50 × 50 cm was cleared from vegetation on each plot. Two parallel lines with 10 cm spacing were established and in each line, five seeds were sown with 5 cm spacing. All seeds were sown during the same day. At the time of planting, the gaps were dominated by a dense tangle of herbaceous plants, shrubs and grasses, such as L. camara and P. purpurea.

The survival and growth of N. macrocalyx was monitored on a monthly basis for the first 19 months and again in 2012. In 2012, the N. macrocalyx canopy areas were also measured using a vertical projection of the tree crowns by measuring the length of two lines across the crown area along the longest axis and perpendicular to the longest axis. In cases where trees formed a continuous canopy, a single canopy area was measured for the entire plot. The mean canopy area was 18 m² (SD ± 3.4 and ranged from 10 to 26 m²).

In August 2012 all naturally established indigenous tree seedlings under the N. macrocalyx patches, or "nuclei", were identified and numbered. Only recruits less than 3 m tall were recorded to ensure that seedlings/saplings had recruited after the establishment of N. macrocalyx nuclei. Recruits between 0.2 and 1 m were recorded as seedlings, and between 1 and 3 m as saplings. Shrubs, such as Ficus asperifolia (Moraceae) and Piper sp. were excluded from the seedling data. For recording, we followed the Botanical names accepted by Tropicos (2015). Growth of the identified seedlings/saplings was monitored every three months for one year. Seedling turnover was monitored by recording all deaths and identifying and tagging all newly found seedlings. Signs of elephant visits and their effect on the established seedlings were

T. Piiroinen et al./Forest Ecology and Management 345 (2015) 21-28

also recorded. The *N. macrocalyx* canopy measurements were used to estimate the average canopy size for each gap. The size of the average canopy area on each gap was then used to establish a control site of the same size within the same gap but randomly located outside the nuclei to enable comparison. The size of each control site was measured with a measuring tape and the site was temporarily marked for the duration of the study. All seedlings in the control sites were identified and monitored. Understory vegetation cover for each *N. macrocalyx* nuclei and control site was visually estimated by three observers using two $1\mathrm{m}^2$ plots per site and a ten-degree scale from $0\%$ to $100\%$ of coverage. The average percentage of the two plots per site and estimates given by the three observers was then used for the analyses. Ground vegetation height was measured for each nuclei and control site from two randomly selected locations.

## 2.4. Data analysis

Paired-samples $t$-test in SPSS version 19.0.0 (SPSS, 2010) was used to examine the differences between the two planting strategies (seeding and transplantation) in terms of *N. macrocalyx* seedling survival and growth. Paired-samples $t$-test was also used to compare the areas under the nuclei and control sites in terms of their ground vegetation cover and vegetation height. The density of recruited seedlings was calculated as the number of seedlings per hectare. Since the density data was zero-skewed, nonparametric analyses were used. Densities were described with medians, but also means were provided to allow comparison with related studies. Wilcoxon signed rank nonparametric test was used to assess differences in densities of naturally recruited seedlings between areas under the nuclei and control sites.

A multidimensional scaling (MDS) was used to visualize, and an unreplicated block design PERMANOVA to test for statistical differences between the seedling communities under the nuclei and control sites. Primer 6 version 6.1.13 and PERMANOVA + version 1.0.3 (Primer, 2009) were used for this analysis. Fourth-root transformed values were used in the analysis in order to down-weight the influence of the most common species and the Bray-Curtis similarity index was calculated with a dummy variable 1 for the tree species counts.

## 3. Results

## 3.1. Establishment of nuclei

Six years after planting, *N. macrocalyx* was present in all 17 gaps. A total of 158 (58%) of the transplanted seedlings and 161 (66%) of the germinated seeds had survived. There was no significant difference between the two planting methods in terms of tree survival or growth (Paired-sample $t$-test; $df = 16$, $P &gt; 0.05$). The mean height of the *N. macrocalyx* trees was $701\mathrm{cm}$ ($\mathrm{SD} \pm 295$ and ranged from 90 to $1210\mathrm{cm}$). The percentage of ground vegetation cover and height were both significantly lower under *N. macrocalyx* nuclei than in the control sites (Paired-sample $t$-test; $df = 16$, $P = 0.001$ and $df = 16$, $P = 0.039$ respectively, Fig. 2a and b).

## 3.2. Recruitment under the nuclei

A total of 636 recruits representing 25 tree species had emerged under the nuclei six years after planting of the nucleus trees. The density of recruits was significantly higher under the nuclei compared to the control sites (Wilcoxon sign rank test; $n = 17$, $z = -2.107$, $P = 0.035$, Fig. 3). The mean density of recruits under *N. macrocalyx* nuclei was $1475.3\mathrm{ha}^{-1}$ ($Mdn = 985.9$, $IQR = 842.7-1497.7$) and in the control sites $849.2\mathrm{ha}^{-1}$ ($Mdn = 555.6$, $IQR = 0-892.9$).

(15%), Rytigynia sp. (6%), Diospyros abyssinica (4%), N. macrocalyx (3%), Millettia dura (3%) and Maesa lanceolata (2%). The remaining 18 species constituted only 8% of the total number of recruits. In control sites, recruits represented only six species, which were also found to recruit under the nuclei. The majority of recruits were seedlings (89%) followed by saplings (11%) and the most common species by far was again A. grandibracteata (69%) followed by D. abyssinica (20%). The remaining four species constituted only 11% of the total number of recruits. N. macrocalyx was found to recruit under the nuclei but not in the control sites.

The PERMANOVA test showed a significant difference in the seedling communities between the areas under  $N$ . macrocalyx nuclei and control sites (PERMANOVA;  $df = 1$ , Pseudo- $F = 16.96$ ,  $R^2 = 30.2$ ,  $P = 0.0001$ , Fig. 4).

Turnover of recruits was high; after the initial survey we marked an additional 244 new recruits but recorded a loss of

![img-4.jpeg](img-4.jpeg)
Fig. 4. Multidimensional scaling (MDS) ordination of indigenous tree seedling communities that had established under the  $N$ . macrocalyx nuclei (N) and adjacent control sites (C) six years after planting of the nucleus trees.

267 seedlings or saplings under the nuclei, and marked an additional four recruits but recorded a loss of 29 in control sites. This indicated an annual mortality rate of  $30\%$  and  $83\%$  of recruits under the nuclei and control sites, respectively. Consequently, at the end of the survey the total number of recruits had reduced from the initial survey by  $3\%$  under the nuclei and by  $86\%$  in control sites. For practical reasons it was not possible to determine death causes for the recruits since this would have required a more frequent monitoring interval. However, we did find that 11 of the 17 nucleus sites and 5 out of the 17 control sites were visited by elephants and the visits had caused damage to or mortality of the naturally recruited seedlings in 9 and 2 sites respectively. The mortality caused by elephants varied considerably. They seemed to have spent more time in some gaps, resulting in the destruction of a large number of recruited seedlings, whereas in some gaps they had just passed through without any damage to the seedlings. In general the seedling mortality caused by elephants constituted a relatively small proportion of the overall mortality.

# 4. Discussion

Applied nucleation is based on the strategy that islands or patches of trees in a degraded area are able to promote seedling recruitment and to restore forest cover (Corbin and Holl, 2012). Compared to other restoration techniques, there are indications that applied nucleation is faster than natural colonization process but cheaper than planting the entire area. Our results support those of e.g. Albornoz et al. (2013), Holl et al. (2013), Zahawi et al. (2013), Holl and Zahawi (2014) and Zwiener et al. (2014) who found that seedling recruitment was higher under the tree patches, i.e. nuclei compared to areas without nucleus trees.

Our results indicate that the characteristics of  $N$  macrocalyx make it a good nucleus tree. Six years after planting of  $N$  macrocalyx in the gaps of the early successional forest we found that the tallest trees were more than  $10\mathrm{m}$  in height and the canopy areas reached up to  $26\mathrm{m}^2$ . We found indications that  $N$  macrocalyx had altered gap conditions, since the difference in the ground vegetation cover and height between areas under  $N$  macrocalyx

nuclei and the adjacent control sites were different (Fig. 2a and b). Study by Bussmann (1999) from Mount Kenya Forest concluded that indigenous pioneer species, such as N. macrocalyx could be highly useful for fast reforestation efforts due to their fast growth rates. Research from other locations has also attempted to identify suitable nucleus species. For example a recently published study by Mullah et al. (2014) from the Mau Forest in Kenya found a positive interaction between abundance and richness of tree saplings and the density of N. macrocalyx, supporting our findings that N. macrocalyx can intensify natural recruitment. Holl et al. (2011) tested nucleation with tree species that have high survival rate, rapid growth and extensive canopy development in a premontane rainforest zone in Costa Rica. The study found that Inga edulis was particularly well suited for restoration due to its rapid canopy development providing shade and a favorable microclimate (Holl et al. 2011) as well as resources for animals (Fink et al. 2009). Toh et al. (1999) recommended planting of large-fruited or wind-dispersed species that might otherwise have difficulty in colonizing degraded sites, provided that they are able to quickly attract seed dispersers.

Many of the ecological and morphological characteristics of N. macrocalyx support its use as a nucleation tree. N. macrocalyx has large leaves, a wide crown and a rapid growth rate and it has been found to be able to grow through a thick tangle of herbaceous plants commonly present in post-logging gaps (Piiroinen et al. 2014). The fruits of N. macrocalyx might attract frugivores that, in addition to foraging on N. macrocalyx fruits, disperse seeds of other trees under the N. macrocalyx canopies in their faeces. In addition, N. macrocalyx grows and forms new leaves more or less throughout the year (Roininen and Kasenene, unpublished study) and has a relatively high level of insect herbivory on its leaves (Kasenene and Roininen, 1999). These might be some of the characteristics of a good nucleus tree.

All species that recruited under the nuclei were indigenous and relatively common in KNP. The most common species, A. grandibracteata, is wind dispersed. This is in line with previous studies where it was recorded as an early colonizer in former pine plantations (e.g. Kasenene, 2007 and references therein). However, most species in this study were animal dispersed and late successional such as C. anisata, Rytigynia sp. and D. abyssinica. In particular, the abundance of the larger seeded, late successional species, such as Monodora myristica (which was not found in control sites), suggest that the nuclei attracted primates, supported by the finding of Balcomb and Chapman (2003) who found that primates dispersed more than 85% of M. myristica seeds in KNP. These findings are important in terms of future development of the gaps, since primates have been found to be the key seed dispersers in KNP (Lambert, 2011). We found that elephants visited the nucleus sites more frequently than the control sites. Previous research from the grasslands of KNP found that elephants often visited isolated trees in search of shelter from the sun and while resting under the crowns, the elephants deposited seeds of species such as Prunus africana, Balanites wilsoniana, Chrysophyllum albidum, Aeglopsis eggelingii, Dovyalis spinossisima, Oncoba spinosa and Dasylepsis eggelingii in their faeces (Majid et al. 2011). From these species, P. africana and B. wilsoniana were also found in our study gaps. Elephant-caused mortality of the recruited seedlings varied considerably across the gaps but our findings indicate that mortality caused by elephants was not substantial and the seed dispersal ability of elephants might overrule their negative effects on tree regeneration. For example, it has been found that B. wilsoniana does not have other effective dispersers in addition to elephants (Cochrane, 2003) and indeed we only found B. wilsoniana seedlings under the nuclei. Similarly, even though elephants visited the N. macrocalyx gaps, they did not debark or actively break or fell N. macrocalyx trees (authors' personal observation). Elephants have been reported to be selective in which trees they damage (Struhsaker et al. 1996, Ssali et al. 2013). A study by from Bwindi Impenetrable National Park by Ssali et al. (2013) found that N. macrocalyx was common in the study area but compared to many other trees such as Newtonia buchananii, Myrianthus holstii and C. albidum, N. macrocalyx was relatively neglected by elephants and thus escaped elephant damage. Since elephants in KNP have been found to favor the post-logging gaps (Struhsaker et al. 1996, Lawes and Chapman, 2006), the finding that N. macrocalyx is not preferred by elephants might further increase its value as a potential nucleus tree.

We also found N. macrocalyx recruits only under the nucleus trees but noted their absence from the control sites. This might imply that the nuclei acted as a seed source and that the N. macrocalyx seedlings were able to establish under the nuclei, but that the denser and taller vegetation in the control sites limited the establishment of the seedlings. This may further demonstrate the need for planting nucleus trees or maintaining such pioneer species to enhance forest restoration.

Our study was conducted in a former pine plantation that had been established for economic purposes on grasslands created by agricultural practices. Several studies conducted at these plantations in KNP before or right after they were clear-cut recorded positive findings indicating that the pine plantation had enhanced natural recruitment when compared to the intact grasslands (e.g. Zanne and Chapman, 2001, Kasenene, 2007). A study conducted shortly after clearing of the plantations by Kasenene (2007) found strong indications of improved natural regeneration of indigenous species, particularly in former Cupressus and Pinus plantations. The study recorded higher densities of Polyscias fulva (n ha^{-1} 23.8 pitsawn and 18.4 sawmilled) and Trema orientalis (n ha^{-1} 21.6 pitsawn and 231.5 sawmilled) which are often identified as the early colonizers in KNP (e.g. Chapman and Chapman, 1997), but we recorded no T. orientalis seedlings in our study plots and only a few P. fulva (11.6 n ha^{-1}) under the N. macrocalyx canopies. Kasenene (2007) also recorded high densities of Albizia sp. C. anisata and D. abyssinica, which is in line with our findings of the most common recruits; but, in general, the densities recorded by our study were lower compared to the densities recorded by Kasenene (2007), particularly at the control sites. The only exception was that we recorded higher densities of N. macrocalyx under the nuclei, likely as a result of seed rain from the nucleus trees. Even though the study by Kasenene (2007) is not directly comparable to our study reported here, a comparison of the two provides indication that the seedling communities in the former pine plantations have changed since the plantation was clear-cut.

A recent study found indications that succession is taking place in these former pine plantation clear-cuts, but that recovery is slow and reaching a later successional stage could take a minimum of 60 years, but most likely hundreds of years (Roininen and Valtonen, University of Eastern Finland, unpublished study). Our results support these projections. We found that indigenous trees recruited to the gaps, but the recruitment was relatively low in the control sites and seedling turnover was higher in the control sites compared to areas under the nuclei. Considering that the areas under the nuclei had higher recruit densities, hosted a higher number of different tree species compared to control sites and that a larger percentage of recruits were at a sapling stage implies that the established nuclei may accelerate forest recovery.

## Conclusions

Applied nucleation is quite poorly studied as a restoration method (Corbin and Holl, 2012) and based on literature review, we found that applied nucleation studies in afrotropical rainforests

T. Piiroinen et al./Forest Ecology and Management 345 (2015) 21-28

seem to be particularly limited even though it has excellent potential as a restoration method. Our results show that planting nuclei of an indigenous tree species, in this case a relatively common, early successional species with animal dispersed seeds, large leaves and a wide crown, was able to establish through a dense cover of herbaceous plants and facilitate natural recruitment of a wide range of other indigenous tree species. This supports findings from previous studies, which found that applied nucleation offers a good alternative to larger-scale re-planting when the aim is natural forest recovery. The loss of tropical forest cover is alarming and there is an urgent need to develop cost-effective restoration strategies since leaving areas under natural regeneration is not always effective. Our study examined whether planting nucleus trees in former pine plantation clear-cuts was able to enhance natural recruitment in gaps where succession was found to be slow. Our results provide positive indications that both transplanted and seeded *N. macrocalyx* nucleus trees were able to survive and form patches of continuous canopy in plantation clear-cuts. Moreover, we found that a viable seedling community of indigenous tree species had been established under the nuclei with a good potential to take over after the nucleus trees eventually die.

# Natural establishment of indigenous trees under planted nuclei: A study from a clear-felled pine plantation in an afrotropical rain forest

CrossMark

T. Piiroinen $^{a,\ast}$, P. Nyeko $^{b}$, H. Roininen $^{a}$

$^{a}$ Faculty of Science and Forestry, Department of Biology, University of Eastern Finland, P.O. Box 111, FI-80101 Joensuu, Finland
$^{b}$ Department of Forestry, Biodiversity and Tourism, Makerere University, P.O. Box 7062, Kampala, Uganda

# ARTICLE INFO

Article history:

Received 21 November 2014

Received in revised form 13 February 2015

Accepted 16 February 2015

Applied nucleation

Logged plantation

Natural succession

Plant colonization

Secondary forest

Tropical forests

# ABSTRACT

Applied nucleation has been proposed as a cost-effective reforestation alternative to large-scale re-planting or establishing plantations with exotic tree species. We tested applied nucleation in a regenerating clear-cut pine plantation in Kibale National Park, Uganda, where natural succession had been slow. We planted Neoboutonia macrocalyx, a relatively common indigenous pioneer tree species with animal dispersed seeds and a wide crown, in the pine plantation clear-cuts as seeds and transplanted seedlings. After six years of monitoring the growth of the nucleus trees we identified all naturally recruited seedlings under the nuclei and adjacent control sites without planted nuclei. We monitored the growth and turnover of the recruited seedlings for one year and examined the ground vegetation structure under the nuclei and control sites. We found that the N. macrocalyx nucleus trees had survived equally well if planted as seeds or transplanted seedlings and had attained heights up to ten meters tall. Understory vegetation structure under the established nuclei was less dense ($P = 0.001$) and shorter ($P = 0.039$) compared to control sites. We also found that natural recruitment of indigenous tree species under the nuclei was higher compared to control sites. The seedling density under the nuclei was significantly higher ($P = 0.035$), and there was a significant difference in the composition of seedling communities ($P = 0.0001$) with a larger number of different tree species found under the nuclei. We found that a viable seedling community had been established with a good potential to take over when planted nucleus trees eventually die. Our results show that planting nucleus trees can increase recruitment of indigenous tree species in locations where natural succession is otherwise slow.

# 1. Introduction

There is an urgent need to develop cost-effective and ecologically sound forest restoration strategies in the tropics in order to curb the loss of ecosystem services (Lamb et al., 2005), conserve biodiversity (Laurance and Useche, 2009), reduce carbon emissions (van der Werf et al., 2009) and reverse altered hydrological cycles (Sheil and Murdiyarso, 2009). More than half of the tropical moist forest cover has been reduced to less than $50\%$ of tree cover (Asner et al., 2009). Achard et al. (2014) estimated forest cover changes in the tropics in 1990–2000 and 2000–2010 and recorded a net forest loss in humid tropical forests to be 4.0 million ha per year in the 1990s and 3.2 million ha per year in the 2000s, whilst the total cover of humid tropical forests in 2010 was 972 million ha. Rightly, restoration of degraded ecosystems has been recognized

as an increasingly important global environmental policy target (Aronson and Alexander, 2013).

The most economic reforestation strategy is to leave logged or otherwise degraded areas to regenerate naturally (Lamb et al., 2005). However, this strategy is sometimes inefficient. Degradation may have resulted in topsoil loss and reduced soil fertility impairing reforestation potential. Woody shrubs and herbaceous plants can also encroach upon the recovering stands, thereby suppressing tree recruitment and resulting in arrested succession (Paul et al., 2004). Moreover, a considerable factor impeding forest recovery is lack of seed dispersal (Holl, 1999; Holl et al., 2000). Most tropical rainforest seeds remain viable only for a short time in the soil, even if they form part of the soil seed bank (Vázquez-Yanes and Orozco-Segovia, 1993). Therefore, succession in degraded lands depends on recently dispersed seeds (Holl, 1999). The majority of tropical tree species depend on animals for dispersal (Howe, 1984); however, most animals avoid open areas since they offer few resources for frugivores, limited shelter from predators and no trees for birds to perch or bats to fly (Schupp et al., 1989).

http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.foreco.2015.02.027

0378-1127/© 2015 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

Active reforestation in the tropics is often carried out by establishing industrial monocultures with a limited number of species belonging to a small number of genera (particularly Pinus, Eucalyptus and Acacia) (Lamb et al. 2005). However, according to Lamb et al. (2005), even though these monocultures may be economically profitable, they fail to provide the same level of goods and services once provided by the indigenous forest. Restoration planting offers an alternative approach and is carried out particularly when attempting to re-establish indigenous forest ecosystems and the services they provide. This can be done by re-planting an entire area either with small number of pioneer tree species or by densely planting a greater number of species representing later successional stages (e.g. Parrotta et al. 1997, Lamb, 1998, Lamb et al. 2005, Rodrigues et al. 2009, Holl, 2012). However, application of these approaches is often limited by their high cost (Holl et al. 2011).

The restoration approach referred to as applied nucleation can offer a cost-effective alternative to extensive re-planting, but despite some promising results it has been relatively little studied (Corbin and Holl, 2012). This technique builds on the nucleation hypothesis (Robinson and Handel, 2000, Zahawi and Augspurger, 2006) by promoting the natural recovery process using a small number of pioneer tree species established in patches to create canopy cover and facilitate recruitment of other tree species (Yarranton and Morrison, 1974). The established tree islands or “nuclei” can also trap wind-dispersed seeds (Franks, 2003, Zahawi et al. 2013) as well as attract animal seed dispersers that would otherwise avoid open areas, allowing natural recruitment and the forested area to expand (Schlawin and Zahawi, 2008). The nuclei then shade out grasses and other competing plants, which favors germination, natural establishment of tree seedlings and increases the rate of forest expansion over time (Elliot et al. 2003). Examples of recent research on applied nucleation include a study by Albornoz et al. (2013) who examined the nucleation process in a burned area of an evergreen temperate rainforest in Chile. The study recorded higher tree regeneration under remnant tree patches compared to open areas and found that whereas open areas were waterlogged, the areas under patches were not and the patches also attracted bird seed-dispersers. Peterson et al. (2014) tested nucleation hypothesis in abandoned pastureland in Costa Rica and found indications that only larger (>40--50 cm DBH and taller than 20 m) isolated trees enhanced recruitment whereas smaller trees did not. The same study also found that in addition to larger trees, patches of other microsites, such as nurse logs and steep slopes promoted tree recruitment to a similar degree compared to larger isolated trees. Similarly, natural tree recruitment was examined on former pasture sites in a tropical premontane forest zone in Costa Rica by applying two restoration strategies, planting trees throughout and planting different sized tree islands and comparing the active restoration sites to control sites undergoing passive restoration (Holl et al. 2011, Holl et al. 2013, Zahawi et al. 2013). The studies found that both active restoration methods increased the abundance and diversity of tree recruitment and the active restoration sites had a higher level of animal-dispersed tree species compared to passive restoration sites. The studies found that the level of tree recruitment in the island treatment was similar to the more intensive plantations, concluding that applied nucleation has good potential as a restoration strategy since it yields similar results to larger scale planting but is less expensive to implement.

Our study examined experimentally if planting patches of an indigenous, early successional tree species in clear-cut pine plantation gaps can facilitate natural forest regeneration by forming recruitment nuclei for other tree species. We asked (i) Do planted N. macrocalyx Pax tree seeds and seedlings survive and grow to form patches of canopy cover in clear-cut plantation gaps where natural succession has been found to be slow? (ii) Is natural establishment of indigenous tree seedlings under the nuclei higher compared to adjacent open areas and hence (iii) Is applied nucleation an effective restoration technique in areas where natural regeneration is slow? According to nucleation hypothesis (Zahawi and Augspurger, 2006), under established nuclei we expected to see less dense and shorter understory vegetation cover, higher density of naturally recruited seedlings and differences in seedling communities when compared to control sites.

## Methods

### Study area

This study was carried out in Kibale National Park (KNP), Uganda (Fig. 1) (0°13′ to 0°41′N and 30°19′ to 30°32′E, 795 km^{2}). The altitude ranges between 1110 and 1590 m above sea level and the area has two distinct rainy seasons from March to April and from September to November (Struhsaker, 1997). The annual rainfall monitored between 1990 and 2011 at the Makerere University Biological Field Station was 1696 mm (Chapman and Chapman unpublished data after Chapman et al. 2013). The soil has been characterized as dark gray to red sandy loams or sandy clays with a soil fertility ranging from fair or favorable to good (McKey et al. 1978). The KNP comprises different habitats including swamps, grasslands, mature forest and colonizing forest patches (Struhsaker, 1997).

The forest also contained exotic softwood plantations (mainly Pinus and Cupressus) that were established in grasslands in the late 1960s and early 1970s (Fimbel and Fimbel, 1996). The grasslands themselves were presumably a result of former agricultural activities in the forest (Kingston, 1967 after Fimbel and Fimbel, 1996). The forest was granted a national park status in 1993 (Struhsaker, 1997) after which the softwood plantations have gradually been logged in order to allow natural forest recovery. The KNP also contains a variety of canopy gaps resulting from logging of the plantations (Chapman et al. 2010) and selective logging of mature forest (Paul et al. 2004). The management strategy was to leave these cleared areas to regenerate naturally, but succession in the gaps has been slow or even arrested, and the gaps are commonly dominated by grasses, shrubs and herbs, such as Pennisetum purpurea and Acanthus pubescens (e.g. Paul et al. 2004, Lawes and Chapman, 2006) and Lantana camara (authors' personal observation).

Our study was established at the vicinity of the Makerere University Biological Field Station, in the former Nyakatojo plantation that was logged during 1995--1999. The study was established in gaps where trees had not recruited naturally.

### Study species

We used Neoboutonia macrocalyx Pax (Euphorbiaceae) since it is a relatively common early successional tree species across East Africa and therefore a tree that one could expect to find in the plantation clear-cuts. The distribution of N. macrocalyx ranges across the montane forests of central and eastern Africa (Lovett et al. 2006), such as Kibale forest in Uganda and Mt. Kenya forest in Kenya where it has been found to colonize post-logging gaps (author's personal observation). It is also found in some lowland rainforests like Kakamega in Kenya and Semuliki National Park in Uganda (Roininen personal observation). It usually grows in open areas, especially along valley bottoms and swamps (Chapman et al. 1999) and in secondary and partially logged forests (Kasenene and Roininen, 1999), but it is uncommon in low-light environments (Chapman et al. 2008). It is a medium sized tree

reaching an average height of 15 m (Lovett et al., 2006) but can grow up to 30 m (Meunier et al., 2010). The rapid growth rate of N. macrocalyx has been reported by Bussmann (1999) who examined the growth of 12 East African forest tree species in Mount Kenya. The study found that the length increment of N. macrocalyx branches (39.1 cm/year) was approximately 75% higher than that of primary forest species included in the study. The diameter at breast height (dbh) increment of 1-5 year old trees was 2.9 cm/year, being highest among all studied trees, the dbh increment of 20-50 year old trees was 1.92 cm/year and for trees older than 50 years, 1.48 cm/year. N. macrocalyx has a short trunk and a wide crown with large leaves. The fruit is a trilobed 1.5 × 1.0 cm capsule bearing three ellipsoid seeds (7 × 5 mm) (Meunier et al., 2010), which are dispersed by animals (Chapman et al., 1999). N. macrocalyx trees in KNP have been found to flower and fruit by the age of 6 years (authors' personal observation).

## 2.3. Experimental design and data collection

Our experiment was established in plantation clear-cuts that had not been colonized by trees. A gap was defined as an open area restricted by a boundary of woody species at least 2 m in height. Where forest boundary was difficult to define, individual large trees or dense woody shrubs were used as boundaries. Seventeen gaps were selected using random stratified sampling of different sized gaps. Gap size was measured by measuring the distance from the gap center to the forest edge toward each cardinal point. The average gap size was 436 m² (SD ± 279.4 and ranged from 113 to 1115 m²).

N. macrocalyx seeds were collected during April-May 2006 from KNP and adjacent areas from multiple trees within 10 km of the park to ensure genetic variation. Seeds were randomly divided into two groups; the first group was dried and stored, and the second group was planted into a grassland soil nursery. The seeds and nursery seedlings were planted in the selected forest gaps in early

September 2006, when the mean height of the seedlings was 34 cm (SD ± 11.6 and ranged from 10.2 to 61.0 cm). Eight randomly selected plots were established in each gap; four with transplanted seedlings (4 seedlings/plot) and four with seeds (10 seeds/plot, lightly covered with soil). The seedlings were planted in a square plot with 2 m spacing. For each seedling, an area of 50 × 50 cm was first cleared from vegetation and the seedlings were planted in the middle of these cleared areas. For the seeds, an area of 50 × 50 cm was cleared from vegetation on each plot. Two parallel lines with 10 cm spacing were established and in each line, five seeds were sown with 5 cm spacing. All seeds were sown during the same day. At the time of planting, the gaps were dominated by a dense tangle of herbaceous plants, shrubs and grasses, such as L. camara and P. purpurea.

The survival and growth of N. macrocalyx was monitored on a monthly basis for the first 19 months and again in 2012. In 2012, the N. macrocalyx canopy areas were also measured using a vertical projection of the tree crowns by measuring the length of two lines across the crown area along the longest axis and perpendicular to the longest axis. In cases where trees formed a continuous canopy, a single canopy area was measured for the entire plot. The mean canopy area was 18 m² (SD ± 3.4 and ranged from 10 to 26 m²).

In August 2012 all naturally established indigenous tree seedlings under the N. macrocalyx patches, or "nuclei", were identified and numbered. Only recruits less than 3 m tall were recorded to ensure that seedlings/saplings had recruited after the establishment of N. macrocalyx nuclei. Recruits between 0.2 and 1 m were recorded as seedlings, and between 1 and 3 m as saplings. Shrubs, such as Ficus asperifolia (Moraceae) and Piper sp. were excluded from the seedling data. For recording, we followed the Botanical names accepted by Tropicos (2015). Growth of the identified seedlings/saplings was monitored every three months for one year. Seedling turnover was monitored by recording all deaths and identifying and tagging all newly found seedlings. Signs of elephant visits and their effect on the established seedlings were

T. Piiroinen et al./Forest Ecology and Management 345 (2015) 21-28

also recorded. The *N. macrocalyx* canopy measurements were used to estimate the average canopy size for each gap. The size of the average canopy area on each gap was then used to establish a control site of the same size within the same gap but randomly located outside the nuclei to enable comparison. The size of each control site was measured with a measuring tape and the site was temporarily marked for the duration of the study. All seedlings in the control sites were identified and monitored. Understory vegetation cover for each *N. macrocalyx* nuclei and control site was visually estimated by three observers using two $1\mathrm{m}^2$ plots per site and a ten-degree scale from $0\%$ to $100\%$ of coverage. The average percentage of the two plots per site and estimates given by the three observers was then used for the analyses. Ground vegetation height was measured for each nuclei and control site from two randomly selected locations.

## 2.4. Data analysis

Paired-samples $t$-test in SPSS version 19.0.0 (SPSS, 2010) was used to examine the differences between the two planting strategies (seeding and transplantation) in terms of *N. macrocalyx* seedling survival and growth. Paired-samples $t$-test was also used to compare the areas under the nuclei and control sites in terms of their ground vegetation cover and vegetation height. The density of recruited seedlings was calculated as the number of seedlings per hectare. Since the density data was zero-skewed, nonparametric analyses were used. Densities were described with medians, but also means were provided to allow comparison with related studies. Wilcoxon signed rank nonparametric test was used to assess differences in densities of naturally recruited seedlings between areas under the nuclei and control sites.

A multidimensional scaling (MDS) was used to visualize, and an unreplicated block design PERMANOVA to test for statistical differences between the seedling communities under the nuclei and control sites. Primer 6 version 6.1.13 and PERMANOVA + version 1.0.3 (Primer, 2009) were used for this analysis. Fourth-root transformed values were used in the analysis in order to down-weight the influence of the most common species and the Bray-Curtis similarity index was calculated with a dummy variable 1 for the tree species counts.

## 3. Results

## 3.1. Establishment of nuclei

Six years after planting, *N. macrocalyx* was present in all 17 gaps. A total of 158 (58%) of the transplanted seedlings and 161 (66%) of the germinated seeds had survived. There was no significant difference between the two planting methods in terms of tree survival or growth (Paired-sample $t$-test; $df = 16$, $P &gt; 0.05$). The mean height of the *N. macrocalyx* trees was $701\mathrm{cm}$ ($\mathrm{SD} \pm 295$ and ranged from 90 to $1210\mathrm{cm}$). The percentage of ground vegetation cover and height were both significantly lower under *N. macrocalyx* nuclei than in the control sites (Paired-sample $t$-test; $df = 16$, $P = 0.001$ and $df = 16$, $P = 0.039$ respectively, Fig. 2a and b).

## 3.2. Recruitment under the nuclei

A total of 636 recruits representing 25 tree species had emerged under the nuclei six years after planting of the nucleus trees. The density of recruits was significantly higher under the nuclei compared to the control sites (Wilcoxon sign rank test; $n = 17$, $z = -2.107$, $P = 0.035$, Fig. 3). The mean density of recruits under *N. macrocalyx* nuclei was $1475.3\mathrm{ha}^{-1}$ ($Mdn = 985.9$, $IQR = 842.7-1497.7$) and in the control sites $849.2\mathrm{ha}^{-1}$ ($Mdn = 555.6$, $IQR = 0-892.9$).
