# METHODS

## Site preparation

The site consists of approximately 15 ha of filled former marshland, surrounded by open water, roads and freeways, in the Hackensack Meadowlands of New Jersey (Plate 1). Most of the site is an abandoned municipal landfill ringed with a reed grass (*Phragmites australis* (Cav.) Trin.) community that slopes into estuarine communities and shallow open water on two sides. The experimental area occupies 6 ha atop the shallow landfill that operated until the early 1960s. Post-closure treatment was apparently limited to a thin layer of coarse cover material, probably composed of excavated subsoil and construction debris (D. Smith, personal communication). A surface fire in summer 1986 burned into the contents, and the combination of fire and lengthy decomposition in this shallow, uncapped landfill probably resulted in the loss of most organic contents. Prior to experimental preparation, the surface consisted of rubble and exposed trash, with a very sparse cover of weedy vegetation (e.g., Stalter 1984). We focused efforts on the development of a native woodland, because wooded sites, which provide critical habitat for many migrating birds, have become scarce in the region (Kane 1991).

The experimental area was surveyed and mapped on a 150 × 400 m grid, and arrangements were made to add sufficient growing medium to support woody plants. Most of the base substrate (94%) arrived from a single source, a deep excavation of buried sandy sediments from Manhattan. Tests of samples indicated a uniformly low organic content (0.058% dry mass), high pH (7.8), low total nitrogen (0.02% dry mass), and high calcium (4700 ppm). The remaining base material arrived from an excavation in Bergen County, New Jersey, USA. This latter material was a clay loam with moderate organic content (4.31% by mass), and considerably lower pH (6.3), but comparably low total nitrogen (0.15% by mass) and calcium (3400 ppm). The top layer was 30 cm of composted leaf mulch (~100% organic matter) that had been stocked in piles for one or more years. To cover the experimental area with new substrate at a depth of 90 cm required ~45000 m³ of transported subsoil and 19000 m³ of composted leaf mulch. Drainage was poor in several locations, resulting in temporary ponds that later evaporated. Experimental plot positions were shifted to avoid planting in waterlogged areas.

The two substrate layers were partially mixed during spreading, but most of the mulch component remained on top. To reduce erosion and as a measure of weed control, the freshly covered site was sown with a commercial annual grass mixture, predominately Japanese millet (*Echinocloa crus-galli*, var. *frumentacea* (Rox.) W. F. Wight), a warm season annual. Sowing took place ~1 wk before experimental planting began. As intended, the annual grass quickly diminished in cover by the following spring, replaced by a mix of native and non-native herbaceous vegetation that varies seasonally and annually (Appendix 1). Propagules of one local weedy tree-of-heaven, *Ailanthus altissima* (Miller) Swingle, apparently arrived in the imported leaf mulch, and we decided to remove its seedlings and sprouts at the outset, to avoid confounding artificial and natural recruitment. In summer 1992, we manually removed ~2000 stems of this species.

Woody plants growing on the immediate periphery (within 50 m) consisted of a sparse, species-poor mix of trees and shrubs. Species native to the region were American ash (*Fraxinus americana* L.), boxelder (*Acer negundo* L.), groundsel bush (*Baccharis halimifolia* L.), hackberry (*Celtis occidentalis* L.), red-berried mulberry (*Morus rubra* L.), quaking aspen (*Populus tremuloides* Michx.), smooth sumac (*Rhus glabra* L.), staghorn sumac (*Rhus typhina* L.), blackberries (*Rubus* spp. L.), pussy willow (*Salix discolor* Muhl.), and el

Steudel.)), black locust (Robinia pseudoacacia L.), and European alder buckthorn (Rhamnus frangula L.). (Nomenclature follows Gleason and Cronquist [1991].) Populations of all 18 taxa were very small, and only four species were represented by more than five individuals—elderberry, red-berried mulberry, smooth sumac, and tree-of-heaven. In addition, a large population of trembling aspen (N &gt; 1000) was located on an elevated wasteland site whose nearest border was ~0.5 km to the west, across two highways.

## Experimental layout and plant installations

After site preparation, we introduced experimental clusters of woody plants in fall 1991, as the initial grass cover crop was germinating. Sixteen plots were planted with 21 woody plants each, according to a two-by-two factorial design. The factors were (1) plant size (larger or smaller) and (2) the inclusion of nitrogen-fixing trees and shrubs (with or without N-fixers). Plant size was determined by selection, with the goal of maintaining average height per species at approximately half-size in plots designated for the smaller plant treatment combinations. All plants were pruned to about two-thirds of original size, to reduce transplant shock. In some cases, tall, thin trees were further pruned to meet the "small" height category. Plants that died were replaced in spring 1992. We watered all installed plants throughout dry periods during the first two growing seasons.

Experimental native plants (Table 1) were chosen to produce abundant fruit soon after transplanting, and to spread fruit production over a full season. For example, black cherry (Prunus serotina) produces ripe fruit in mid-summer, while arrowwood (Viburnum dentatum) and grey dogwood (Cornus racemosa) have fruits that ripen in late summer, and ripe fruits of winged sumac (Rhus copallina) are displayed throughout winter. The trees and larger shrubs were obtained from commercial nurseries, while some of the smaller plants (R. copallina, Rubus spp. and Sambucus canadensis) were excavated from successional old fields or on the perimeter

of the experimental site. For all transplants, an effort was made to include large root volumes (none were bare-root transplants), that not only aid in establishment, but also help ensure that soil-borne mutualists were included.

To reduce damage by browsing eastern cottontail rabbits (Sylvilagus floridanus), we constructed a wire fence surrounding each planted plot. Eight empty plots were laid out, four with fencing (which had the potential to serve as a perch for avian frugivores) and four without fencing. The 24 plots were placed on a 150 × 400 m grid in a random array, stratified to prevent neighboring plots with the same treatment. The final plot arrangement is presented in Fig. 2. Spacing was somewhat irregular, in order to avoid spots with insufficient substrate or impeded drainage. Site margins and all plot centers were mapped on a two-dimensional grid (±1 m resolution). On the site periphery, the nearest potential source plants for woody seedling recruitment were identified and mapped on the same grid.

Once installed, all 336 trees and shrubs were measured (basal diameters, stem counts, and maximum stem height after pruning), and tagged. Insect pests were found on several of the experimental species, notably the locust borer (Megacyllene robiniae) and the eastern tent caterpillar (Malocosma americanum). These pests arrived with nursery material, and spread rapidly. When possible, these were controlled by hand-picking. However, their activities reduced the growth and reproduction of several trees, and in extreme cases led to mortality.

On two sides of each plot, a 4 × 20 m strip was surveyed, and a lengthwise half of each strip was cleared of herbaceous vegetation using a rotary cultivator. Our aim was to examine whether natural recruitment of new plants varied with distance, and whether disturbance enhanced recruitment. In subsequent years, sampling was extended to 25 m, but tilling was not repeated.

## Sampling and analytical methods

Sampling began in spring, 1992. All experimental plants were measured in fall of the first two years to track annual growth. Subsets of plants were studied to determine fruit production, as a measure of reproduc

tive potential, and as an estimate of pollinator visitation. Recruitment of new woody plants was recorded in fall censuses during 1993–1995. An additional census was made in spring 1993, to determine seasonal turnover of recruits. Within each plot and its two adjoining strip transects, all stems were identified to species and assigned to height classes. For a direct measure of growth and survivorship, a subset of 320 recruiting plants, representing 10 species, were marked and measured (height, ±1 cm) in spring 1994 and re-measured in fall 1994, inside 16 plots and 16 strip transects. In summer, 1996, we examined 25 additional 4 m wide strip transects (varying in length from 35 to 100 m), extended between edges of pairs of plots, counting and measuring all woody plant recruits.

The majority of the experimental species are clonal, sending up multiple stems from roots or rhizomes. Four of these (elderberry, winged sumac, and the two species of Rubus) are capable of lengthy horizontal expansion, and can be said to disperse clonally. Clonal growth was measured with sequential stem counts in late summer 1993 and 1994. In addition, recruitment of clonal stems into plot peripheries was recorded each year. Clonal shoots were distinguished from seedlings by probing the soil for rhizomatous connections.

Seed rain was monitored throughout most of the fruiting season (June through November) in 1994. One seed trap was placed within each of the 16 planted plots

and the four fenced, unplanted plots. Seed traps were 1 m² wooden frames with a bottom layer of 3 mm fiberglass mesh. All seeds from each trap were collected every 14 d and removed to the laboratory for identification and counting.

Woody plant recruitment data were analyzed with univariate tests of main treatment effects (planted vs. unplanted plots, small vs. large plants), and also compared by dispersal mode (wind vs. animal dispersal). Recruitment within plots was analyzed separately from recruitment on plot exteriors, which was examined on the basis of distance from plots, distance from site periphery, and distance to nearest putative source plant. Repeated-measures ANOVA was used to examine sequential treatment data. For contingency tests of proportional contributions of wind, avian, and clonal dispersal, G statistics were calculated as chi-square values corrected for continuity. Contours of interplot recruitment levels were mapped on a diagram of the site grid, using density contours smoothed with a quadratic function (Wilkinson et al. 1992). In addition to indirect evidence of bird visitation provided by plant recruitment rates, we kept an inventory of all bird species observed on the site.

# RESULTS

Growth and reproduction of experimental plants

Among the experimental plants, all but 18 shrubs survived through the first full growing season (1992),

although many trees suffered considerable dieback, probably due to desiccation and poor root establishment. The actinorrhizal shrub, bayberry, was the species most prone to mortality. These losses, coupled with the realization that the nutrient-rich leaf mulch could mask any short-term contribution of N-fixers, led us to restrict analyses of plot treatments to plant size effects only, for the duration reported here. Injured trees, which continued to function as perches for avian dispersers, were not pruned.

Most surviving plants were reproductive in 1993, yielding at least a few flowers each. However, the outcrossing, insect-pollinated shrubs—grey dogwood, elderberry, and arrowwood—accounted for most (90%) of the observed flower production that year. Among the inflorescences studied among the three species, fruits were produced from 4802 of 17 960 flowers, a fruit set rate of 27%. Subsequent work on pollination and pollinator diversity is reported elsewhere (Yurlina 1998).

## Recruitment and plot treatments

Plots with trees and shrubs had much higher recruitment of new woody plants than empty plots. On average, over twice as many new plants were observed in plots planted with trees and shrubs, and by 1995 we found a three- to four-fold difference (Fig. 3), primarily due to differences in avian-dispersed seedlings (Table 2). Counts of recruits fluctuated annually, indicating substantial losses in 1994, followed by some compensatory gains. Of the 737 colonizing plants found in 1995 samples of plot centers, 212 (29%) originated as

clones, only one of which occurred in an unplanted plot. Plots with large experimental plants had higher average recruitment densities at the outset, but that relationship weakened with time (Fig. 3).

Within the strip transects extending from plot edges, recruitment densities were higher in those portions that were cleared by tilling. However, this difference was limited to the first pulse of recruitment measured at the outset of sampling (Fig. 4). Densities of recruits within transects were highly correlated with recruit densities in plot centers for all planted plots (Pearson's R = 0.77 to 0.92, over the four censuses). The same was not true of unplanted plots (Pearson's R = -0.02 to 0.35), another indication that the plantings had an attractive function.

## Seed rain patterns

Seventeen species were found in 1994 seed rain samples, nine from external sources, six from planted species, and two that probably originated from both sources (elderberry and winged sumac). Most seeds (7650 of 8519) were captured during a 1-mo period from early August to early September. Mean annual seed densities were 18.3/m² in fenced controls and 527.9/m² in planted plots, where cumulative counts varied from 32 to 5116/m² per plot. The correlation between seed rain density and the density of recruits in the following year was weak (Pearson's R = 0.194). Planted plots with the most seed species had the highest total seed counts (regression: ln[seed count] = 2.89 + 1.39[ln(species)]; regression coefficient SE = 0.571;

## Growth and survivorship of recruiting plants

Among the marked and measured recruits, 12.5% (40 of 320) were missing or confirmed dead at the end of the season. The most susceptible species was elderberry, a species very sensitive to desiccation (Dirr 1983), which lost 15 of 67 individuals. Height increments for survivors ranged from −32 cm to 49 cm, with an overall mean of 8.1 cm. Positive growth inside plots was greater than in the transects, with a mean increment of 9.6 (±8.4) cm vs. 6.7 (±8.1) cm. Size distributions of recruits shifted quickly, with older recruits contributing proportionately more each year (Fig. 5). Annual size distributions were comparable for planted or unplanted plots (and their respective peripheries) in 1993. However, by 1996 the planted plots had a substantially larger percentage of recruits in the smallest (0.5 m) size class (17.3% vs. 3.1%).

## Recruitment modes

Forty-eight bird species were observed within the experimental site, 34 of which have the potential to disperse seeds of fruit-bearing plants (Appendix 2). Recruitment attributed to avian dispersal was clustered in and around plots, whereas wind-dispersed recruitment was more evenly spread. For planted plots, mean density of wind-dispersed recruits in 1995 was 351/ha within plots and 512/ha on plot margins. During the same period, mean density of bird-dispersed recruits was 2301/ha within plots and 625/ha on plot margins. Clonal dispersal contributed substantially within, but not surrounding the planted plots (mean recruitment densities of 1319 and 398 stems/ha, respectively).

A fence effect was consistently apparent, in that the

proportional contribution of avian dispersal was significantly higher in fenced vs. unfenced control (unplanted) plots. In fall 1993, 46 of 83 recruits inside fenced controls were bird-dispersed, compared to a much smaller proportion (11 of 62) in unfenced plots ($G_{1,0} = 19.57; P &lt; 0.0001$). Similar proportions carried into 1995 (31 of 48 vs. 12 of 54; $G_{1,0} = 17.00; P &lt; 0.0001$). Extrapolating from densities in the unplanted plots, we estimate that of the 1029 avian-dispersed recruits within planted plots in 1995, 12.4% could be indirectly attributed to background seed rain and 34.6% to a fence effect.

Recruitment densities were lower between plots, where the proportion of wind-dispersed trees and shrubs was much higher. The 1996 interplot transect surveys yielded a total of 493 new woody plants in a census area of 6160/m², for an average inter-plot density of 800/ha. Of these, 53.5% were wind-dispersed species, 35.9% avian-dispersed, and 10.6% clonally generated (usually extending from planted plots).

## Recruitment and site species diversity

The flux of new species added to the experimental site was rapid and brief (Fig. 6). Sixteen of the 17 woody species found on the site margin had colonized by 1995 (the exception was hackberry, Celtis occidentalis). Prior to 1994, seedlings of elderberry and black locust could be attributed exclusively to natural populations, but experimental transplants may have served as seed sources thereafter. Only four other experimental planted species—grey dogwood, winged sumac, and the two Rubus species—had contributed by 1995, the latter three primarily by clonal reproduction.

The six additional recruiting species were American ash, black cherry (Prunus serotina Ehrh.), bitter nightshade (Solanum dulcamara L.), hawthorn (Crataegus sp.), Virginia creeper (Parthenocissus quinquefolia (L.) Planchon), and poison ivy (Toxicodendron radicans (L.) Kunze). The latter two were first observed growing at the base of experimental transplants, and were probably introduced with nursery soils. With the exception

With respect to relative abundances, a few species were dominant. Among all 1995 plot and transect censuses, 83% of nonclonal recruitment was attributable to five plant species, American ash, trembling aspen, elderberry (S. canadensis), and the two mulberry species (M. alba and M. rubra). Within the interplot transects studied in the 1996 census, these same five species accounted for 93% of the nonclonal recruits.

## Spatial patterns of recruitment

The relative attractive function of the experimental plots appeared to be highly localized. A direct measure of this is the relationship between recruitment density of bird-dispersed species and proximity to plot edges. Density of avian dispersed woody plants declined with distance from plot edges, as indicated by significantly

negative regression coefficients (Table 3). In contrast, wind-dispersed recruits were distributed more-or-less evenly over the same distances, as indicated by slopes indistinguishable from zero (Table 3).

The general spatial patterns of recruitment are portrayed in Fig. 7, which depicts density and height contours determined from the 1996 inter-plot surveys. Strong directionality is evident for both wind- and bird-dispersed plants. Wind-dispersed plants were heavily clustered near edges of the experimental field (Fig. 7a), particularly in the southern corner. In contrast, bird-dispersed recruits, although better-distributed in the center of the field, were strongly clustered in the eastern corner. The most successful bird-dispersed recruit (representing 57.7% of the total) was elderberry (S. canadensis), a shrub that grows profusely on the site's eastern margin (Fig. 7b).

## DISCUSSION

Plant propagule movement can regulate community composition over multiple spatial and temporal scales (e.g., Willson 1993, Pitelka et al. 1997, Clark et al. 1998), and the early stages of land reclamation and restoration are no exception (Montalvo et al. 1997). Effective natural dispersal can lead to remarkable increases in the pace of succession on degraded lands (Bradshaw 1988, Robinson and Handel 1993, van Aarde et al. 1997), but dispersal barriers may impede succession following both natural and anthropogenic disturbance (Janzen 1988, Woodwell 1992, Ash et al. 1994, Ray and Brown 1994, Franklin et al. 1995, Dobson et al. 1997, Clarke et al. 1998). When a reclaimed site is embedded in a relatively intact natural landscape, little or no intervention may be required beyond site preparation (Bell et al. 1997), whereas isolated sites are bound to pose larger challenges (Handel et al. 1994, Holl 1995, Jackson et al. 1995). a means to overcome dispersal barriers by attracting dispersal agents to target islands in a reclamation site.

Part of the inspiration for this study can be found in simulation models of biotic invasions that have found a significant role for colonization by small, satellite populations (Moody and Mack 1988, Vitousek et al. 1996). Satellites form nuclear "foci" (Yarranton and Morrison 1974) for the spread of invaders—a more rapid form of invasion than simple diffusive growth on the perimeter of a single population (Auld and Coote 1980). Our experimental clusters of plants were influential in directing seed dispersal, although the spatial patterns of seed deposition and seedling recruitment were complex. Wind-dispersed plants were more likely to be found on the periphery of the field, and were not associated with experimental treatments. Avian-dispersed recruitment was focused around experimental planted plots (the concentric model of Fig. 1c), indicating an attractive function.

Recruitment was also associated with a strong source-proximity component (as in Fig. 1d). Seed deposition itself appeared highly variable, and could not be explained on the basis of plant size treatment effects, nor was it well correlated with subsequent recruitment.

Of the plant species that did arrive, none were unexpected (in the sense of arriving from obviously distant sources), and only a few contributed seedlings in abundance. During many attempts at ecological restoration, general successes or failures may depend critically on the activity or inactivity of nearby natural populations, which bolster and often rescue the efforts of practitioners. At the same time, restoration/rehabilitation projects can also provide important windows on local biodiversity, offering a functional assay of local natural populations. For example, in a related study of a reclamation project on Staten Island, New York, we found that the seed rain volume within clustered experimental plantings depended on the proximity and extent of nearby source plant populations. Seed numbers were substantially higher in plantings closer to the putative source (a small native woodland), and, following the loss of approximately half of the source habitat, seed rain decreased commensurably (Mattei and Handel 1997).

We connect recruitment to the behavior of avian dispersers only by inference, and offer no direct evidence of links between bird behavior and dispersal. However, frugivore behavior may have been a key determinant

GEORGE R. ROBINSON AND STEVEN N. HANDEL
Ecological Applications Vol. 10, No. 1
184

of the relative contributions of different woody plant species to recruitment. While specialization may be the exception among North American frugivores (Willson 1986, Malmborg and Willson 1988), the habits of many species (especially flocking birds) are difficult to predict, as are their local abundances (Willson and Whelan 1990a, b). Therefore, the food preferences of one or a few bird species may have been a driving force. Nonetheless, against a background of large temporal variability, many experimental effects were statistically significant and woodland succession was under way, with the establishment of several thousand new woody plants in a few years.

The experimental plantings did not serve well as recruitment sources, however, and most new recruits came from peripheral species. This latter finding has an interesting practical implication for restoration ecology. Plots with taller, more massive plantings had higher recruitment rates, but only at the end of year one. Larger plants are more costly, more difficult to install, and more vulnerable to transplant shock. In this particular setting, the combination of exposure to strong winds and the unnatural substrate may have stressed larger plants disproportionately. Therefore, given these disadvantages, the modest benefits seem insufficient to outweigh the practical value of using smaller plants.

In many cases, restorationists do not want their planted materials to take over a site, because the plantings represent mixes of genotypes that may not be well suited for the full range of ecological interactions that characterize a reviving ecosystem (Larson 1996, Montalvo et al. 1997). In our study, wild populations contributed substantially to the early gene pool, and planted materials seem unlikely to overwhelm the site, judging from their limited spread. Nevertheless, genetic mismatches are a growing concern in land restoration and reclamation (e.g., Gordon and Rice 1998) and an important issue for future research (Montalvo et al. 1997).

Recruiting seedlings were more prevalent at first in cleared strips, but these were quickly colonized by herbaceous species, and woody plant densities declined, matching those in uncleared areas. Although a herbaceous cover crop can shelter woody seedlings and promote their survival (Choi and Wali 1995), competitive effects of herbaceous vegetation on woody plants are often expressed at the seedling stage (Facelli and Pickett 1991, Eliason and Allen 1997). Available safe sites for seedling establishment may have declined over time throughout the experimental field, as seen in the general increase in average plant size commensurate with a fall in the number of recruits censused. The general problem of safe site limitations appears to be a significant impediment to reclamation efforts (Urbanska 1997). Another threat may have been posed by the growing populations of small mammals observed on our site, notably *Microtus pennsylvanicus* (G. Robinson and S. Handel, unpublished data), and an influential role for seedling predation cannot be discounted.

In comparison to seed dispersal, clonal reproduction contributed much less to overall recruitment, and added little to the spatial spread of woody plants. Clonal growth might be a particularly effective dispersal method in land reclamation, because a disperser's survival is greatly enhanced by connections to a parent plant (Hutchings and Wijesinghe 1997). However, rates of clonal spread rarely match the potential of dispersed seeds, and low-density plantings like ours are not likely to quickly propagate a woodland.

The N-fixer treatments were apparently ineffective, at least for the period reported here. Studies of the potential for nitrogen-fixing plants in forest succession indicate that fertilizing effects may be gradual and incremental, important for establishing long-term nutrient pools (Morris et al. 1974, Skeffington and Bradshaw 1980, Boring and Swank 1984, Ashby et al. 1985), but less likely to show immediate measurable effects on adjacent vegetation (Fimbel 1992, Bradshaw 1997).

Perhaps more significant than declining rates of recruitment, woody plant species richness reached an early and shallow threshold. The background landscape was quite depauperate, as seen in the small number of native woody species added to the site. A few species have dominated, at least in the early stages, and the development of a more diverse woodland may require further intervention. In a more natural setting, a comparable inoculation technique ought to be more effective. A broader issue is the narrowing window of opportunity to draw on natural dispersal resources, as background natural populations continue to decline (Tilman et al. 1994, Hughes et al. 1997, Nee and May 1997). Our study shows that basic ecological processes can be directed to supply woody plant recruits even in a degraded urban setting. However, in such settings the ultimate structural and functional targets must be realistically defined (Clark 1997), with the expectation that long-distance dispersal events may be too infrequent to raise site diversity to levels associated with historic natural communities.

## Evidence extraction (verbatim quotes)

- Spatial measurement precision:
  - “Site margins and all plot centers were **mapped on a two-dimensional grid (±1 m resolution)**. On the site periphery, the nearest potential source plants for woody seedling recruitment were identified and mapped on the same grid.”

- Measurement precision for some biological variables (not necessarily confounders, but shows general measurement approach):
  - “Once installed, all 336 trees and shrubs were measured (basal diameters, stem counts, and maximum stem height after pruning), and tagged.”
  - “For a direct measure of growth and survivorship, a subset of 320 recruiting plants… were marked and measured (**height, ±1 cm**)…”
  - “Seed traps were **1 m²** wooden frames… All seeds from each trap were collected every **14 d** and removed to the laboratory for identification and counting.”

- A key process relevant to confounding (bird behavior) was not directly measured:
  - “**We connect recruitment to the behavior of avian dispersers only by inference, and offer no direct evidence of links between bird behavior and dispersal.**”

## Reasoning (step-by-step)

1. The question asks whether *potential confounders* were measured accurately and precisely enough.
2. The paper provides explicit precision for **some** measurements that could relate to confounding in spatial analyses—most clearly, plot and margin positions were “mapped… (±1 m resolution).” This supports that **distance-related variables** (e.g., distance to plot edge/periphery/source plants) were measured with stated precision.
3. However, the paper does **not** comprehensively list all potential confounders nor does it systematically report the accuracy/precision of measurements for each (e.g., factors like herbaceous competition intensity, microtopography/drainage variation, animal activity).
4. Importantly, for a major plausible confounding influence in this study (bird visitation/behavior), the authors explicitly state they have “no direct evidence of links between bird behavior and dispersal,” indicating that at least this potentially confounding process was **not directly measured**, so its measurement accuracy/precision cannot be judged as sufficient from the paper.
5. Because precision is reported for some variables but not for confounders as a whole—and at least one key confounding process is only inferred—the paper text does not allow a clear determination that confounders were measured accurately/precisely enough overall.

--- PAPER TEXT ---
Ecological Applications, 10(1), 2000, pp. 174-188 © 2000 by the Ecological Society of America

# DIRECTING SPATIAL PATTERNS OF RECRUITMENT DURING AN EXPERIMENTAL URBAN WOODLAND RECLAMATION

GEORGE R. ROBINSON¹,³ AND STEVEN N. HANDEL²

¹Department of Biological Sciences, State University of New York at Albany, Albany, New York 12222, USA
²Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Natural Resources, Rutgers University, One College Farm Road, New Brunswick, New Jersey 08901-1582 USA

Abstract. Studies of biological invasions indicate that natural recruitment of new species can occur as a “nucleation” phenomenon, in which scattered colonization foci spread and coalesce. Ecological reclamation of damaged lands might make use of this potential for enhanced natural dispersal, by inoculating sites with multiple small plantings to attract animal dispersers and other mutualists from nearby remnants of natural habitat. We conducted an experimental test of this proposition.

On a 6-ha section of an abandoned municipal landfill in the New Jersey Meadowlands, we installed 16 clusters of 21 trees and shrubs in an array of fenced plots. Clusters contained seven native species known to: (1) attract bird dispersers to introduce propagules from remnants of off-site habitat; (2) contribute propagules by virtue of high reproductive output and clonal growth; and (3) accelerate woodland succession on open, degraded habitats. Average plant size was varied, with half the plots receiving larger trees and shrubs, to test whether woody plant size would enhance any attractive function. An additional eight empty plots were studied to estimate background rates of recruitment and to test for a fencing effect. Site preparation included the addition of 90 cm of fresh substrate, including organic matter, and a cover crop of annual grasses. Recruitment of woody plants inside and surrounding the experimental plots was examined for five years, and results were compared on the basis of treatment and recruitment mode (avian, wind, or clonal dispersal).

Woody plant recruitment into experimental plots was rapid and substantial, primarily via dispersal from natural sources. Plots with larger plants attracted significantly more recruits at the outset, but this difference diminished over time. Fall seed rain samples yielded a mean estimate of 426 seeds/m² within plots. However, size distributions of recruiting woody species increasingly shifted toward larger individuals each year. Experimental manipulations that opened seed beds for woody plant recruitment had short-lived effects, indicating a narrow window of opportunity for establishment. Spread of the planted species themselves was generally weak, although clonal growth contributed substantially to spread on the margins of plots.

Most recruitment outside experimental plots was from external sources. A strong proximity component was found for bird-dispersed recruits, which were highly clustered near planted plots, with the highest densities near source populations on the site margin. Wind-dispersed trees and shrubs, by contrast, were not associated with planted plots and were concentrated near one corner of the site. Discounting plot interiors, total recruitment density for the site after 5 yr was ~800 woody stems/ha, 36% via avian dispersal, 10% via clonal spread, and the remainder via wind-borne propagules. New recruits represented 26 woody plant species, all but four from external sources, and only five common species contributed more than a few recruits. We conclude that techniques for manipulating natural seed dispersal hold promise for ecological restoration, provided that background populations are available to supply colonists.

Key words: clonal growth; dispersal; experimental reclamation; nucleation; safe sites; seed sources; spatial pattern; surrounding landscape.

# INTRODUCTION

## The ecological context of woodland restoration

Ecological restoration can be likened to accelerated succession, in part because it aims to pass over the early phases of community development, when recovery can be delayed by the effects of past degradation (Aber 1987, Allen 1988, Bradshaw 1989, Luken 1990, Parker 1997). Following severe habitat damage, the reclamation phase closely resembles primary succession, in which most organisms colonize from external source populations. Indeed, a common goal of ecological restoration is to initiate natural populations as dispersing immigrants (Bradshaw 1988, Harris et al. 1993,

Handel 1997). Two areas of ecological research are especially pertinent here: propagule dispersal and the spatial dynamics of natural populations. In this study, we examined the potential to attract recruits from surrounding habitats as a means of stimulating succession from open field to woodland. Our focus was on avian frugivores and the trees and shrubs they disperse in northeastern North America.

Inaugurating populations by drawing from natural sources is particularly challenging when attempted within a depauperate natural background. In such cases, experiments can be used to test the strength of ecological connections—whether processes like dispersal and pollination are sufficiently robust to initiate wild populations on reclaimed habitats (Handel et al. 1994, Handel 1997). Urban areas present some of the greater challenges, in part because remaining natural populations are in decline (Robinson et al. 1994, Drayton and Primack 1996) and tend to occur in patches, isolated by distances that limit exchange by natural dispersal (Sharpe et al. 1986).

The ways in which small, isolated plant populations function and interact are of great interest to restoration ecology, because the newly introduced populations must survive and reproduce under unusual physical circumstances. Furthermore, the formative plant community is unlikely to grow and persist without external biotic inputs, such as mutualists or new individuals to rescue small populations. Recruits from natural sources, however, may arrive slowly or not at all. We explored the spatial and temporal patterns of natural dispersal into an isolated reclaimed site, using artificial patches of vegetation, designated as habitat islands.

## Habitat islands as tools for ecological reclamation

When the invasion process of succession is short-circuited, the use of small artificial islands designed to grow and spread may boost rates of invasion (Yarranton and Morrison 1974). We are exploring how ecological attributes of artificial habitat islands affect their interactions with background natural populations, and following recruitment among habitat islands to study the spatial character of dispersal. For example, when dispersal agents pass frequently among islands, propagules may travel with no directional pattern (Fig. 1a), or in the extreme become concentrated among clusters of islands (Fig. 1b). Concentric spread (Fig. 1c) is more likely when dispersal agents are scarce (so that most

propagules fall near parent plants), or when spread is driven by clonal growth. Dispersal can also be highly directional (Fig. 1d), in cases where most dispersal agents arrive from one major source.

## Seed dispersal by frugivores

Many trees and shrubs of eastern North America depend on avian dispersers to move seeds to new establishment sites (Stapanian 1986, Stiles 1989). These plants have short-lived seed banks and rely on frugivorous birds to maintain and establish populations (Sørensen 1981, Howe and Smallwood 1982, James and Wamer 1982, Jordano 1982, Estrada and Fleming 1986, Stapanian 1986, Willson 1986, Sallbanks 1992). One of the commonly-observed results is that avian dispersers contribute substantially to the progress of woodland succession (McAtee 1947, Bard 1952, Johnston and Odum 1956, Buell et al. 1971, Smith 1975, Marks 1983, Morris et al. 1986, Brown and Archer 1987, 1989, Holt et al. 1995). Their contributions can be enhanced by the presence of elevated perches, as demonstrated experimentally in old fields of northeastern North America (McDonnell and Stiles 1983, McDonnell 1986), and observed in similar settings throughout the world (Livingston 1972, Uhl et al. 1982, Werner and Harbeck 1982, Finegan 1984, Guevara et al. 1986, McClanahan and Wolfe 1987, 1993, Campbell et al. 1990, Debussche and Isenmann 1990, Izhaki et al. 1991, Nepstad et al. 1991). Large or otherwise apparent fruit displays also attract avian dispersers (e.g., Moore and Willson 1980, Sargeant 1990), and this leads to the possibility that fleshy-fruited woody plants, which may serve as both perches and food sources, can be arranged to maximize frugivore visits.

In two studies of woodland succession onto derelict lands, we found that modest plantings of trees and shrubs led to substantial recruitment of avian-dispersed woody species. In one case, in a 14-yr-old clustered planting of 19 tree species, natural dispersal had added 18 new woody species at densities of over 6000 stems/ha (Robinson et al. 1992). In another case, following a scattered planting of trees and shrubs, 20 new woody species were added at densities of 640 stems/ha after a single year (Robinson and Handel 1993).

As a rule, it appears that avian dispersers are sensitive to landscape patterns. For example, patch size influences the likelihood of disperser visits (Leck 1976a, b, Santos and Tellaria 1994), and large openings may be slow to undergo succession, because dispersers pass over or avoid them (McClanahan 1986, Da Silva et al. 1996). Patch connectivity also may be required, and isolated successional sites may be disconnected because dispersers will not cross unfamiliar territory (e.g., Darley-Hill and Johnson 1981, Johnson and Adkisson 1985).

## Post-dispersal limitations to recruitment

A growing literature on restoring native species to degraded sites points to severe limitations imposed by

site characteristics, such as deficient soils (Bradshaw and Chadwick 1980), exposure to overwhelming herbivory (Waller and Alverson 1997), and competitive interactions with established plants, particularly the weedy species that occupy or invade reclamation sites (Schmitz et al. 1997, Sauer 1998). Simply boosting dispersal could therefore prove insufficient to accelerate woodland succession, without taking steps to identify potential safe site limitations (Harper 1977), to test their relative effects and to ameliorate the most influential limiting factors. In some cases, the plants chosen for reclamation may improve site properties, such as nutrient mineralization (Bradshaw and Chadwick 1980), while in others site preparation requirements may include manipulating the substrate to ensure abundant safe sites (Parsons and Zedler 1997, Urbanska 1997).

## Experimental objectives

We tested the following questions on an isolated, degraded urban reclamation site. First, are frugivores available to act as reliable seed dispersers, and can they be attracted into an experimental site? Second, can we influence rates and spatial patterns of avian frugivore visits (and thereby woody plant recruitment) by inoculating a site with scattered clusters of trees and shrubs? Third, will the experimental clusters of plants themselves spread quickly enough to contribute to woodland succession? We also examined whether structural and ecological properties of the experimental plants would influence their effectiveness as attractants and propagule sources. To test whether dispersers were available and effective, we (1) monitored avian species diversity, (2) compared seed rain and seedling recruitment of woody plants in plots with and without plantings, (3) examined recruitment density as a function of distance from experimental plots, and (4) compared recruitment of fruit-bearing woody species with wind-dispersed trees and shrubs.

To further test whether properties of the experimental plants would influence recruitment, we adjusted average plant size per cluster as a means of controlling perch height and fruit display. Clonally-dispersing species were included, to test whether clonal propagation was comparable to seedling recruitment.

To compare the contributions of internal and external seed sources, we examined recruitment density on the basis of source category, and distance from sources, to test (1) whether densities would vary throughout the site as a function of source (on-site vs. off-site), and (2) whether densities of externally-derived recruits would vary with either proximity to site periphery or distance to nearest source population.

Potential post-dispersal limitations were addressed in three ways. (1) Nitrogen-fixing species were included in planted clusters, to test for N limitations on growth, reproduction, and recruitment. (2) Mechanical cultivation was introduced to reduce herbaceous veg

# METHODS

## Site preparation

The site consists of approximately 15 ha of filled former marshland, surrounded by open water, roads and freeways, in the Hackensack Meadowlands of New Jersey (Plate 1). Most of the site is an abandoned municipal landfill ringed with a reed grass (*Phragmites australis* (Cav.) Trin.) community that slopes into estuarine communities and shallow open water on two sides. The experimental area occupies 6 ha atop the shallow landfill that operated until the early 1960s. Post-closure treatment was apparently limited to a thin layer of coarse cover material, probably composed of excavated subsoil and construction debris (D. Smith, personal communication). A surface fire in summer 1986 burned into the contents, and the combination of fire and lengthy decomposition in this shallow, uncapped landfill probably resulted in the loss of most organic contents. Prior to experimental preparation, the surface consisted of rubble and exposed trash, with a very sparse cover of weedy vegetation (e.g., Stalter 1984). We focused efforts on the development of a native woodland, because wooded sites, which provide critical habitat for many migrating birds, have become scarce in the region (Kane 1991).

The experimental area was surveyed and mapped on a 150 × 400 m grid, and arrangements were made to add sufficient growing medium to support woody plants. Most of the base substrate (94%) arrived from a single source, a deep excavation of buried sandy sediments from Manhattan. Tests of samples indicated a uniformly low organic content (0.058% dry mass), high pH (7.8), low total nitrogen (0.02% dry mass), and high calcium (4700 ppm). The remaining base material arrived from an excavation in Bergen County, New Jersey, USA. This latter material was a clay loam with moderate organic content (4.31% by mass), and considerably lower pH (6.3), but comparably low total nitrogen (0.15% by mass) and calcium (3400 ppm). The top layer was 30 cm of composted leaf mulch (~100% organic matter) that had been stocked in piles for one or more years. To cover the experimental area with new substrate at a depth of 90 cm required ~45000 m³ of transported subsoil and 19000 m³ of composted leaf mulch. Drainage was poor in several locations, resulting in temporary ponds that later evaporated. Experimental plot positions were shifted to avoid planting in waterlogged areas.

The two substrate layers were partially mixed during spreading, but most of the mulch component remained on top. To reduce erosion and as a measure of weed control, the freshly covered site was sown with a commercial annual grass mixture, predominately Japanese millet (*Echinocloa crus-galli*, var. *frumentacea* (Rox.) W. F. Wight), a warm season annual. Sowing took place ~1 wk before experimental planting began. As intended, the annual grass quickly diminished in cover by the following spring, replaced by a mix of native and non-native herbaceous vegetation that varies seasonally and annually (Appendix 1). Propagules of one local weedy tree-of-heaven, *Ailanthus altissima* (Miller) Swingle, apparently arrived in the imported leaf mulch, and we decided to remove its seedlings and sprouts at the outset, to avoid confounding artificial and natural recruitment. In summer 1992, we manually removed ~2000 stems of this species.

Woody plants growing on the immediate periphery (within 50 m) consisted of a sparse, species-poor mix of trees and shrubs. Species native to the region were American ash (*Fraxinus americana* L.), boxelder (*Acer negundo* L.), groundsel bush (*Baccharis halimifolia* L.), hackberry (*Celtis occidentalis* L.), red-berried mulberry (*Morus rubra* L.), quaking aspen (*Populus tremuloides* Michx.), smooth sumac (*Rhus glabra* L.), staghorn sumac (*Rhus typhina* L.), blackberries (*Rubus* spp. L.), pussy willow (*Salix discolor* Muhl.), and el

Seven species were non-indigenous: tree-of-heaven, Russian olive (Eleagnus angustifolia L.), honey locust (Gleditsia tricanthos L.), Asian mulberry (Morus alba L.), princess tree (Paulownia tomentosa (Thunb. Steudel.)), black locust (Robinia pseudoacacia L.), and European alder buckthorn (Rhamnus frangula L.). (Nomenclature follows Gleason and Cronquist [1991].) Populations of all 18 taxa were very small, and only four species were represented by more than five individuals—elderberry, red-berried mulberry, smooth sumac, and tree-of-heaven. In addition, a large population of trembling aspen (N &gt; 1000) was located on an elevated wasteland site whose nearest border was ~0.5 km to the west, across two highways.

## Experimental layout and plant installations

After site preparation, we introduced experimental clusters of woody plants in fall 1991, as the initial grass cover crop was germinating. Sixteen plots were planted with 21 woody plants each, according to a two-by-two factorial design. The factors were (1) plant size (larger or smaller) and (2) the inclusion of nitrogen-fixing trees and shrubs (with or without N-fixers). Plant size was determined by selection, with the goal of maintaining average height per species at approximately half-size in plots designated for the smaller plant treatment combinations. All plants were pruned to about two-thirds of original size, to reduce transplant shock. In some cases, tall, thin trees were further pruned to meet the "small" height category. Plants that died were replaced in spring 1992. We watered all installed plants throughout dry periods during the first two growing seasons.

Experimental native plants (Table 1) were chosen to produce abundant fruit soon after transplanting, and to spread fruit production over a full season. For example, black cherry (Prunus serotina) produces ripe fruit in mid-summer, while arrowwood (Viburnum dentatum) and grey dogwood (Cornus racemosa) have fruits that ripen in late summer, and ripe fruits of winged sumac (Rhus copallina) are displayed throughout winter. The trees and larger shrubs were obtained from commercial nurseries, while some of the smaller plants (R. copallina, Rubus spp. and Sambucus canadensis) were excavated from successional old fields or on the perimeter

of the experimental site. For all transplants, an effort was made to include large root volumes (none were bare-root transplants), that not only aid in establishment, but also help ensure that soil-borne mutualists were included.

To reduce damage by browsing eastern cottontail rabbits (Sylvilagus floridanus), we constructed a wire fence surrounding each planted plot. Eight empty plots were laid out, four with fencing (which had the potential to serve as a perch for avian frugivores) and four without fencing. The 24 plots were placed on a 150 × 400 m grid in a random array, stratified to prevent neighboring plots with the same treatment. The final plot arrangement is presented in Fig. 2. Spacing was somewhat irregular, in order to avoid spots with insufficient substrate or impeded drainage. Site margins and all plot centers were mapped on a two-dimensional grid (±1 m resolution). On the site periphery, the nearest potential source plants for woody seedling recruitment were identified and mapped on the same grid.

Once installed, all 336 trees and shrubs were measured (basal diameters, stem counts, and maximum stem height after pruning), and tagged. Insect pests were found on several of the experimental species, notably the locust borer (Megacyllene robiniae) and the eastern tent caterpillar (Malocosma americanum). These pests arrived with nursery material, and spread rapidly. When possible, these were controlled by hand-picking. However, their activities reduced the growth and reproduction of several trees, and in extreme cases led to mortality.

On two sides of each plot, a 4 × 20 m strip was surveyed, and a lengthwise half of each strip was cleared of herbaceous vegetation using a rotary cultivator. Our aim was to examine whether natural recruitment of new plants varied with distance, and whether disturbance enhanced recruitment. In subsequent years, sampling was extended to 25 m, but tilling was not repeated.

## Sampling and analytical methods

Sampling began in spring, 1992. All experimental plants were measured in fall of the first two years to track annual growth. Subsets of plants were studied to determine fruit production, as a measure of reproduc

tive potential, and as an estimate of pollinator visitation. Recruitment of new woody plants was recorded in fall censuses during 1993–1995. An additional census was made in spring 1993, to determine seasonal turnover of recruits. Within each plot and its two adjoining strip transects, all stems were identified to species and assigned to height classes. For a direct measure of growth and survivorship, a subset of 320 recruiting plants, representing 10 species, were marked and measured (height, ±1 cm) in spring 1994 and re-measured in fall 1994, inside 16 plots and 16 strip transects. In summer, 1996, we examined 25 additional 4 m wide strip transects (varying in length from 35 to 100 m), extended between edges of pairs of plots, counting and measuring all woody plant recruits.

The majority of the experimental species are clonal, sending up multiple stems from roots or rhizomes. Four of these (elderberry, winged sumac, and the two species of Rubus) are capable of lengthy horizontal expansion, and can be said to disperse clonally. Clonal growth was measured with sequential stem counts in late summer 1993 and 1994. In addition, recruitment of clonal stems into plot peripheries was recorded each year. Clonal shoots were distinguished from seedlings by probing the soil for rhizomatous connections.

Seed rain was monitored throughout most of the fruiting season (June through November) in 1994. One seed trap was placed within each of the 16 planted plots

and the four fenced, unplanted plots. Seed traps were 1 m² wooden frames with a bottom layer of 3 mm fiberglass mesh. All seeds from each trap were collected every 14 d and removed to the laboratory for identification and counting.

Woody plant recruitment data were analyzed with univariate tests of main treatment effects (planted vs. unplanted plots, small vs. large plants), and also compared by dispersal mode (wind vs. animal dispersal). Recruitment within plots was analyzed separately from recruitment on plot exteriors, which was examined on the basis of distance from plots, distance from site periphery, and distance to nearest putative source plant. Repeated-measures ANOVA was used to examine sequential treatment data. For contingency tests of proportional contributions of wind, avian, and clonal dispersal, G statistics were calculated as chi-square values corrected for continuity. Contours of interplot recruitment levels were mapped on a diagram of the site grid, using density contours smoothed with a quadratic function (Wilkinson et al. 1992). In addition to indirect evidence of bird visitation provided by plant recruitment rates, we kept an inventory of all bird species observed on the site.

# RESULTS

Growth and reproduction of experimental plants

Among the experimental plants, all but 18 shrubs survived through the first full growing season (1992),

although many trees suffered considerable dieback, probably due to desiccation and poor root establishment. The actinorrhizal shrub, bayberry, was the species most prone to mortality. These losses, coupled with the realization that the nutrient-rich leaf mulch could mask any short-term contribution of N-fixers, led us to restrict analyses of plot treatments to plant size effects only, for the duration reported here. Injured trees, which continued to function as perches for avian dispersers, were not pruned.

Most surviving plants were reproductive in 1993, yielding at least a few flowers each. However, the outcrossing, insect-pollinated shrubs—grey dogwood, elderberry, and arrowwood—accounted for most (90%) of the observed flower production that year. Among the inflorescences studied among the three species, fruits were produced from 4802 of 17 960 flowers, a fruit set rate of 27%. Subsequent work on pollination and pollinator diversity is reported elsewhere (Yurlina 1998).

## Recruitment and plot treatments

Plots with trees and shrubs had much higher recruitment of new woody plants than empty plots. On average, over twice as many new plants were observed in plots planted with trees and shrubs, and by 1995 we found a three- to four-fold difference (Fig. 3), primarily due to differences in avian-dispersed seedlings (Table 2). Counts of recruits fluctuated annually, indicating substantial losses in 1994, followed by some compensatory gains. Of the 737 colonizing plants found in 1995 samples of plot centers, 212 (29%) originated as

clones, only one of which occurred in an unplanted plot. Plots with large experimental plants had higher average recruitment densities at the outset, but that relationship weakened with time (Fig. 3).

Within the strip transects extending from plot edges, recruitment densities were higher in those portions that were cleared by tilling. However, this difference was limited to the first pulse of recruitment measured at the outset of sampling (Fig. 4). Densities of recruits within transects were highly correlated with recruit densities in plot centers for all planted plots (Pearson's R = 0.77 to 0.92, over the four censuses). The same was not true of unplanted plots (Pearson's R = -0.02 to 0.35), another indication that the plantings had an attractive function.

## Seed rain patterns

Seventeen species were found in 1994 seed rain samples, nine from external sources, six from planted species, and two that probably originated from both sources (elderberry and winged sumac). Most seeds (7650 of 8519) were captured during a 1-mo period from early August to early September. Mean annual seed densities were 18.3/m² in fenced controls and 527.9/m² in planted plots, where cumulative counts varied from 32 to 5116/m² per plot. The correlation between seed rain density and the density of recruits in the following year was weak (Pearson's R = 0.194). Planted plots with the most seed species had the highest total seed counts (regression: ln[seed count] = 2.89 + 1.39[ln(species)]; regression coefficient SE = 0.571;

## Growth and survivorship of recruiting plants

Among the marked and measured recruits, 12.5% (40 of 320) were missing or confirmed dead at the end of the season. The most susceptible species was elderberry, a species very sensitive to desiccation (Dirr 1983), which lost 15 of 67 individuals. Height increments for survivors ranged from −32 cm to 49 cm, with an overall mean of 8.1 cm. Positive growth inside plots was greater than in the transects, with a mean increment of 9.6 (±8.4) cm vs. 6.7 (±8.1) cm. Size distributions of recruits shifted quickly, with older recruits contributing proportionately more each year (Fig. 5). Annual size distributions were comparable for planted or unplanted plots (and their respective peripheries) in 1993. However, by 1996 the planted plots had a substantially larger percentage of recruits in the smallest (0.5 m) size class (17.3% vs. 3.1%).

## Recruitment modes

Forty-eight bird species were observed within the experimental site, 34 of which have the potential to disperse seeds of fruit-bearing plants (Appendix 2). Recruitment attributed to avian dispersal was clustered in and around plots, whereas wind-dispersed recruitment was more evenly spread. For planted plots, mean density of wind-dispersed recruits in 1995 was 351/ha within plots and 512/ha on plot margins. During the same period, mean density of bird-dispersed recruits was 2301/ha within plots and 625/ha on plot margins. Clonal dispersal contributed substantially within, but not surrounding the planted plots (mean recruitment densities of 1319 and 398 stems/ha, respectively).

A fence effect was consistently apparent, in that the

proportional contribution of avian dispersal was significantly higher in fenced vs. unfenced control (unplanted) plots. In fall 1993, 46 of 83 recruits inside fenced controls were bird-dispersed, compared to a much smaller proportion (11 of 62) in unfenced plots ($G_{1,0} = 19.57; P &lt; 0.0001$). Similar proportions carried into 1995 (31 of 48 vs. 12 of 54; $G_{1,0} = 17.00; P &lt; 0.0001$). Extrapolating from densities in the unplanted plots, we estimate that of the 1029 avian-dispersed recruits within planted plots in 1995, 12.4% could be indirectly attributed to background seed rain and 34.6% to a fence effect.

Recruitment densities were lower between plots, where the proportion of wind-dispersed trees and shrubs was much higher. The 1996 interplot transect surveys yielded a total of 493 new woody plants in a census area of 6160/m², for an average inter-plot density of 800/ha. Of these, 53.5% were wind-dispersed species, 35.9% avian-dispersed, and 10.6% clonally generated (usually extending from planted plots).

## Recruitment and site species diversity

The flux of new species added to the experimental site was rapid and brief (Fig. 6). Sixteen of the 17 woody species found on the site margin had colonized by 1995 (the exception was hackberry, Celtis occidentalis). Prior to 1994, seedlings of elderberry and black locust could be attributed exclusively to natural populations, but experimental transplants may have served as seed sources thereafter. Only four other experimental planted species—grey dogwood, winged sumac, and the two Rubus species—had contributed by 1995, the latter three primarily by clonal reproduction.

The six additional recruiting species were American ash, black cherry (Prunus serotina Ehrh.), bitter nightshade (Solanum dulcamara L.), hawthorn (Crataegus sp.), Virginia creeper (Parthenocissus quinquefolia (L.) Planchon), and poison ivy (Toxicodendron radicans (L.) Kunze). The latter two were first observed growing at the base of experimental transplants, and were probably introduced with nursery soils. With the exception

With respect to relative abundances, a few species were dominant. Among all 1995 plot and transect censuses, 83% of nonclonal recruitment was attributable to five plant species, American ash, trembling aspen, elderberry (S. canadensis), and the two mulberry species (M. alba and M. rubra). Within the interplot transects studied in the 1996 census, these same five species accounted for 93% of the nonclonal recruits.

## Spatial patterns of recruitment

The relative attractive function of the experimental plots appeared to be highly localized. A direct measure of this is the relationship between recruitment density of bird-dispersed species and proximity to plot edges. Density of avian dispersed woody plants declined with distance from plot edges, as indicated by significantly

negative regression coefficients (Table 3). In contrast, wind-dispersed recruits were distributed more-or-less evenly over the same distances, as indicated by slopes indistinguishable from zero (Table 3).

The general spatial patterns of recruitment are portrayed in Fig. 7, which depicts density and height contours determined from the 1996 inter-plot surveys. Strong directionality is evident for both wind- and bird-dispersed plants. Wind-dispersed plants were heavily clustered near edges of the experimental field (Fig. 7a), particularly in the southern corner. In contrast, bird-dispersed recruits, although better-distributed in the center of the field, were strongly clustered in the eastern corner. The most successful bird-dispersed recruit (representing 57.7% of the total) was elderberry (S. canadensis), a shrub that grows profusely on the site's eastern margin (Fig. 7b).

## DISCUSSION

Plant propagule movement can regulate community composition over multiple spatial and temporal scales (e.g., Willson 1993, Pitelka et al. 1997, Clark et al. 1998), and the early stages of land reclamation and restoration are no exception (Montalvo et al. 1997). Effective natural dispersal can lead to remarkable increases in the pace of succession on degraded lands (Bradshaw 1988, Robinson and Handel 1993, van Aarde et al. 1997), but dispersal barriers may impede succession following both natural and anthropogenic disturbance (Janzen 1988, Woodwell 1992, Ash et al. 1994, Ray and Brown 1994, Franklin et al. 1995, Dobson et al. 1997, Clarke et al. 1998). When a reclaimed site is embedded in a relatively intact natural landscape, little or no intervention may be required beyond site preparation (Bell et al. 1997), whereas isolated sites are bound to pose larger challenges (Handel et al. 1994, Holl 1995, Jackson et al. 1995). Our experiment tested

a means to overcome dispersal barriers by attracting dispersal agents to target islands in a reclamation site.

Part of the inspiration for this study can be found in simulation models of biotic invasions that have found a significant role for colonization by small, satellite populations (Moody and Mack 1988, Vitousek et al. 1996). Satellites form nuclear "foci" (Yarranton and Morrison 1974) for the spread of invaders—a more rapid form of invasion than simple diffusive growth on the perimeter of a single population (Auld and Coote 1980). Our experimental clusters of plants were influential in directing seed dispersal, although the spatial patterns of seed deposition and seedling recruitment were complex. Wind-dispersed plants were more likely to be found on the periphery of the field, and were not associated with experimental treatments. Avian-dispersed recruitment was focused around experimental planted plots (the concentric model of Fig. 1c), indicating an attractive function.

Recruitment was also associated with a strong source-proximity component (as in Fig. 1d). Seed deposition itself appeared highly variable, and could not be explained on the basis of plant size treatment effects, nor was it well correlated with subsequent recruitment.

Of the plant species that did arrive, none were unexpected (in the sense of arriving from obviously distant sources), and only a few contributed seedlings in abundance. During many attempts at ecological restoration, general successes or failures may depend critically on the activity or inactivity of nearby natural populations, which bolster and often rescue the efforts of practitioners. At the same time, restoration/rehabilitation projects can also provide important windows on local biodiversity, offering a functional assay of local natural populations. For example, in a related study of a reclamation project on Staten Island, New York, we found that the seed rain volume within clustered experimental plantings depended on the proximity and extent of nearby source plant populations. Seed numbers were substantially higher in plantings closer to the putative source (a small native woodland), and, following the loss of approximately half of the source habitat, seed rain decreased commensurably (Mattei and Handel 1997).

We connect recruitment to the behavior of avian dispersers only by inference, and offer no direct evidence of links between bird behavior and dispersal. However, frugivore behavior may have been a key determinant

GEORGE R. ROBINSON AND STEVEN N. HANDEL
Ecological Applications Vol. 10, No. 1
184

of the relative contributions of different woody plant species to recruitment. While specialization may be the exception among North American frugivores (Willson 1986, Malmborg and Willson 1988), the habits of many species (especially flocking birds) are difficult to predict, as are their local abundances (Willson and Whelan 1990a, b). Therefore, the food preferences of one or a few bird species may have been a driving force. Nonetheless, against a background of large temporal variability, many experimental effects were statistically significant and woodland succession was under way, with the establishment of several thousand new woody plants in a few years.

The experimental plantings did not serve well as recruitment sources, however, and most new recruits came from peripheral species. This latter finding has an interesting practical implication for restoration ecology. Plots with taller, more massive plantings had higher recruitment rates, but only at the end of year one. Larger plants are more costly, more difficult to install, and more vulnerable to transplant shock. In this particular setting, the combination of exposure to strong winds and the unnatural substrate may have stressed larger plants disproportionately. Therefore, given these disadvantages, the modest benefits seem insufficient to outweigh the practical value of using smaller plants.

In many cases, restorationists do not want their planted materials to take over a site, because the plantings represent mixes of genotypes that may not be well suited for the full range of ecological interactions that characterize a reviving ecosystem (Larson 1996, Montalvo et al. 1997). In our study, wild populations contributed substantially to the early gene pool, and planted materials seem unlikely to overwhelm the site, judging from their limited spread. Nevertheless, genetic mismatches are a growing concern in land restoration and reclamation (e.g., Gordon and Rice 1998) and an important issue for future research (Montalvo et al. 1997).

Recruiting seedlings were more prevalent at first in cleared strips, but these were quickly colonized by herbaceous species, and woody plant densities declined, matching those in uncleared areas. Although a herbaceous cover crop can shelter woody seedlings and promote their survival (Choi and Wali 1995), competitive effects of herbaceous vegetation on woody plants are often expressed at the seedling stage (Facelli and Pickett 1991, Eliason and Allen 1997). Available safe sites for seedling establishment may have declined over time throughout the experimental field, as seen in the general increase in average plant size commensurate with a fall in the number of recruits censused. The general problem of safe site limitations appears to be a significant impediment to reclamation efforts (Urbanska 1997). Another threat may have been posed by the growing populations of small mammals observed on our site, notably *Microtus pennsylvanicus* (G. Robinson and S. Handel, unpublished data), and an influential role for seedling predation cannot be discounted.

In comparison to seed dispersal, clonal reproduction contributed much less to overall recruitment, and added little to the spatial spread of woody plants. Clonal growth might be a particularly effective dispersal method in land reclamation, because a disperser's survival is greatly enhanced by connections to a parent plant (Hutchings and Wijesinghe 1997). However, rates of clonal spread rarely match the potential of dispersed seeds, and low-density plantings like ours are not likely to quickly propagate a woodland.

The N-fixer treatments were apparently ineffective, at least for the period reported here. Studies of the potential for nitrogen-fixing plants in forest succession indicate that fertilizing effects may be gradual and incremental, important for establishing long-term nutrient pools (Morris et al. 1974, Skeffington and Bradshaw 1980, Boring and Swank 1984, Ashby et al. 1985), but less likely to show immediate measurable effects on adjacent vegetation (Fimbel 1992, Bradshaw 1997).

Perhaps more significant than declining rates of recruitment, woody plant species richness reached an early and shallow threshold. The background landscape was quite depauperate, as seen in the small number of native woody species added to the site. A few species have dominated, at least in the early stages, and the development of a more diverse woodland may require further intervention. In a more natural setting, a comparable inoculation technique ought to be more effective. A broader issue is the narrowing window of opportunity to draw on natural dispersal resources, as background natural populations continue to decline (Tilman et al. 1994, Hughes et al. 1997, Nee and May 1997). Our study shows that basic ecological processes can be directed to supply woody plant recruits even in a degraded urban setting. However, in such settings the ultimate structural and functional targets must be realistically defined (Clark 1997), with the expectation that long-distance dispersal events may be too infrequent to raise site diversity to levels associated with historic natural communities.

- **Fence as a potential confounder and that it had an effect:**  
  “*To reduce damage by browsing eastern cottontail rabbits (Sylvilagus floridanus), we constructed a wire fence surrounding each planted plot. Eight empty plots were laid out, four with fencing (which had the potential to serve as a perch for avian frugivores) and four without fencing.*”  
  “*A fence effect was consistently apparent, in that the proportional contribution of avian dispersal was significantly higher in fenced vs. unfenced control (unplanted) plots.*”  
  “*Extrapolating from densities in the unplanted plots, we estimate that of the 1029 avian-dispersed recruits within planted plots in 1995, 12.4% could be indirectly attributed to background seed rain and 34.6% to a fence effect.*”

- **Example of a main inferential analysis that does not show adjustment for fence or other confounders (planted vs unplanted):**  
  “*TABLE 2. Results of repeated-measures ANOVA comparing avian-dispersed recruitment inside planted (n = 16) and unplanted (n = 8) plots.*”

## 2) Reasoning (step-by-step, strictly from the paper)

1. The study acknowledges at least one important potential confounder: **fencing**, because fences “had the potential to serve as a perch for avian frugivores,” and the authors later report a “consistently apparent” **fence effect** on avian-dispersed recruitment.

2. The authors report that recruitment data were analyzed primarily using **“univariate tests of main treatment effects”** (e.g., planted vs. unplanted; small vs. large). Univariate tests, as described here, do not inherently indicate that confounders (like fencing, spatial gradients, proximity to sources, etc.) were included simultaneously in an adjusted model.

3. The key repeated-measures ANOVA shown (Table 2) is described as comparing **planted (n=16) vs unplanted (n=8)** plots. From the methods, unplanted plots include **both fenced and unfenced** controls (“four with fencing… and four without fencing”), but Table 2 does not indicate that fencing was included as a factor/covariate or that the comparison was restricted to only fenced controls. Therefore, from the text provided, it is **not explicit** that the planted vs. unplanted effect estimate was adjusted for the fence effect.

4. Although the authors **quantify** the likely magnitude of the fence effect by an extrapolation (“we estimate… 34.6%… to a fence effect”), this is presented as a separate calculation/interpretation rather than clearly as part of the primary inferential analysis estimating treatment effects with confounder adjustment.

5. The paper also notes that analyses of one designed factor (N-fixers) were dropped (“restrict analyses… to plant size effects”), but this is not the same as demonstrating that confounding was handled appropriately; it shows a change in which effects were analyzed, not an explicit confounder-adjusted analysis.

**Overall:** The paper demonstrates awareness of confounding (especially fencing) and runs separate tests/estimates related to it, but it does not explicitly describe an analysis approach where the main treatment effect is estimated **while adjusting for confounders** (e.g., multivariable model including fencing and/or spatial/source covariates). Therefore, whether confounders were appropriately taken into account in the effect analysis cannot be determined from the text.

Ecological Applications, 10(1), 2000, pp. 174-188 © 2000 by the Ecological Society of America

# DIRECTING SPATIAL PATTERNS OF RECRUITMENT DURING AN EXPERIMENTAL URBAN WOODLAND RECLAMATION

GEORGE R. ROBINSON¹,³ AND STEVEN N. HANDEL²

¹Department of Biological Sciences, State University of New York at Albany, Albany, New York 12222, USA
²Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Natural Resources, Rutgers University, One College Farm Road, New Brunswick, New Jersey 08901-1582 USA

Abstract. Studies of biological invasions indicate that natural recruitment of new species can occur as a “nucleation” phenomenon, in which scattered colonization foci spread and coalesce. Ecological reclamation of damaged lands might make use of this potential for enhanced natural dispersal, by inoculating sites with multiple small plantings to attract animal dispersers and other mutualists from nearby remnants of natural habitat. We conducted an experimental test of this proposition.

On a 6-ha section of an abandoned municipal landfill in the New Jersey Meadowlands, we installed 16 clusters of 21 trees and shrubs in an array of fenced plots. Clusters contained seven native species known to: (1) attract bird dispersers to introduce propagules from remnants of off-site habitat; (2) contribute propagules by virtue of high reproductive output and clonal growth; and (3) accelerate woodland succession on open, degraded habitats. Average plant size was varied, with half the plots receiving larger trees and shrubs, to test whether woody plant size would enhance any attractive function. An additional eight empty plots were studied to estimate background rates of recruitment and to test for a fencing effect. Site preparation included the addition of 90 cm of fresh substrate, including organic matter, and a cover crop of annual grasses. Recruitment of woody plants inside and surrounding the experimental plots was examined for five years, and results were compared on the basis of treatment and recruitment mode (avian, wind, or clonal dispersal).

Woody plant recruitment into experimental plots was rapid and substantial, primarily via dispersal from natural sources. Plots with larger plants attracted significantly more recruits at the outset, but this difference diminished over time. Fall seed rain samples yielded a mean estimate of 426 seeds/m² within plots. However, size distributions of recruiting woody species increasingly shifted toward larger individuals each year. Experimental manipulations that opened seed beds for woody plant recruitment had short-lived effects, indicating a narrow window of opportunity for establishment. Spread of the planted species themselves was generally weak, although clonal growth contributed substantially to spread on the margins of plots.

Most recruitment outside experimental plots was from external sources. A strong proximity component was found for bird-dispersed recruits, which were highly clustered near planted plots, with the highest densities near source populations on the site margin. Wind-dispersed trees and shrubs, by contrast, were not associated with planted plots and were concentrated near one corner of the site. Discounting plot interiors, total recruitment density for the site after 5 yr was ~800 woody stems/ha, 36% via avian dispersal, 10% via clonal spread, and the remainder via wind-borne propagules. New recruits represented 26 woody plant species, all but four from external sources, and only five common species contributed more than a few recruits. We conclude that techniques for manipulating natural seed dispersal hold promise for ecological restoration, provided that background populations are available to supply colonists.

Key words: clonal growth; dispersal; experimental reclamation; nucleation; safe sites; seed sources; spatial pattern; surrounding landscape.

# INTRODUCTION

## The ecological context of woodland restoration

Ecological restoration can be likened to accelerated succession, in part because it aims to pass over the early phases of community development, when recovery can be delayed by the effects of past degradation (Aber 1987, Allen 1988, Bradshaw 1989, Luken 1990, Parker 1997). Following severe habitat damage, the reclamation phase closely resembles primary succession, in which most organisms colonize from external source populations. Indeed, a common goal of ecological restoration is to initiate natural populations as dispersing immigrants (Bradshaw 1988, Harris et al. 1993,
