explained well by the abundance of mature plants at our plots. Cause and effect might possibly go both ways in these relationships, with areas of intense seed rain leading to large adult populations or areas with many adult plants causing high seed rain. Seed rain of R. cathartica was related to seedling density, suggesting that high seed rain might lead to high seedling densities. However, seed rain of R. cathartica was not related to sapling density. In a population of Olea europaea the spatial distributions of seedlings and mature plants differed, suggesting non-random post-dispersal survivorship (Rey and Alcantara 2000). Differences in distribution between seedlings and saplings of the invasive Prunus serotina in Belgium may have been related to differential response to light

(Godefroid et al. 2005). Similarly, we suggest that conditions promoting dispersal and germination of  $R$  cathartica, including proximity to shrubs, may increase mortality of seedlings and reduce likelihood of maturation.

Local density of adult plants, which are potential seed sources, did not affect propagule pressure of Lonicera. Mature  $(&gt;1\mathrm{m})$  L. morrowii were very common, found at 11 of our 12 plots. It may be that Lonicera fruits make up a significant portion of the diets of birds in our area, and dispersal is generally high in all habitats. Fruits of L. morrowii are sugary and may provide an important energetic resource for certain frugivores during the autumn and winter (Witmer and Van Soest 1998), as the fruits of the invasive L. tatarica do in other areas of North America (Drummond 2005).

Unlike many authors working in early-successional and disturbed systems (McDonnell and Stiles 1983; Holl 1998; Shiels and Walker 2003), we found that perch presence had a small effect on seed rain relative to large spatial variability for most species. The perches that we used were similar to the cross-bar type artificial perch used by Holl (1998), which was less effective than natural perches constructed of dead tree branches. However, McDonnell and Stiles (1983) found similar rates of seed deposition under natural and cross-bar type artificial perches. Our perches may have generally increased seed rain across the entire plot, thus being reflected in both traps with artificial perches and those without artificial perches. McDonnell and Stiles (1983) found that the introduction of perches generally elevated rates of dispersal in large areas surrounding the perch. Our traps without perches also may have attracted birds (Kollmann and Goetze 1998). Most investigators noting an increase in dispersal with artificial perches worked in areas with few natural perches (McDonnell and Stiles 1983; Holl 1998). It is noteworthy that our perches seem to have had a greater positive effect on seed capture in old fields than other habitats. Natural perches were more available at forested plots, potentially freeing birds from the use of artificial perches.

Our results did not document the identity of dispersal agents or the success of dispersal, including subsequent germination. Seeds of the invasive Lonicera maackii were not inhibited by passage by American robins but were inhibited by cedar waxwings (Bartuszevige and Gorchov 2006). There may

Springer

Plant Ecol (2009) 203:59-67

be important associations between identity and habitat use of dispersal agents and the survival of seeds of particular exotic plants in our landscape.

The remote location of our plots and large number of traps used in the study prevented us from frequent collection of seeds. The time between visits to traps may have allowed granivores to predate seeds, which would cause us to underestimate seed rain. Kollmann and Goetze (1998) summarized the strong evidence that seed predation can markedly influence seed-capture rates and that seed predation can vary among habitats. In our case, this may have exaggerated small seed-capture rates in maple-beech forests because mammalian granivores likely were most common in that habitat. In contrast, Stevenson and Vargas (2008) found seed predation rates lower in seed traps than at the nearby forest floor in tropical forests. Unfortunately we did not quantify rates of seed loss with labeled seeds. Time between visits also may have allowed fruits to degrade and mammal feces to disintegrate, especially during warm months. It is therefore possible that some of the seed deposition that we attribute to secondary seed rain by birds is primary seed rain or secondary seed rain by mammals.

The most common types of ornithochorous seeds dispersed to all ecosystems in central New York were of invasive, exotic plants. Seed rain of *E. umbellata*, *R. multiflora*, and *R. cathartica* reflected the local density of adult plants that might serve as sources of propagules. Managers aiming to control the spread of these species in our area might, therefore, consider selective removal of propagule sources (Gosper et al. 2005). The seed rain of *L. morrowii* was generally high regardless of the local density of seed sources. However, the abundance of mature *L. morrowii* was much greater in old fields and plantations than maple-beech forests, possibly reflecting greater post-dispersal mortality in mature forests. The control of *Lonicera* might therefore involve physical removal or management for mature, closed-canopy habitats, which are poorly invaded by members of this genus (Robertson et al. 1994; Hutchinson and Vankat 1997).

Plant Ecol (2009) 203:59-67

# Deposition of exotic bird-dispersed seeds into three habitats of a fragmented landscape in the northeastern United States

Timothy S. McCay · Deanna H. McCay · Jessica L. Czajka

Received: 15 May 2008/Accepted: 12 September 2008/Published online: 30 September 2008
© Springer Science+Business Media B.V. 2008

Abstract Dispersal by frugivorous birds facilitates invasion by many exotic plants. We measured the seed rain of ornithochorous native and exotic plants at three habitats of a fragmented landscape of the northeastern United States for 1 year. We studied maple-beech forests, old fields, and abandoned conifer plantations. Across all sites we collected 2,196 ornithochorous seeds, including seeds from six exotic species and 10 native species. The majority (90%) of collected seeds were from exotic species. Seed dispersal was broadly similar among habitats, though seed rain of exotic species was higher in old fields than forested habitats. Seed rain was not strongly influenced by artificial perches for most species. However, seeds of exotic species were more commonly found in traps under an artificial perch in old fields. Seed rains for the exotic Elaeagnus umbellata, Rhamnus cathartica, and Rosa multiflora were positively associated with local density of mature plants. Seed rain of R. cathartica was positively associated with abundance of seedlings but not saplings, suggesting that post-dispersal mortality was important. Seed dispersal of the exotic Lonicera spp. was

high in all habitats, accounting for 66% of all seeds collected. With the exception of Lonicera spp., seed rain of common exotic invaders was affected by the abundance of seed sources, and these species might be effectively controlled by elimination of local fruiting plants. Fruits of Lonicera morrowii, which has extensively invaded our area, are apparently a common component in the diet of frugivores.

Keywords Exotic species · Fragmented forest landscape · Invasion · Old fields · Plantations · Seed dispersal

# Introduction

Colonization of new sites by invasive plants depends on dispersal of propagules and successful germination, growth, and reproduction. Although suitability of microsites clearly is important, propagule pressure may be a factor of primary importance in certain plant invasions (Rouget and Richardson 2003; Lambrinos 2006; DiVittorio et al. 2007; Milton et al. 2007). Exotic plants that produce fleshy fruits and are dispersed by animal vectors likely exist in the absence of historical dispersal agents within their new range (but see Simberloff and Von Holle 1999; Richardson et al. 2000). However, frugivorous vertebrates typically have catholic diets, and coevolved dispersal systems are generally flexible (Wheelwright and Orians 1982; Herrera 1985; Jordano 1995; Witmer

1996; Renne et al. 2002). Aronson et al. (2007) found that woody exotic plants with fleshy fruits were more successful in increasing their distributions than other exotic and native plants in the New York metropolitan region, suggesting that frugivores are frequently unwitting accomplices in the expansion of invaders.

Northeastern North America is inhabited by a suite of bird-dispersed (ornithochorous) exotic shrubs, including members of Berberis, Elaeagnus, Lonicera, Rhamnus, and Rosa. White and Stiles (1992) found that about one-third of the plant species dispersed by frugivorous birds in central New Jersey were exotic. Lonicera maackii (Amur honeysuckle) is successfully dispersed by the American robin (Turdus migratorius), hermit thrush (Catharus guttatus), northern mockingbird (Mimus polyglottos), European starling (Sturnus vulgaris), and cedar waxwing (Bombycilla cedrorum) in Ohio (Bartuszevige and Gorchov 2006); the northern mockingbird is a dispersal agent for Rosa multiflora (multiflora rose; Stiles 1982); the American robin readily consumes fruits of the invasive Rhamnus frangula (glossy buckthorn; LaFleur et al. 2007); and cedar waxwings (Bombycilla cedrorum) have incorporated Berberis vulgaris and Rhamnus cathartica into their diet (Witmer 1996). Birds of eastern North America clearly illustrate the common flexibility within coevolved avian--plant dispersal systems. The European starling (Sturnus vulgaris) is an effective frugivore that has become naturalized and common in much of North America. It consumes the fruits of a variety of native and exotic plants, including some occurring within its native range, in North America (McIlhenny 1936; Lindsey 1939; Russell 1971).

Frugivorous birds are more likely to defecate or regurgitate seeds near perches (McDonnell and Stiles 1983; Holl 1998; Shiels and Walker 2003). This tendency makes certain microsites—such as under shrubs, fencerows, and power lines—more likely to receive bird-dispersed seeds (Glyphis et al. 1981; Dean and Milton 2000). Perch use by frugivorous birds affects the rate and spatial pattern of encroachment by woody plants into old fields (Yarranton and Morrison 1974; McDonnell and Stiles 1983) and may affect the invasibility of different ecosystems by ornithochorous exotic plants (Milton et al. 2007; Deckers et al. 2008).

The landscape of central New York State is typical of much of eastern North America, including second-growth forest interspersed with agricultural land, abandoned agricultural land (old fields), plantations of trees managed for timber, and abandoned plantations. Areas recovering from disturbance, including old fields and abandoned plantations, may be more susceptible to invasion by exotics than more mature ecosystems (Fox and Fox 1986; Huebner and Tobin 2006). We measured the rate at which seeds of fleshy-fruited plants entered old fields, abandoned conifer plantations, and second-growth maple-beech forests of central New York State by bird dispersal in the presence and absence of artificial perches. We also related seed rain to the abundance of common exotics in these habitats. This study was part of a larger effort to understand invasion by R. cathartica (European buckthorn) at these sites (T.S. McCay, unpubl. results). Thus, particular emphasis was placed on understanding the role of propagule pressure in facilitating invasion by this species.

## Methods

### Study area

Our study area was in Madison County, near the geometric center of New York State, on properties owned by Colgate University (47°39′N, 75°35′W). Twelve plots were established, with one plot in each of maple-beech forest, old field, and conifer plantation within each of four study areas: natural areas adjacent to the Colgate University campus (Campus), the Parker Farm natural area (Parker Farm), the southern end of the Bewkes Nature Preserve (Bewkes South), and the northern end of the Bewkes Nature Preserve (Bewkes North). Density of exotic species at these plots was typical of similar habitats in our landscape. Plots at northern hardwood forests and old fields were 30 × 50 m; plots at plantations were 30 × 30 m. Unmanageably large densities of R. cathartica, which were completely censused, precluded the use of 30 × 50-m plots in plantations.

Maple-beech forest stands were 60--120 years old based on increment cores of the largest individuals in the plots. Common overstory trees included Acer saccharum (sugar maple), Fagus grandifolia (American beech), and Fraxinus americanus (white ash). Herbaceous cover was sparse (18 ± 12% [SD]) and shrubs were uncommon in maple-beech forests. Plantations were 35--45 years old and had not been

thinned since aforestation. Plantations were Larix decidua (European larch; Bewkes South and Bewkes North) or a mix of Pinus resinosa (red pine) and Picea glauca (white spruce; Campus and Parker Farm). High mortality of overstory trees resulted in canopy-gap formation and higher herbaceous cover (57 ± 21%) than in maple-beech forests. Plantation abandonment is common in our area, and these plantation species are not regenerating within stands (Goldblum 1998). Shrubs, including L. morrowii and R. cathartica, were common in plantations (shrub density 0.08 ± 0.07 m^{-2}). Old fields were abandoned from cultivation or grazing 10--30 years ago based on age of woody vegetation. Old fields were dominated by grasses and other herbaceous plants (86 ± 11% herbaceous cover); however, L. morrowii, R. cathartica, F. americanus, and L. decidua were common woody colonizers (shrub density 0.05 ± 0.03 m^{-2}, tree density 0.03 ± 0.04 m^{-2}; species classified as shrubs and trees based on growth form).

### Sampling of seed rain

Ten 1-m^{2} seed traps were established at random locations within each site. Traps consisted of a wooden frame made of untreated hemlock and a bottom made of nylon screen supported by 0.6-cm mesh galvanized steel hardware cloth. Traps were elevated 25 cm from the ground with wooden stakes. One half of the traps at each plot (5) included a bird perch emerging from their center, modified from the “horizontal” design of McDonnell and Stiles (1983). Perches consisted of 3 × 3-cm pressure-treated pine, were 2 m tall, and were topped with a single 1-m horizontal cross bar.

Seeds were recovered from traps approximately every 2 months between June 2, 2003 and June 15, 2004. Seeds were identified using Martin and Barkley (1961), and Young and Young (1992). Only seeds of ornithochorous plants were considered in the current analysis. We only considered seeds that were free of intact fruits and that were likely dispersed by birds (secondary seed rain, Kollmann and Pirl 1995). Thus, we disregarded entire fruits that fell into traps. We also disregarded a single large deposit of seeds that resulted from raccoon (Procyon lotor) defecation. We did not attempt sub-generic identification of seeds from the genera Vitis, Lonicera, and Rubus because of similarity in seed morphology among congeneric species. The only species of Lonicera growing at our plots was L. morrowii. Plants were divided into exotic and native categories following Mitchell and Tucker (1997).

### Sampling of vegetation

Plots were systematically searched during the summers of 2001 (Parker Farm), 2002 (Campus and Bewkes South), and 2003 (Bewkes North). All individuals of R. cathartica were tallied and measured for basal diameter pursuant to other aims of the work at these plots. Buckthorn individuals were separated into seedling (≤5 mm basal diameter [BD]), sapling (0.5 < BD < 1.5 cm), and adult (≥1.5 cm BD) life history stages. The threshold separating adults and saplings was based on the observation that the smallest R. cathartica to reproduce were 1.5 cm BD. The threshold separating seedlings and saplings reflected what we perceived to be a natural break in the distribution of plant sizes. All other plants were tallied if they were >1 m tall.

### Analysis

Data were only considered for those species for which we recovered ≥3 total seeds over all plots. We compared numbers of seeds for exotic and native species among habitat types and between traps with perches and traps without perches using analysis of variance (ANOVA) after square root transformation ($\sqrt{\text{y + 0.5}}$). This transformation effectively normalizes variables that are expected to be distributed as a Poisson random variable and is common for count data (Sokal and Rohlf 1995). When differences among habitats were found, we evaluated specific contrasts using the Tukey method of multiple comparisons (T-method, Sokal and Rohlf 1995). Analyses were conducted using SPSS 14.0^{©}. We did not conduct hypothesis tests for individual species to avoid inflation of experiment-wide error rate (Sokal and Rohlf 1995; García 2004).

We related seed rain of our most common exotic taxa to the abundance of those taxa, and life-history stages for R. cathartica, using ranged major axis (RMA) regression. RMA regression is a type of model II regression appropriate when (1) both variables include random error variance, (2) variables are not in the same physical units, and (3) it can be reasonably assumed that the error variance is proportional to the

Plant Ecol (2009) 203:59-67

variance of the variable (Legendre and Legendre 1998). RMA regression is similar to standard major axis regression (Sokal and Rohlf 1995), except that RMA allows testing of the null hypothesis that the slope = 0. The data were inspected for outliers prior to analysis and log-transformed to meet statistical assumptions. These analyses were conducted using Model II, a program by Legendre (2001).

# Results

We collected and identified 2,196 seeds representing 10 native and six exotic taxa of ornithochorous

plants, along with Rubus, which might have included native or exotic species in our area (Table 1). We collected an additional 12,596 seeds of non-ornithochorous plants in the course of this study, primarily reflecting dominant wind-dispersed plants in each habitat (e.g., Acer saccharum in maple-beech forests). Thus, seeds of ornithochorous plants made up approximately 15% of the numerical seed rain measured at these plots.

More seeds of exotic plants were collected in old fields than the other habitats (FHabitat = 13.79, df = 2,18, P &lt; 0.01; Tukey Method P &lt; 0.05), and perches were positively associated with seed rain at old fields but not other habitats (FH×P = 3.56, df = 2,18, P = 0.05). These trends were strongly influenced by the most common exotic taxon, Lonicera spp., which accounted for 73% of exotic seeds. Seed rain of Lonicera spp. was markedly higher at old fields and was apparently influenced by perches in old fields but not other habitats. Seeds of Elaeagnus umbellata, Rhamnus cathartica, and Rosa multiflora also were markedly more common at old fields than in forested habitats. Seeds of B. thunbergii were more commonly collected in plantations than other habitats.

Annual seed rain of Elaeagnus and Rosa each were explained well by the abundance of those taxa at our plots (Elaeagnus: slope = 0.84, P &lt; 0.01; Rosa: slope = 0.89, P &lt; 0.01; Fig. 1). Seed rain of R. cathartica was positively related to the density of R. cathartica seedlings (slope = 0.70, P = 0.01) and adults (slope = 0.79, P = 0.03) but not saplings (P = 0.32) at our plots (Fig. 2). Seed rain of Lonicera was consistently high among all plots regardless of the density of large (&gt;1 m tall) L. morrowii (Fig. 1), which varied markedly among maple-beech forests (median = 7 ha⁻¹, range = [0, 13]), old fields (150 ha⁻¹, [53, 467]), and plantations (378 ha⁻¹, [189, 1767]). Lonicera morrowii was the most widespread exotic shrub at our plots, detected at 11 of our 12 plots.

# Discussion

Rejmanek (1996) identified effective vertebrate seed dispersal as a factor associated with invasion success by exotic seed plants. We found that several of the most common woody exotic invaders of our landscape are dispersed by local avian frugivores. Thirty-eight percent (6/16) of ornithochorous plant species recovered in our seed traps were exotic to our area. Similarly, White and Stiles (1992) found that one-third of ornithochorous species collected in seed traps in central New Jersey were exotic. A large fraction of seeds (90%) dispersed by birds in our area were from exotic plants, particularly Lonicera spp. White and Stiles (1992) estimated that fruits of exotic plants made up  $\leq 14\%$  of estimated fruit biomass consumed by birds in central New Jersey during 1977-1986.

We found greater seed rain, particularly for exotic plants, in old fields than in forests. This is likely due to the patterns of habitat use by birds. Seed rain of  $E$  umbellata,  $R$  cathartica, and  $R$  multiflora were

explained well by the abundance of mature plants at our plots. Cause and effect might possibly go both ways in these relationships, with areas of intense seed rain leading to large adult populations or areas with many adult plants causing high seed rain. Seed rain of R. cathartica was related to seedling density, suggesting that high seed rain might lead to high seedling densities. However, seed rain of R. cathartica was not related to sapling density. In a population of Olea europaea the spatial distributions of seedlings and mature plants differed, suggesting non-random post-dispersal survivorship (Rey and Alcantara 2000). Differences in distribution between seedlings and saplings of the invasive Prunus serotina in Belgium may have been related to differential response to light

(Godefroid et al. 2005). Similarly, we suggest that conditions promoting dispersal and germination of  $R$  cathartica, including proximity to shrubs, may increase mortality of seedlings and reduce likelihood of maturation.

Local density of adult plants, which are potential seed sources, did not affect propagule pressure of Lonicera. Mature  $(&gt;1\mathrm{m})$  L. morrowii were very common, found at 11 of our 12 plots. It may be that Lonicera fruits make up a significant portion of the diets of birds in our area, and dispersal is generally high in all habitats. Fruits of L. morrowii are sugary and may provide an important energetic resource for certain frugivores during the autumn and winter (Witmer and Van Soest 1998), as the fruits of the invasive L. tatarica do in other areas of North America (Drummond 2005).

Unlike many authors working in early-successional and disturbed systems (McDonnell and Stiles 1983; Holl 1998; Shiels and Walker 2003), we found that perch presence had a small effect on seed rain relative to large spatial variability for most species. The perches that we used were similar to the cross-bar type artificial perch used by Holl (1998), which was less effective than natural perches constructed of dead tree branches. However, McDonnell and Stiles (1983) found similar rates of seed deposition under natural and cross-bar type artificial perches. Our perches may have generally increased seed rain across the entire plot, thus being reflected in both traps with artificial perches and those without artificial perches. McDonnell and Stiles (1983) found that the introduction of perches generally elevated rates of dispersal in large areas surrounding the perch. Our traps without perches also may have attracted birds (Kollmann and Goetze 1998). Most investigators noting an increase in dispersal with artificial perches worked in areas with few natural perches (McDonnell and Stiles 1983; Holl 1998). It is noteworthy that our perches seem to have had a greater positive effect on seed capture in old fields than other habitats. Natural perches were more available at forested plots, potentially freeing birds from the use of artificial perches.

Our results did not document the identity of dispersal agents or the success of dispersal, including subsequent germination. Seeds of the invasive Lonicera maackii were not inhibited by passage by American robins but were inhibited by cedar waxwings (Bartuszevige and Gorchov 2006). There may

Springer

Plant Ecol (2009) 203:59-67

be important associations between identity and habitat use of dispersal agents and the survival of seeds of particular exotic plants in our landscape.

The remote location of our plots and large number of traps used in the study prevented us from frequent collection of seeds. The time between visits to traps may have allowed granivores to predate seeds, which would cause us to underestimate seed rain. Kollmann and Goetze (1998) summarized the strong evidence that seed predation can markedly influence seed-capture rates and that seed predation can vary among habitats. In our case, this may have exaggerated small seed-capture rates in maple-beech forests because mammalian granivores likely were most common in that habitat. In contrast, Stevenson and Vargas (2008) found seed predation rates lower in seed traps than at the nearby forest floor in tropical forests. Unfortunately we did not quantify rates of seed loss with labeled seeds. Time between visits also may have allowed fruits to degrade and mammal feces to disintegrate, especially during warm months. It is therefore possible that some of the seed deposition that we attribute to secondary seed rain by birds is primary seed rain or secondary seed rain by mammals.

The most common types of ornithochorous seeds dispersed to all ecosystems in central New York were of invasive, exotic plants. Seed rain of *E. umbellata*, *R. multiflora*, and *R. cathartica* reflected the local density of adult plants that might serve as sources of propagules. Managers aiming to control the spread of these species in our area might, therefore, consider selective removal of propagule sources (Gosper et al. 2005). The seed rain of *L. morrowii* was generally high regardless of the local density of seed sources. However, the abundance of mature *L. morrowii* was much greater in old fields and plantations than maple-beech forests, possibly reflecting greater post-dispersal mortality in mature forests. The control of *Lonicera* might therefore involve physical removal or management for mature, closed-canopy habitats, which are poorly invaded by members of this genus (Robertson et al. 1994; Hutchinson and Vankat 1997).

# Deposition of exotic bird-dispersed seeds into three habitats of a fragmented landscape in the northeastern United States

Timothy S. McCay · Deanna H. McCay · Jessica L. Czajka

Received: 15 May 2008/Accepted: 12 September 2008/Published online: 30 September 2008
© Springer Science+Business Media B.V. 2008

Abstract Dispersal by frugivorous birds facilitates invasion by many exotic plants. We measured the seed rain of ornithochorous native and exotic plants at three habitats of a fragmented landscape of the northeastern United States for 1 year. We studied maple-beech forests, old fields, and abandoned conifer plantations. Across all sites we collected 2,196 ornithochorous seeds, including seeds from six exotic species and 10 native species. The majority (90%) of collected seeds were from exotic species. Seed dispersal was broadly similar among habitats, though seed rain of exotic species was higher in old fields than forested habitats. Seed rain was not strongly influenced by artificial perches for most species. However, seeds of exotic species were more commonly found in traps under an artificial perch in old fields. Seed rains for the exotic Elaeagnus umbellata, Rhamnus cathartica, and Rosa multiflora were positively associated with local density of mature plants. Seed rain of R. cathartica was positively associated with abundance of seedlings but not saplings, suggesting that post-dispersal mortality was important. Seed dispersal of the exotic Lonicera spp. was

high in all habitats, accounting for 66% of all seeds collected. With the exception of Lonicera spp., seed rain of common exotic invaders was affected by the abundance of seed sources, and these species might be effectively controlled by elimination of local fruiting plants. Fruits of Lonicera morrowii, which has extensively invaded our area, are apparently a common component in the diet of frugivores.

Keywords Exotic species · Fragmented forest landscape · Invasion · Old fields · Plantations · Seed dispersal

# Introduction

Colonization of new sites by invasive plants depends on dispersal of propagules and successful germination, growth, and reproduction. Although suitability of microsites clearly is important, propagule pressure may be a factor of primary importance in certain plant invasions (Rouget and Richardson 2003; Lambrinos 2006; DiVittorio et al. 2007; Milton et al. 2007). Exotic plants that produce fleshy fruits and are dispersed by animal vectors likely exist in the absence of historical dispersal agents within their new range (but see Simberloff and Von Holle 1999; Richardson et al. 2000). However, frugivorous vertebrates typically have catholic diets, and coevolved dispersal systems are generally flexible (Wheelwright and Orians 1982; Herrera 1985; Jordano 1995; Witmer

1996; Renne et al. 2002). Aronson et al. (2007) found that woody exotic plants with fleshy fruits were more successful in increasing their distributions than other exotic and native plants in the New York metropolitan region, suggesting that frugivores are frequently unwitting accomplices in the expansion of invaders.

Northeastern North America is inhabited by a suite of bird-dispersed (ornithochorous) exotic shrubs, including members of Berberis, Elaeagnus, Lonicera, Rhamnus, and Rosa. White and Stiles (1992) found that about one-third of the plant species dispersed by frugivorous birds in central New Jersey were exotic. Lonicera maackii (Amur honeysuckle) is successfully dispersed by the American robin (Turdus migratorius), hermit thrush (Catharus guttatus), northern mockingbird (Mimus polyglottos), European starling (Sturnus vulgaris), and cedar waxwing (Bombycilla cedrorum) in Ohio (Bartuszevige and Gorchov 2006); the northern mockingbird is a dispersal agent for Rosa multiflora (multiflora rose; Stiles 1982); the American robin readily consumes fruits of the invasive Rhamnus frangula (glossy buckthorn; LaFleur et al. 2007); and cedar waxwings (Bombycilla cedrorum) have incorporated Berberis vulgaris and Rhamnus cathartica into their diet (Witmer 1996). Birds of eastern North America clearly illustrate the common flexibility within coevolved avian--plant dispersal systems. The European starling (Sturnus vulgaris) is an effective frugivore that has become naturalized and common in much of North America. It consumes the fruits of a variety of native and exotic plants, including some occurring within its native range, in North America (McIlhenny 1936; Lindsey 1939; Russell 1971).

Frugivorous birds are more likely to defecate or regurgitate seeds near perches (McDonnell and Stiles 1983; Holl 1998; Shiels and Walker 2003). This tendency makes certain microsites—such as under shrubs, fencerows, and power lines—more likely to receive bird-dispersed seeds (Glyphis et al. 1981; Dean and Milton 2000). Perch use by frugivorous birds affects the rate and spatial pattern of encroachment by woody plants into old fields (Yarranton and Morrison 1974; McDonnell and Stiles 1983) and may affect the invasibility of different ecosystems by ornithochorous exotic plants (Milton et al. 2007; Deckers et al. 2008).

The landscape of central New York State is typical of much of eastern North America, including second-growth forest interspersed with agricultural land, abandoned agricultural land (old fields), plantations of trees managed for timber, and abandoned plantations. Areas recovering from disturbance, including old fields and abandoned plantations, may be more susceptible to invasion by exotics than more mature ecosystems (Fox and Fox 1986; Huebner and Tobin 2006). We measured the rate at which seeds of fleshy-fruited plants entered old fields, abandoned conifer plantations, and second-growth maple-beech forests of central New York State by bird dispersal in the presence and absence of artificial perches. We also related seed rain to the abundance of common exotics in these habitats. This study was part of a larger effort to understand invasion by R. cathartica (European buckthorn) at these sites (T.S. McCay, unpubl. results). Thus, particular emphasis was placed on understanding the role of propagule pressure in facilitating invasion by this species.

## Methods

### Study area

Our study area was in Madison County, near the geometric center of New York State, on properties owned by Colgate University (47°39′N, 75°35′W). Twelve plots were established, with one plot in each of maple-beech forest, old field, and conifer plantation within each of four study areas: natural areas adjacent to the Colgate University campus (Campus), the Parker Farm natural area (Parker Farm), the southern end of the Bewkes Nature Preserve (Bewkes South), and the northern end of the Bewkes Nature Preserve (Bewkes North). Density of exotic species at these plots was typical of similar habitats in our landscape. Plots at northern hardwood forests and old fields were 30 × 50 m; plots at plantations were 30 × 30 m. Unmanageably large densities of R. cathartica, which were completely censused, precluded the use of 30 × 50-m plots in plantations.

Maple-beech forest stands were 60--120 years old based on increment cores of the largest individuals in the plots. Common overstory trees included Acer saccharum (sugar maple), Fagus grandifolia (American beech), and Fraxinus americanus (white ash). Herbaceous cover was sparse (18 ± 12% [SD]) and shrubs were uncommon in maple-beech forests. Plantations were 35--45 years old and had not been

thinned since aforestation. Plantations were Larix decidua (European larch; Bewkes South and Bewkes North) or a mix of Pinus resinosa (red pine) and Picea glauca (white spruce; Campus and Parker Farm). High mortality of overstory trees resulted in canopy-gap formation and higher herbaceous cover (57 ± 21%) than in maple-beech forests. Plantation abandonment is common in our area, and these plantation species are not regenerating within stands (Goldblum 1998). Shrubs, including L. morrowii and R. cathartica, were common in plantations (shrub density 0.08 ± 0.07 m^{-2}). Old fields were abandoned from cultivation or grazing 10--30 years ago based on age of woody vegetation. Old fields were dominated by grasses and other herbaceous plants (86 ± 11% herbaceous cover); however, L. morrowii, R. cathartica, F. americanus, and L. decidua were common woody colonizers (shrub density 0.05 ± 0.03 m^{-2}, tree density 0.03 ± 0.04 m^{-2}; species classified as shrubs and trees based on growth form).

### Sampling of seed rain

Ten 1-m^{2} seed traps were established at random locations within each site. Traps consisted of a wooden frame made of untreated hemlock and a bottom made of nylon screen supported by 0.6-cm mesh galvanized steel hardware cloth. Traps were elevated 25 cm from the ground with wooden stakes. One half of the traps at each plot (5) included a bird perch emerging from their center, modified from the “horizontal” design of McDonnell and Stiles (1983). Perches consisted of 3 × 3-cm pressure-treated pine, were 2 m tall, and were topped with a single 1-m horizontal cross bar.

Seeds were recovered from traps approximately every 2 months between June 2, 2003 and June 15, 2004. Seeds were identified using Martin and Barkley (1961), and Young and Young (1992). Only seeds of ornithochorous plants were considered in the current analysis. We only considered seeds that were free of intact fruits and that were likely dispersed by birds (secondary seed rain, Kollmann and Pirl 1995). Thus, we disregarded entire fruits that fell into traps. We also disregarded a single large deposit of seeds that resulted from raccoon (Procyon lotor) defecation. We did not attempt sub-generic identification of seeds from the genera Vitis, Lonicera, and Rubus because of similarity in seed morphology among congeneric species. The only species of Lonicera growing at our plots was L. morrowii. Plants were divided into exotic and native categories following Mitchell and Tucker (1997).

### Sampling of vegetation

Plots were systematically searched during the summers of 2001 (Parker Farm), 2002 (Campus and Bewkes South), and 2003 (Bewkes North). All individuals of R. cathartica were tallied and measured for basal diameter pursuant to other aims of the work at these plots. Buckthorn individuals were separated into seedling (≤5 mm basal diameter [BD]), sapling (0.5 < BD < 1.5 cm), and adult (≥1.5 cm BD) life history stages. The threshold separating adults and saplings was based on the observation that the smallest R. cathartica to reproduce were 1.5 cm BD. The threshold separating seedlings and saplings reflected what we perceived to be a natural break in the distribution of plant sizes. All other plants were tallied if they were >1 m tall.

### Analysis

Data were only considered for those species for which we recovered ≥3 total seeds over all plots. We compared numbers of seeds for exotic and native species among habitat types and between traps with perches and traps without perches using analysis of variance (ANOVA) after square root transformation ($\sqrt{\text{y + 0.5}}$). This transformation effectively normalizes variables that are expected to be distributed as a Poisson random variable and is common for count data (Sokal and Rohlf 1995). When differences among habitats were found, we evaluated specific contrasts using the Tukey method of multiple comparisons (T-method, Sokal and Rohlf 1995). Analyses were conducted using SPSS 14.0^{©}. We did not conduct hypothesis tests for individual species to avoid inflation of experiment-wide error rate (Sokal and Rohlf 1995; García 2004).

We related seed rain of our most common exotic taxa to the abundance of those taxa, and life-history stages for R. cathartica, using ranged major axis (RMA) regression. RMA regression is a type of model II regression appropriate when (1) both variables include random error variance, (2) variables are not in the same physical units, and (3) it can be reasonably assumed that the error variance is proportional to the

Plant Ecol (2009) 203:59-67

variance of the variable (Legendre and Legendre 1998). RMA regression is similar to standard major axis regression (Sokal and Rohlf 1995), except that RMA allows testing of the null hypothesis that the slope = 0. The data were inspected for outliers prior to analysis and log-transformed to meet statistical assumptions. These analyses were conducted using Model II, a program by Legendre (2001).

# Results

We collected and identified 2,196 seeds representing 10 native and six exotic taxa of ornithochorous

plants, along with Rubus, which might have included native or exotic species in our area (Table 1). We collected an additional 12,596 seeds of non-ornithochorous plants in the course of this study, primarily reflecting dominant wind-dispersed plants in each habitat (e.g., Acer saccharum in maple-beech forests). Thus, seeds of ornithochorous plants made up approximately 15% of the numerical seed rain measured at these plots.

More seeds of exotic plants were collected in old fields than the other habitats (FHabitat = 13.79, df = 2,18, P &lt; 0.01; Tukey Method P &lt; 0.05), and perches were positively associated with seed rain at old fields but not other habitats (FH×P = 3.56, df = 2,18, P = 0.05). These trends were strongly influenced by the most common exotic taxon, Lonicera spp., which accounted for 73% of exotic seeds. Seed rain of Lonicera spp. was markedly higher at old fields and was apparently influenced by perches in old fields but not other habitats. Seeds of Elaeagnus umbellata, Rhamnus cathartica, and Rosa multiflora also were markedly more common at old fields than in forested habitats. Seeds of B. thunbergii were more commonly collected in plantations than other habitats.

Annual seed rain of Elaeagnus and Rosa each were explained well by the abundance of those taxa at our plots (Elaeagnus: slope = 0.84, P &lt; 0.01; Rosa: slope = 0.89, P &lt; 0.01; Fig. 1). Seed rain of R. cathartica was positively related to the density of R. cathartica seedlings (slope = 0.70, P = 0.01) and adults (slope = 0.79, P = 0.03) but not saplings (P = 0.32) at our plots (Fig. 2). Seed rain of Lonicera was consistently high among all plots regardless of the density of large (&gt;1 m tall) L. morrowii (Fig. 1), which varied markedly among maple-beech forests (median = 7 ha⁻¹, range = [0, 13]), old fields (150 ha⁻¹, [53, 467]), and plantations (378 ha⁻¹, [189, 1767]). Lonicera morrowii was the most widespread exotic shrub at our plots, detected at 11 of our 12 plots.

# Discussion

Rejmanek (1996) identified effective vertebrate seed dispersal as a factor associated with invasion success by exotic seed plants. We found that several of the most common woody exotic invaders of our landscape are dispersed by local avian frugivores. Thirty-eight percent (6/16) of ornithochorous plant species recovered in our seed traps were exotic to our area. Similarly, White and Stiles (1992) found that one-third of ornithochorous species collected in seed traps in central New Jersey were exotic. A large fraction of seeds (90%) dispersed by birds in our area were from exotic plants, particularly Lonicera spp. White and Stiles (1992) estimated that fruits of exotic plants made up  $\leq 14\%$  of estimated fruit biomass consumed by birds in central New Jersey during 1977-1986.

We found greater seed rain, particularly for exotic plants, in old fields than in forests. This is likely due to the patterns of habitat use by birds. Seed rain of  $E$  umbellata,  $R$  cathartica, and  $R$  multiflora were

explained well by the abundance of mature plants at our plots. Cause and effect might possibly go both ways in these relationships, with areas of intense seed rain leading to large adult populations or areas with many adult plants causing high seed rain. Seed rain of R. cathartica was related to seedling density, suggesting that high seed rain might lead to high seedling densities. However, seed rain of R. cathartica was not related to sapling density. In a population of Olea europaea the spatial distributions of seedlings and mature plants differed, suggesting non-random post-dispersal survivorship (Rey and Alcantara 2000). Differences in distribution between seedlings and saplings of the invasive Prunus serotina in Belgium may have been related to differential response to light

(Godefroid et al. 2005). Similarly, we suggest that conditions promoting dispersal and germination of  $R$  cathartica, including proximity to shrubs, may increase mortality of seedlings and reduce likelihood of maturation.

Local density of adult plants, which are potential seed sources, did not affect propagule pressure of Lonicera. Mature  $(&gt;1\mathrm{m})$  L. morrowii were very common, found at 11 of our 12 plots. It may be that Lonicera fruits make up a significant portion of the diets of birds in our area, and dispersal is generally high in all habitats. Fruits of L. morrowii are sugary and may provide an important energetic resource for certain frugivores during the autumn and winter (Witmer and Van Soest 1998), as the fruits of the invasive L. tatarica do in other areas of North America (Drummond 2005).

Unlike many authors working in early-successional and disturbed systems (McDonnell and Stiles 1983; Holl 1998; Shiels and Walker 2003), we found that perch presence had a small effect on seed rain relative to large spatial variability for most species. The perches that we used were similar to the cross-bar type artificial perch used by Holl (1998), which was less effective than natural perches constructed of dead tree branches. However, McDonnell and Stiles (1983) found similar rates of seed deposition under natural and cross-bar type artificial perches. Our perches may have generally increased seed rain across the entire plot, thus being reflected in both traps with artificial perches and those without artificial perches. McDonnell and Stiles (1983) found that the introduction of perches generally elevated rates of dispersal in large areas surrounding the perch. Our traps without perches also may have attracted birds (Kollmann and Goetze 1998). Most investigators noting an increase in dispersal with artificial perches worked in areas with few natural perches (McDonnell and Stiles 1983; Holl 1998). It is noteworthy that our perches seem to have had a greater positive effect on seed capture in old fields than other habitats. Natural perches were more available at forested plots, potentially freeing birds from the use of artificial perches.

Our results did not document the identity of dispersal agents or the success of dispersal, including subsequent germination. Seeds of the invasive Lonicera maackii were not inhibited by passage by American robins but were inhibited by cedar waxwings (Bartuszevige and Gorchov 2006). There may

Springer

Plant Ecol (2009) 203:59-67

be important associations between identity and habitat use of dispersal agents and the survival of seeds of particular exotic plants in our landscape.

The remote location of our plots and large number of traps used in the study prevented us from frequent collection of seeds. The time between visits to traps may have allowed granivores to predate seeds, which would cause us to underestimate seed rain. Kollmann and Goetze (1998) summarized the strong evidence that seed predation can markedly influence seed-capture rates and that seed predation can vary among habitats. In our case, this may have exaggerated small seed-capture rates in maple-beech forests because mammalian granivores likely were most common in that habitat. In contrast, Stevenson and Vargas (2008) found seed predation rates lower in seed traps than at the nearby forest floor in tropical forests. Unfortunately we did not quantify rates of seed loss with labeled seeds. Time between visits also may have allowed fruits to degrade and mammal feces to disintegrate, especially during warm months. It is therefore possible that some of the seed deposition that we attribute to secondary seed rain by birds is primary seed rain or secondary seed rain by mammals.

The most common types of ornithochorous seeds dispersed to all ecosystems in central New York were of invasive, exotic plants. Seed rain of *E. umbellata*, *R. multiflora*, and *R. cathartica* reflected the local density of adult plants that might serve as sources of propagules. Managers aiming to control the spread of these species in our area might, therefore, consider selective removal of propagule sources (Gosper et al. 2005). The seed rain of *L. morrowii* was generally high regardless of the local density of seed sources. However, the abundance of mature *L. morrowii* was much greater in old fields and plantations than maple-beech forests, possibly reflecting greater post-dispersal mortality in mature forests. The control of *Lonicera* might therefore involve physical removal or management for mature, closed-canopy habitats, which are poorly invaded by members of this genus (Robertson et al. 1994; Hutchinson and Vankat 1997).

Plant Ecol (2009) 203:59-67
DOI 10.1007/s11258-008-9509-8

# Deposition of exotic bird-dispersed seeds into three habitats of a fragmented landscape in the northeastern United States

Timothy S. McCay · Deanna H. McCay · Jessica L. Czajka

Received: 15 May 2008/Accepted: 12 September 2008/Published online: 30 September 2008
© Springer Science+Business Media B.V. 2008

Abstract Dispersal by frugivorous birds facilitates invasion by many exotic plants. We measured the seed rain of ornithochorous native and exotic plants at three habitats of a fragmented landscape of the northeastern United States for 1 year. We studied maple-beech forests, old fields, and abandoned conifer plantations. Across all sites we collected 2,196 ornithochorous seeds, including seeds from six exotic species and 10 native species. The majority (90%) of collected seeds were from exotic species. Seed dispersal was broadly similar among habitats, though seed rain of exotic species was higher in old fields than forested habitats. Seed rain was not strongly influenced by artificial perches for most species. However, seeds of exotic species were more commonly found in traps under an artificial perch in old fields. Seed rains for the exotic Elaeagnus umbellata, Rhamnus cathartica, and Rosa multiflora were positively associated with local density of mature plants. Seed rain of R. cathartica was positively associated with abundance of seedlings but not saplings, suggesting that post-dispersal mortality was important. Seed dispersal of the exotic Lonicera spp. was

high in all habitats, accounting for 66% of all seeds collected. With the exception of Lonicera spp., seed rain of common exotic invaders was affected by the abundance of seed sources, and these species might be effectively controlled by elimination of local fruiting plants. Fruits of Lonicera morrowii, which has extensively invaded our area, are apparently a common component in the diet of frugivores.

Keywords Exotic species · Fragmented forest landscape · Invasion · Old fields · Plantations · Seed dispersal

# Introduction

Colonization of new sites by invasive plants depends on dispersal of propagules and successful germination, growth, and reproduction. Although suitability of microsites clearly is important, propagule pressure may be a factor of primary importance in certain plant invasions (Rouget and Richardson 2003; Lambrinos 2006; DiVittorio et al. 2007; Milton et al. 2007). Exotic plants that produce fleshy fruits and are dispersed by animal vectors likely exist in the absence of historical dispersal agents within their new range (but see Simberloff and Von Holle 1999; Richardson et al. 2000). However, frugivorous vertebrates typically have catholic diets, and coevolved dispersal systems are generally flexible (Wheelwright and Orians 1982; Herrera 1985; Jordano 1995; Witmer

T. S. McCay (✉) · J. L. Czajka
Department of Biology, Colgate University, Hamilton, NY 13346, USA
e-mail: tmccay@mail.colgate.edu

D. H. McCay
Department of Geography, Colgate University, Hamilton, NY 13346, USA

Springer

1996; Renne et al. 2002). Aronson et al. (2007) found that woody exotic plants with fleshy fruits were more successful in increasing their distributions than other exotic and native plants in the New York metropolitan region, suggesting that frugivores are frequently unwitting accomplices in the expansion of invaders.

Northeastern North America is inhabited by a suite of bird-dispersed (ornithochorous) exotic shrubs, including members of Berberis, Elaeagnus, Lonicera, Rhamnus, and Rosa. White and Stiles (1992) found that about one-third of the plant species dispersed by frugivorous birds in central New Jersey were exotic. Lonicera maackii (Amur honeysuckle) is successfully dispersed by the American robin (Turdus migratorius), hermit thrush (Catharus guttatus), northern mockingbird (Mimus polyglottos), European starling (Sturnus vulgaris), and cedar waxwing (Bombycilla cedrorum) in Ohio (Bartuszevige and Gorchov 2006); the northern mockingbird is a dispersal agent for Rosa multiflora (multiflora rose; Stiles 1982); the American robin readily consumes fruits of the invasive Rhamnus frangula (glossy buckthorn; LaFleur et al. 2007); and cedar waxwings (Bombycilla cedrorum) have incorporated Berberis vulgaris and Rhamnus cathartica into their diet (Witmer 1996). Birds of eastern North America clearly illustrate the common flexibility within coevolved avian--plant dispersal systems. The European starling (Sturnus vulgaris) is an effective frugivore that has become naturalized and common in much of North America. It consumes the fruits of a variety of native and exotic plants, including some occurring within its native range, in North America (McIlhenny 1936; Lindsey 1939; Russell 1971).

Frugivorous birds are more likely to defecate or regurgitate seeds near perches (McDonnell and Stiles 1983; Holl 1998; Shiels and Walker 2003). This tendency makes certain microsites—such as under shrubs, fencerows, and power lines—more likely to receive bird-dispersed seeds (Glyphis et al. 1981; Dean and Milton 2000). Perch use by frugivorous birds affects the rate and spatial pattern of encroachment by woody plants into old fields (Yarranton and Morrison 1974; McDonnell and Stiles 1983) and may affect the invasibility of different ecosystems by ornithochorous exotic plants (Milton et al. 2007; Deckers et al. 2008).

The landscape of central New York State is typical of much of eastern North America, including second-growth forest interspersed with agricultural land, abandoned agricultural land (old fields), plantations of trees managed for timber, and abandoned plantations. Areas recovering from disturbance, including old fields and abandoned plantations, may be more susceptible to invasion by exotics than more mature ecosystems (Fox and Fox 1986; Huebner and Tobin 2006). We measured the rate at which seeds of fleshy-fruited plants entered old fields, abandoned conifer plantations, and second-growth maple-beech forests of central New York State by bird dispersal in the presence and absence of artificial perches. We also related seed rain to the abundance of common exotics in these habitats. This study was part of a larger effort to understand invasion by R. cathartica (European buckthorn) at these sites (T.S. McCay, unpubl. results). Thus, particular emphasis was placed on understanding the role of propagule pressure in facilitating invasion by this species.

## Methods

### Study area

Our study area was in Madison County, near the geometric center of New York State, on properties owned by Colgate University (47°39′N, 75°35′W). Twelve plots were established, with one plot in each of maple-beech forest, old field, and conifer plantation within each of four study areas: natural areas adjacent to the Colgate University campus (Campus), the Parker Farm natural area (Parker Farm), the southern end of the Bewkes Nature Preserve (Bewkes South), and the northern end of the Bewkes Nature Preserve (Bewkes North). Density of exotic species at these plots was typical of similar habitats in our landscape. Plots at northern hardwood forests and old fields were 30 × 50 m; plots at plantations were 30 × 30 m. Unmanageably large densities of R. cathartica, which were completely censused, precluded the use of 30 × 50-m plots in plantations.

Maple-beech forest stands were 60--120 years old based on increment cores of the largest individuals in the plots. Common overstory trees included Acer saccharum (sugar maple), Fagus grandifolia (American beech), and Fraxinus americanus (white ash). Herbaceous cover was sparse (18 ± 12% [SD]) and shrubs were uncommon in maple-beech forests. Plantations were 35--45 years old and had not been

thinned since aforestation. Plantations were Larix decidua (European larch; Bewkes South and Bewkes North) or a mix of Pinus resinosa (red pine) and Picea glauca (white spruce; Campus and Parker Farm). High mortality of overstory trees resulted in canopy-gap formation and higher herbaceous cover (57 ± 21%) than in maple-beech forests. Plantation abandonment is common in our area, and these plantation species are not regenerating within stands (Goldblum 1998). Shrubs, including L. morrowii and R. cathartica, were common in plantations (shrub density 0.08 ± 0.07 m^{-2}). Old fields were abandoned from cultivation or grazing 10--30 years ago based on age of woody vegetation. Old fields were dominated by grasses and other herbaceous plants (86 ± 11% herbaceous cover); however, L. morrowii, R. cathartica, F. americanus, and L. decidua were common woody colonizers (shrub density 0.05 ± 0.03 m^{-2}, tree density 0.03 ± 0.04 m^{-2}; species classified as shrubs and trees based on growth form).

### Sampling of seed rain

Ten 1-m^{2} seed traps were established at random locations within each site. Traps consisted of a wooden frame made of untreated hemlock and a bottom made of nylon screen supported by 0.6-cm mesh galvanized steel hardware cloth. Traps were elevated 25 cm from the ground with wooden stakes. One half of the traps at each plot (5) included a bird perch emerging from their center, modified from the “horizontal” design of McDonnell and Stiles (1983). Perches consisted of 3 × 3-cm pressure-treated pine, were 2 m tall, and were topped with a single 1-m horizontal cross bar.

Seeds were recovered from traps approximately every 2 months between June 2, 2003 and June 15, 2004. Seeds were identified using Martin and Barkley (1961), and Young and Young (1992). Only seeds of ornithochorous plants were considered in the current analysis. We only considered seeds that were free of intact fruits and that were likely dispersed by birds (secondary seed rain, Kollmann and Pirl 1995). Thus, we disregarded entire fruits that fell into traps. We also disregarded a single large deposit of seeds that resulted from raccoon (Procyon lotor) defecation. We did not attempt sub-generic identification of seeds from the genera Vitis, Lonicera, and Rubus because of similarity in seed morphology among congeneric species. The only species of Lonicera growing at our plots was L. morrowii. Plants were divided into exotic and native categories following Mitchell and Tucker (1997).

### Sampling of vegetation

Plots were systematically searched during the summers of 2001 (Parker Farm), 2002 (Campus and Bewkes South), and 2003 (Bewkes North). All individuals of R. cathartica were tallied and measured for basal diameter pursuant to other aims of the work at these plots. Buckthorn individuals were separated into seedling (≤5 mm basal diameter [BD]), sapling (0.5 < BD < 1.5 cm), and adult (≥1.5 cm BD) life history stages. The threshold separating adults and saplings was based on the observation that the smallest R. cathartica to reproduce were 1.5 cm BD. The threshold separating seedlings and saplings reflected what we perceived to be a natural break in the distribution of plant sizes. All other plants were tallied if they were >1 m tall.

### Analysis

Data were only considered for those species for which we recovered ≥3 total seeds over all plots. We compared numbers of seeds for exotic and native species among habitat types and between traps with perches and traps without perches using analysis of variance (ANOVA) after square root transformation ($\sqrt{\text{y + 0.5}}$). This transformation effectively normalizes variables that are expected to be distributed as a Poisson random variable and is common for count data (Sokal and Rohlf 1995). When differences among habitats were found, we evaluated specific contrasts using the Tukey method of multiple comparisons (T-method, Sokal and Rohlf 1995). Analyses were conducted using SPSS 14.0^{©}. We did not conduct hypothesis tests for individual species to avoid inflation of experiment-wide error rate (Sokal and Rohlf 1995; García 2004).

We related seed rain of our most common exotic taxa to the abundance of those taxa, and life-history stages for R. cathartica, using ranged major axis (RMA) regression. RMA regression is a type of model II regression appropriate when (1) both variables include random error variance, (2) variables are not in the same physical units, and (3) it can be reasonably assumed that the error variance is proportional to the

Plant Ecol (2009) 203:59-67

variance of the variable (Legendre and Legendre 1998). RMA regression is similar to standard major axis regression (Sokal and Rohlf 1995), except that RMA allows testing of the null hypothesis that the slope = 0. The data were inspected for outliers prior to analysis and log-transformed to meet statistical assumptions. These analyses were conducted using Model II, a program by Legendre (2001).

# Results

We collected and identified 2,196 seeds representing 10 native and six exotic taxa of ornithochorous

plants, along with Rubus, which might have included native or exotic species in our area (Table 1). We collected an additional 12,596 seeds of non-ornithochorous plants in the course of this study, primarily reflecting dominant wind-dispersed plants in each habitat (e.g., Acer saccharum in maple-beech forests). Thus, seeds of ornithochorous plants made up approximately 15% of the numerical seed rain measured at these plots.

Collection totals of all native seeds combined did not differ among habitats or between traps with perches and those without perches (P &gt; 0.05, Table 1). Sambucus racemosa was collected at all four plantation plots but no maple-beech or old field

More seeds of exotic plants were collected in old fields than the other habitats (FHabitat = 13.79, df = 2,18, P &lt; 0.01; Tukey Method P &lt; 0.05), and perches were positively associated with seed rain at old fields but not other habitats (FH×P = 3.56, df = 2,18, P = 0.05). Seed rain of Lonicera spp. was markedly higher at old fields and was apparently influenced by perches in old fields but not other habitats. Seeds of Elaeagnus umbellata, Rhamnus cathartica, and Rosa multiflora also were markedly more common at old fields than in forested habitats. Seeds of B. thunbergii were more commonly collected in plantations than other habitats.

Seed rain of Lonicera was consistently high among all plots regardless of the density of large (&gt;1 m tall) L. morrowii (Fig. 1), which varied markedly among maple-beech forests (median = 7 ha⁻¹, range = [0, 13]), old fields (150 ha⁻¹, [53, 467]), and plantations (378 ha⁻¹, [189, 1767]). Lonicera morrowii was the most widespread exotic shrub at our plots, detected at 11 of our 12 plots.

Total seed captures also were affected by habitat ( $F_{\text{Habitat}} = 10.20$ , df = 2,36,  $P &lt; 0.01$ ), with more seeds collected at old fields than other habitats (Tukey Method,  $P &lt; 0.05$ ). The interaction between origin and habitat was significant ( $F_{\text{O} \times \text{H}} = 15.41$ , df = 2,36,  $P &lt; 0.01$ ), with relatively more exotic seeds collected in old fields than other habitats (Fig. 3). Finally, artificial perches influenced total seed capture positively in old fields but negligibly in other habitats ( $F_{\text{P} \times \text{H}} = 4.08$ , df = 2,36,  $P = 0.03$ ; Fig. 4). These trends were all strongly influenced by seed rain of Lonicera spp., which accounted for  $66\%$  of total seeds.

# Discussion

Rejmanek (1996) identified effective vertebrate seed dispersal as a factor associated with invasion success by exotic seed plants. We found that several of the most common woody exotic invaders of our landscape are dispersed by local avian frugivores. Thirty-eight percent (6/16) of ornithochorous plant species recovered in our seed traps were exotic to our area. Similarly, White and Stiles (1992) found that one-third of ornithochorous species collected in seed traps in central New Jersey were exotic. A large fraction of seeds (90%) dispersed by birds in our area were from exotic plants, particularly Lonicera spp. White and Stiles (1992) estimated that fruits of exotic plants made up  $\leq 14\%$  of estimated fruit biomass consumed by birds in central New Jersey during 1977-1986.

We found greater seed rain, particularly for exotic plants, in old fields than in forests. This is likely due to the patterns of habitat use by birds. Seed rain of  $E$  umbellata,  $R$  cathartica, and  $R$  multiflora were

explained well by the abundance of mature plants at our plots. Cause and effect might possibly go both ways in these relationships, with areas of intense seed rain leading to large adult populations or areas with many adult plants causing high seed rain. Seed rain of R. cathartica was related to seedling density, suggesting that high seed rain might lead to high seedling densities. However, seed rain of R. cathartica was not related to sapling density. In a population of Olea europaea the spatial distributions of seedlings and mature plants differed, suggesting non-random post-dispersal survivorship (Rey and Alcantara 2000). Differences in distribution between seedlings and saplings of the invasive Prunus serotina in Belgium may have been related to differential response to light

(Godefroid et al. 2005). Similarly, we suggest that conditions promoting dispersal and germination of  $R$  cathartica, including proximity to shrubs, may increase mortality of seedlings and reduce likelihood of maturation.

Local density of adult plants, which are potential seed sources, did not affect propagule pressure of Lonicera. Mature  $(&gt;1\mathrm{m})$  L. morrowii were very common, found at 11 of our 12 plots. It may be that Lonicera fruits make up a significant portion of the diets of birds in our area, and dispersal is generally high in all habitats. Fruits of L. morrowii are sugary and may provide an important energetic resource for certain frugivores during the autumn and winter (Witmer and Van Soest 1998), as the fruits of the invasive L. tatarica do in other areas of North America (Drummond 2005).

Unlike many authors working in early-successional and disturbed systems (McDonnell and Stiles 1983; Holl 1998; Shiels and Walker 2003), we found that perch presence had a small effect on seed rain relative to large spatial variability for most species. The perches that we used were similar to the cross-bar type artificial perch used by Holl (1998), which was less effective than natural perches constructed of dead tree branches. However, McDonnell and Stiles (1983) found similar rates of seed deposition under natural and cross-bar type artificial perches. Our perches may have generally increased seed rain across the entire plot, thus being reflected in both traps with artificial perches and those without artificial perches. McDonnell and Stiles (1983) found that the introduction of perches generally elevated rates of dispersal in large areas surrounding the perch. Our traps without perches also may have attracted birds (Kollmann and Goetze 1998). Most investigators noting an increase in dispersal with artificial perches worked in areas with few natural perches (McDonnell and Stiles 1983; Holl 1998). It is noteworthy that our perches seem to have had a greater positive effect on seed capture in old fields than other habitats. Natural perches were more available at forested plots, potentially freeing birds from the use of artificial perches.

Our results did not document the identity of dispersal agents or the success of dispersal, including subsequent germination. Seeds of the invasive Lonicera maackii were not inhibited by passage by American robins but were inhibited by cedar waxwings (Bartuszevige and Gorchov 2006). There may

Springer

Plant Ecol (2009) 203:59-67

be important associations between identity and habitat use of dispersal agents and the survival of seeds of particular exotic plants in our landscape.

The remote location of our plots and large number of traps used in the study prevented us from frequent collection of seeds. The time between visits to traps may have allowed granivores to predate seeds, which would cause us to underestimate seed rain. Kollmann and Goetze (1998) summarized the strong evidence that seed predation can markedly influence seed-capture rates and that seed predation can vary among habitats. In our case, this may have exaggerated small seed-capture rates in maple-beech forests because mammalian granivores likely were most common in that habitat. In contrast, Stevenson and Vargas (2008) found seed predation rates lower in seed traps than at the nearby forest floor in tropical forests. Unfortunately we did not quantify rates of seed loss with labeled seeds. Time between visits also may have allowed fruits to degrade and mammal feces to disintegrate, especially during warm months. It is therefore possible that some of the seed deposition that we attribute to secondary seed rain by birds is primary seed rain or secondary seed rain by mammals.

The most common types of ornithochorous seeds dispersed to all ecosystems in central New York were of invasive, exotic plants. Seed rain of *E. umbellata*, *R. multiflora*, and *R. cathartica* reflected the local density of adult plants that might serve as sources of propagules. Managers aiming to control the spread of these species in our area might, therefore, consider selective removal of propagule sources (Gosper et al. 2005). The seed rain of *L. morrowii* was generally high regardless of the local density of seed sources. However, the abundance of mature *L. morrowii* was much greater in old fields and plantations than maple-beech forests, possibly reflecting greater post-dispersal mortality in mature forests. The control of *Lonicera* might therefore involve physical removal or management for mature, closed-canopy habitats, which are poorly invaded by members of this genus (Robertson et al. 1994; Hutchinson and Vankat 1997).

# Deposition of exotic bird-dispersed seeds into three habitats of a fragmented landscape in the northeastern United States

Timothy S. McCay · Deanna H. McCay · Jessica L. Czajka

Received: 15 May 2008/Accepted: 12 September 2008/Published online: 30 September 2008
© Springer Science+Business Media B.V. 2008

Abstract Dispersal by frugivorous birds facilitates invasion by many exotic plants. We measured the seed rain of ornithochorous native and exotic plants at three habitats of a fragmented landscape of the northeastern United States for 1 year. We studied maple-beech forests, old fields, and abandoned conifer plantations. Across all sites we collected 2,196 ornithochorous seeds, including seeds from six exotic species and 10 native species. The majority (90%) of collected seeds were from exotic species. Seed dispersal was broadly similar among habitats, though seed rain of exotic species was higher in old fields than forested habitats. Seed rain was not strongly influenced by artificial perches for most species. However, seeds of exotic species were more commonly found in traps under an artificial perch in old fields. Seed rains for the exotic Elaeagnus umbellata, Rhamnus cathartica, and Rosa multiflora were positively associated with local density of mature plants. Seed rain of R. cathartica was positively associated with abundance of seedlings but not saplings, suggesting that post-dispersal mortality was important. Seed dispersal of the exotic Lonicera spp. was

high in all habitats, accounting for 66% of all seeds collected. With the exception of Lonicera spp., seed rain of common exotic invaders was affected by the abundance of seed sources, and these species might be effectively controlled by elimination of local fruiting plants. Fruits of Lonicera morrowii, which has extensively invaded our area, are apparently a common component in the diet of frugivores.

Keywords Exotic species · Fragmented forest landscape · Invasion · Old fields · Plantations · Seed dispersal

# Introduction

Colonization of new sites by invasive plants depends on dispersal of propagules and successful germination, growth, and reproduction. Although suitability of microsites clearly is important, propagule pressure may be a factor of primary importance in certain plant invasions (Rouget and Richardson 2003; Lambrinos 2006; DiVittorio et al. 2007; Milton et al. 2007). Exotic plants that produce fleshy fruits and are dispersed by animal vectors likely exist in the absence of historical dispersal agents within their new range (but see Simberloff and Von Holle 1999; Richardson et al. 2000). However, frugivorous vertebrates typically have catholic diets, and coevolved dispersal systems are generally flexible (Wheelwright and Orians 1982; Herrera 1985; Jordano 1995; Witmer
